#3490. Jennifer Connelly's Forgotten '90s Disney Superhero Movie Deserved Its Own Franchise

After Tim Burton's "Batman" film became an inescapably huge success in the summer of 1989 and set off to expand into its weirdly experimental sequel in 1992, there was a mad rush by other studios to hop a trend and get their own piece of that lucrative superhero pie — sort of. Studio executives of the early '90s seem to have been drawn more to Burton's retro aesthetics than the actual idea of a superhero, so rather than expanding into bringing other iconic DC characters like Wonder Woman to the big screen, or heading across the street to give the Marvel universe a shot at cinematic glory, we got a rush of big-screen revivals of other throwback comic strip heroes. The results were, well, let's just put it nicely and say they were pretty mixed in terms of quality.

While they undoubtedly have their fans out there, pulp hero movies like 1990's "Dick Tracy," 1994's "The Shadow," and 1996's "The Phantom" simply were not able to reach the same levels of success. It may have been that audiences just liked Batman way more than they liked characters who had never been as popular as the Caped Crusader, or that these movies just weren't very good. Maybe people were just simply not prepared to slam evil. Whatever it was, none of those movies managed to launch their heroes into a franchise.

There is, however, one member of that crowd that absolutely deserved better: 1991's "The Rocketeer," in which Jennifer Connelly, Billy Campbell, and a rocket-powered jetpack faced off against Nazis in Los Angeles circa 1938.

One big difference that set "The Rocketeer" apart from the surrounding crop of pulp hero flicks was that its source material was actually pretty contemporary. Cliff Secord and his supporting cast were created in 1982 by the legendary comics creator Dave Stevens, and had been an indie favorite since its introduction. All things considered, Stevens produced a relatively small number of comics about the Rocketeer — his entire run with the character fits into a single 120-page hardcover — but his lavish, gorgeous art and incredible storytelling make it a timeless classic even today. Sadly, Stevens passed away in 2008 after a long battle with leukemia, which had long affected his output.

Looking back, it's easy to see why Disney jumped on "The Rocketeer." Since it was a throwback to the adventure serials and comic strip heroes of the '30s and '40s, Stevens' work already had the modern spin on the kind of pulpy action that movies like "Dick Tracy" and "The Shadow" struggled with, and incorporated a lot of the same elements. In fact, the "Rocketeer" comics even included thinly veiled versions of pulp heroes like The Shadow and Doc Savage in supporting roles, with just enough of their serial numbers filed off to avoid a copyright lawsuit. (Needless to say, those characters didn't make it into the film version.)

There were real-life influences, too; in the film, the jetpack was created by Howard Hughes, and Timothy Dalton's villainous Neville Sinclair was based on actor (and real-life villain) Errol Flynn. Connelly's character, appropriately renamed Jenny, was based on Cliff's comics girlfriend Betty, who was in turn inspired by pin-up icon Bettie Page, of whom Stevens was a dedicated and unabashed fan.

As for the film, while it lacks the lushness of Stevens' comics art, it told the classic story of "boy loves girl, boy finds rocket pack, boy has to rescue girl from an evil Nazi actor played by one of the lesser James Bonds" in a fun, engaging way that made it a cult classic. It also has a connection to the modern Marvel Cinematic Universe. Two decades after "The Rocketeer," its director, Joe Johnston, would direct another, more successful retro-inspired superhero movie, 2011's "Captain America: The First Avenger."

According to an interview with Stevens, the original plan for "The Rocketeer" had been to make a trilogy that would've skewed slightly more adult:

"So, we had a lot of interesting meetings with executives who passed on it but gave us some good criticisms. The last studio on the list was Disney. They took one look at it, and said 'toys!' So ... that's where we eventually made the deal. We originally signed on as a trilogy at Touchstone, the division of Disney doing more adult-themed films. [...] As soon as we all signed on, [Disney executive Jeffrey] Katzenberg pulled a switch and said, 'Nope, it's going to be a Disney release, because Disney needs a live-action hit.' So immediately, Betty and anything else "adult" went right out with the bathwater."

We'll never know if a more adult-oriented version of "The Rocketeer" that kept elements like Betty's glamour modeling day job intact would've been successful enough to get us that trilogy, but the movie we got is well worth revisiting, even though it was crushed by "Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves" and "Terminator 2" at the box office.

#3488. Netflix Adds The 2026 Horror Movie That Made Over 500x Its Budget At The Box Office

"Obsession" passed a box office milestone only five other horror films ever have when it crossed the $500 million mark. That would be an achievement regardless of its budget, but this movie only cost $600,000 to $750,000 to make. That means that when "Obsession" brought in $524.4 million by the end of its unprecedented box office run, it had made more than 500 times its budget.

For a while, that made "Obsession" the most profitable movie ever at the box office, until it was technically dethroned by the low-budget Chinese movie "Niu Lai." Still, it remains one of the most stunning horror success stories of recent years, which is especially impressive considering we've seen multiple low-budget horror movies become hits of late. But if you somehow managed to miss out on all of this, or just want to revisit one of the best horror movies of 2026, Netflix has you covered.

"Obsession" has a relatively simple premise, yet its execution and the lead performances elevate it beyond your typical low-budget horror fare. The film stars Michael Johnston as Baron "Bear" Bailey, a luckless music store worker who has a major crush on his friend/co-worker Nikki Freeman (Inde Navarrette). After buying a One Wish Willow toy, he wishes that Nikki loved him more than anyone in the world and gets everything he asked for and more. The only problem is, Nikki becomes absolutely obsessed with him, to the extent she's willing to hurt anyone who gets in her way.

It's well worth doing so. "Obsession" is a confident crowd-pleaser with a killer lead performance from Navarette. In fact the actor's portrayal of Nikki proved to be her breakout turn, landing Navarrette a role as Rogue in the Marvel Cinematic Universe's upcoming "X-Men" movie reboot. No doubt, more high-profile roles await. As such, even if you're not too intrigued by the prospect of a twisted girlfriend causing violent chaos, you should at least check out "Obsession" to see one of the best performances of 2026 and the beginning of a star's ascendence. The film is streaming on Netflix as of November 17, 2026.

#3487. 5 Reasons Why Robert Pattinson Could Be The Best James Bond Yet

Robert Pattinson has officially been cast as James Bond, beating out several promising contenders to take the coveted role. Denis Villeneuve will oversee the upcoming 26th Bond installment, and he couldn't have chosen a more dynamic and interesting leading man.

Thus far, Bond fans have reacted to Pattinson's casting with both excitement and wariness — which is to be expected. After all, the British actor is one of the biggest stars in Hollywood and is therefore unlike any actor to be cast in the role throughout the franchise's more than 60-year history. But clearly Villeneuve and new Bond custodians Amazon MGM have been impressed by the actor, and frankly it's not hard to see why.

The "Primetime" star has been delivering consistently compelling performances for years now, and if nothing else it will be fascinating to see what he does to make England's greatest spy his own. Sure, on the surface he seems like a safe choice — A-lister white guy with a string of hits to his name. But part of what makes Pattinson so exciting as an actor is his unpredictability. Beyond that, there are myriad reasons why he could not only make a great 007, but might just give us the best Bond yet. Here are five of them.

Robert Pattinson is a big star with the kind of look you'd associate with James Bond. But he's made no secret of the fact he's also a bit of a weirdo underneath it all, and in that sense he shares something in common with Bond.

007 is a similarly deceptive character. Like Pattinson, he's a refined, handsome white guy with an urbane manner. But in the first Bond book, "Casino Royale," author Ian Fleming described him as a "blunt instrument." That element has been integral to the character since his inception. That is to say, Bond is much more than a posh boy with a licence to kill. He's damaged, troubled, maybe a little rough around the edges. Sure, his cinematic history has proved the character lends himself to interpretation, but the best Bond performances have integrated that dark side to some extent.

Pattinson could give us the best version of that to date. Remember that short film he made for GQ about his mounting anxiety over leaving his hotel room to get a hotdog? Something's up with this guy in the best way possible, and every role he's taken since then has been testament to that fact. From his lecherous, questionably-accented preacher in "The Devil all the Time" to his delightfully unhinged nineteenth-Century lighthouse keeper in "The Lighthouse," Pattinson has clearly been having a ball playing crazy (and that's not to mention some of his most Pattinsoniest performances in films such as "Good Time" and "The King"). He'll have to keep it under control for Bond, but 007 needs an edge to be interesting, and Pattinson has a wild unpredictability could be the best thing to ever happen to the character.

Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond breaks a 60-year tradition of unknown actors being given the role. For Bond purists, such a thing is basically sacrilegious. For everyone else, it might just be the most exciting thing to happen to Bond since 1962's "Dr. No" kicked off cinema's most enduring franchise.

Look, there's a chance Pattinson could be distracting as 007. Bond is a male fantasy come to life, and part of the series' success could well be attributed to the fact it's easier for audiences to project themselves onto relative unknowns. On the other hand, it only takes one Bond movie for an actor to become a major star, so there'll always be diminishing returns in that respect. What's more, I think it's fair to say we need big changes after the multiple duds that characterized Daniel Craig's last few years as Bond. The franchise was in danger of becoming less relevant than it once was, and casting a star of Pattinson's standing, in a movie directed by the similarly esteemed Denis Villeneuve is a way to remind people of the saga's blue chip status.

What's more, we're not talking about any A-lister here. Pattinson has proved time and again he has the ability to completely disappear into a role. So, what we're actually getting is an actor with the gravitas and appeal of a megastar who is simultaneously able to become a cinematic cipher onto which we can all project our fantasies of becoming the most lethal instrument the Secret Intelligence Service has at its disposal. As the first millennial Bond, and the first major star to take on the role, Pattinson could prove to be a master stroke of casting on Villeneuve's part.

There was a major turning point in Robert Pattinson's career whereby he seemed to throw caution to the wind and embrace the most challenging, unusual, and downright insane roles he could. In 2017, the year "Good Time" debuted, GQ exclaimed that "the new Rob Pattinson is defined by his willingness to go berserk or go home." Ever since then he has delivered back to back unforgettable performances that have seen the middle class London boy disappear into some of the most unique characters to appear on-screen in the last decade.

Part of it was an attempt to escape the shadow of the "Twilight" saga, with which he'd made his name. But his portrayals of these more off-kilter characters that came in the wake of his decision to recalibrate felt so natural and honest that it was like he was finally able to be himself, paradoxically by playing people so completely unlike himself.

What's even more impressive is that he hasn't slowed down since deciding to "go berserk." 2026 saw him deliver yet another electric performance in the dark, unsettling media satire thriller "Primetime," in which he completely disappeared behind the mask of "To Catch a Predator" host Chris Hanson. Pattinson just can't seem to deliver a bad performance. Wild, sure. Unpredictable? Absolutely. But he's never been anything less than magnetic and seems incapable of being boring. That should be hugely exciting for James Bond fans.

"Tenet" was full of confusing moments but Robert Pattinson's ability to portray a debonair spy with a quietly simmering intensity was not in question. The actor played Neil in Christopher Nolan's thriller. A mysterious operative who helps John David Washington's Protagonist throughout the film, Neil possesses all the charisma of James Bond and even seems to have a bit of a dark side.

All you need to see to be convinced Pattinson has what it takes to play Bond is the scene in which Neil scopes out the freeport where he plans to steal a priceless art piece. As he's shown around the facility, Pattinson's agent simultaneously exudes a polite charm and a kind of palpable ruthlessness, smiling at his tour guide before staring intently at possible escape routes and security measures. You can feel the cogs turning as he looks around, with Pattinson managing to convey a real sense of Neil's thought processes. When he's told about the freeport's security system, which sucks the air out of a room within 10 seconds, he simply says "Blimey," an ironic understatement accompanied by a wry smile more than worthy of 007.

Surely nobody ever doubted Pattinson could play an urbane sleuth who looks remarkably sharp in a suit. But his "Tenet" performance hints at something more interesting. The brief moments when Pattinson's agent drops the charming facade and focuses his attention on various parts of the building's design convey a cold, calculating intensity that bodes well for a Bond with a truly dark side. Nolan's confounding thriller is an exciting proof of concept for Pattinson's Bond and his ability to exude both charisma and a striking cold-bloodedness unlike any 007 yet seen on-screen.

If you were told Robert Pattinson went to Eton and Oxford you probably wouldn't have a hard time believing it. He didn't, but it feels like he'd be very much at home in the public school boy milieu. That's interesting because while previous James Bond actors have managed to affect that kind of high-born aura, Pattinson is the first to just sort of have it from the get go.

He's an upper-middle class white Londoner with a Received Pronunciation accent and an urbane, sophisticated manner. Sure, he's also the guy who can't stop nervously laughing in interviews and who seems to run on pure anxiety most of the time. But there's no denying he has the sort of heritage you'd associate with Bond.

Roger Moore — the only other London-born actor to play Bond — had something similar, but undercut it with his famously tongue-in-cheek portrayal. Sean Connery was, of course, Scottish, Timothy Dalton was born in Wales, Pierce Brosnan is Irish, and Daniel Craig is from Chester in North England. Each of them brought something unique to the role, but of all the James Bond actors Pattinson seems like the first who won't have to work too hard at exuding the kind of aura we've come to expect from a character Idles frontman Joe Talbot described as a "murderous toff."

#3486. Humanity Prepares For Alien War In Netflix's 3 Body Problem Season 2

Netflix has released a first trailer for 3 Body Problem season 2, which sees humanity on the brink of conflict with a hyper-intelligent alien race. Based on the Remembrance of Earth's Past trilogy by Liu Cixin, the Netflix series sees humanity dealing with the approaching arrival of an extraterrestrial civilization that wants to conquer the planet over the span of decades. 3 Body Problem season 2 was recently confirmed to be arriving soon,. The show was given a definitive release date of January 14, 2027.

Now, Netflix has released a full trailer for 3 Body Problem season 2, which sees the conflict with the core alien race about to grow into an ever bigger problem for humanity. The trailer sees the aliens deciding to send an emissary down to Earth for peace talks, a ploy that some important figures, such as Thomas Wade (Liam Cunningham), don't believe is in good faith. The trailer teases more events in space, while on Earth, operations to protect the planet begin to unfold. This includes missions on the ground, alongside tense discussions of what humanity should prepare for.

3 Body Problem season 2 pulls from the second book in Remembrance of Earth's Past, titled The Dark Forest. As seen in the trailer, it appears some additional Earthly events will be unfolding as space takes on a bigger role. This includes new alien characters getting introduced, with some hints that the emissary is, in fact, not there to prevent a larger war from taking place. Based on the events of the trailer, it seems like whatever happens in season 2, humanity will never be the same.

The cast of 3 Body Problem will expand in season 2, with Claudia Doumit portraying Captain Van Rijin and Ellie de Lange joining as Alya. Both will have main roles in the show, making them vital additions to the larger cast. Recurring roles will also be fleshed out as Alfie Allen, David Yip, and Jordan Sunshine join as undisclosed characters. Netflix also recently confirmed season 2 will be shorter than season 1, clocking in at 6 episodes. This puts it two shy of the sci-fi show's debut batch.

David Benioff and D.B. Weiss return as showrunners following the end of 3 Body Problem season 1. The first three episodes of season 2 will be directed by Jeremy Podeswa, while Miguel Sapochnik will direct the second half of the season. Writers include Benioff, Weiss, and Alexander Woo for episode 1, Rose Cartwright for episode 2, Woo for episode 3, Nichelle Tramble Spellman for episode 4, and Benioff and Weiss for episodes 5 and 6. Season 2 was filmed back-to-back with season 3, which will end the series.

The trailer for 3 Body Problem season 2 indicates the story will be pushed forward in a massive new way, as the conflict between humanity and its ever-present outside threat continues. It remains to be seen how the series will measure up to the books, but it appears certain this adaptation of the novel series will have plenty of memorable moments in its middle third.

#3485. 'GTA 6' Runs Best on This Console

Grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time. It's been 13 years since Rockstar dropped GTA 5, and after years of rumors, leaks, and official announcements, the sixth mainstream installment in the series is nearly here. In fact, anyone who pre-ordered the game digitally can now pre-load it onto their console, if you want to ensure you're ready to play the second the game comes out.

Now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox. (The PC version of the game isn't expected until at least early 2027.) But, as it turns out, there's one specific console that can run GTA 6 better than the rest.

Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game. But, interestingly, it spurred a discussion about the performance of the game itself, as well as which consoles are best to run it.

No matter which console you play GTA 6 on, Rockstar says that the game will only target 30 fps (frames per second). That's decided slow for a mainstream game in 2026. GTA 5 also shipped at 30 fps in 2013, but newer consoles can run it at higher frame rates. In fact, most games that launch on the latest generation of consoles can run at 60 fps, if not higher. While it's certainly not a dealbreaker, it is interesting that Rockstar's latest game can't run at a faster frame rate even on the PS5 Pro or the Xbox Series X.

To that point, Rockstar called out the PS5 Pro specifically in its post, announcing, "The PlayStation 5 Pro offers breathtaking visuals, with improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro."

PSSR is Sony's AI upscaler, similar to options like DLSS from Nvidia, which uses AI to add extra graphical information to games in real time. That allows developers like Rockstar to run the game at a lower resolution to save on processing power, but still boost the visuals to reach a higher perceived resolution. As such, it's not as ideal as running the game at a higher resolution natively, but it can help improve the visuals without pushing the hardware beyond its limits. Meanwhile, ray-tracing offers realistic lighting effects and can also be graphically intense.

While PlayStation and Xbox players alike will be stuck at 30 fps, it seems only PS5 Pro gamers will be able to play the game with ray-tracing effects and AI upscaling. It's surprising that Xbox Series X players don't have similar benefits, as the hardware is more powerful than Xbox Series S. Rockstar didn't specify why only the PS5 Pro gets these upgrades.

In the post, Rockstar also announced that the PS5 version of GTA 6 takes advantage of other PlayStation-exclusive perks, like high-fidelity haptic feedback in the DualSense controller, spatial audio rendering using the PlayStation's Tempest 3D audio, as well as improved load times—though Rockstar didn't specify what those load times would be. These perks apply to all PS5 consoles, not just PS5 Pros. Rockstar goes so far as to say that GTA 6 plays best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

That's not to say that Microsoft's consoles are totally left out of the perks. Rockstar says that GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both Xbox Series X and S, as well as Xbox One. In addition, both PlayStation and Xbox gamers can play GTA 6 using Remote Play, so no one has to physically play on their console if they want to game on the go.

Again, there's no reason to go out and buy a specific console for GTA 6, so long as you have something that can run the game. After all, PS5 Pros are difficult to find, especially without wildly overpaying. But it's interesting that Rockstar has managed to give Sony's consoles the extra perks here, particularly since the company hasn't explained why that is.

#3484. The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Review: Haymitch's Prequel Delivers

Suzanne Collins, the woman behind the young adult dystopian phenomenon known as the Hunger Games franchise, seems like she's pretty calculated with her prequels. I mean this as a good thing. Instead of pumping out endless content and prequels that don't really serve the original narrative (ahem, the apparently permanently unfinished Fantastic Beasts franchise), Collins sticks to stories that help us understand key characters and stories from the first three novels ("The Hunger Games" and its sequels "Catching Fire" and "Mockingjay").

This was true of the 2023 big-screen prequel "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," which casts Tom Blyth as future Panem president Coriolanus Snow and explains how and why he grew into the villain faced by Jennifer Lawrence's Katniss in the original films (where he's played by Donald Sutherland). This is, thankfully, also true of the Haymitch Abernathy prequel "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," based on the 2025 novel "Sunrise on the Reaping."

Haymitch — a role originated by Woody Harrelson and played spectacularly by "We Were Liars" and "East of Eden" alum Joseph Zada in this new film — is sixteen during the Second Quarter Quell, a sort of demented "special edition" of the titular Games that take place every 25 years. For the 50th Games, the all-powerful Capitol in charge of Panem reaps double the number of tributes from each of the totalitarian nation's 12 districts, meaning that 48 kids will enter the arena and only one will survive. Frankly, this premise is immediately intriguing, but director Francis Lawrence and screenwriters Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie ensure that, beyond the shock value, this story remains human, emotional, and gripping from beginning to end. Much of that is also thanks to Zada, who delivers an unforgettable performance.

Playing an established franchise character — especially one originated by an incredibly famous and acclaimed actor — must be a tough undertaking, and I'll get back to the highlights and lowlights of that exact situation before long. First, though, I want to soundly and unrestrainedly praise Joseph Zada, an actor with a massive responsibility in this film. Without a good Haymitch, "Sunrise on the Reaping" fails.

Thankfully, Zada is more than up to the task, and the movie's extremely speedy — but not overly so — pacing means that he has to go through a massive emotional journey in a relatively short amount of time. Zada sells every second as Haymitch, whether he's promising his District 12 girlfriend Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak) that he'll see her after the reaping to breaking down crying just before he enters an arena filled with, presumably, 47 kids who hope to kill him.

Zada is great, but much like Haymitch, he doesn't do it alone. Because, again, "Sunrise on the Reaping" moves at such a quick clip — to be fair, it packs 400 pages into about 2 hours and 40 minutes — he's the character we bond with the most, and the character Haymitch himself bonds with the most is arguably Maysilee Donner, his fellow District 12 tribute played by Mckenna Grace. Despite being enemies back home, where Maysilee is a sort of petty schoolyard bully, the two become unlikely allies who end up making it to the end of the Games together, and Grace brings a steeliness to her role that eventually falls away to reveal an understandably scared young girl. It certainly helps that Francis Lawrence and his team built an astounding world for his performers.

Joseph Zada and Mckenna Grace, the standouts among the tributes — with respect to Ben Wang, Molly McCann, and Iona Bell, the first of whom plays District 12 tribute Wyatt Callow and the rest of whom play Louella and "Lou Lou" McCoy, they, uh, aren't in the movie as much for reasons you can probably ascertain — deliver exceptional performances, but respect must be paid to Francis Lawrence's overall vision and the stunning world-building that he and his creative team deliver in "Sunrise on the Reaping."

When I spoke to Lawrence about the film and other dystopian teen movies he's directed (or is set to direct), he said, "I think the dystopian aspect of these worlds, a lot of it, for me, is about the world-building." This love of the game is evident, because "Sunrise on the Reaping" looks and feels phenomenal.

If you're familiar with the Hunger Games franchise, you know that we've gotten to see two very different eras of Panem, which come with understandably different technical developments. In "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," everything is relatively primitive; beginning in "The Hunger Games," the tech is much more advanced after several decades. "Sunrise on the Reaping" falling pretty squarely in the middle here is particularly cool because of the small details of the world; one such example that I really appreciated is the tributes being lifted into the arena on small platforms as opposed to the tubes we see Katniss and other tributes enter years later. Without spoilers, the technical logistics of the arena play an outsized role in "Sunrise on the Reaping," and the world feels rich, full, and disturbingly real in the best way.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is chock-a-block full of characters you'll remember from previous installments like "The Hunger Games: Catching Fire" and both parts of "The Hunger Games: Mockingjay," and the results are ... a bit mixed. (It was confirmed, long before the film's release, that Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson would reprise their roles as Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark; how exactly that transpires will remain a secret until you sit down and see the movie.) I'm going to mention the breakneck pacing again here, and it's not a bad thing, but it does mean that a lot of characters are introduced and summarily disappear; this is also true of Billy Porter's larger-than-life Capitol stylist Magno Stift, though his legal wife and nemesis Drusilla Sickle, a plastic surgery nightmare gamely played by a vamping Glenn Close, gets much more play.

I wish we'd seen more of Elle Fanning's take on Effie Trinket, a character originally played by Elizabeth Banks, but she's reliably great in her scenes; Kieran Culkin plays a pre-Stanley Tucci version of Caesar Flickerman and is bombastic, over-the-top, and undeniably sharp and dynamic. Jesse Plemons does great work, as always, stepping into Philip Seymour Hoffman's shoes as the taciturn turncoat Plutarch Heavensbee, echoing Hoffman's performance while making it his own.

The best and worst performers behind recurring characters, though, are Ralph Fiennes and Kelvin Harrison Jr. Fiennes manages to bridge the gap between Tom Blyth and Donald Sutherland as Panem's president Coriolanus Snow, but Harrison Jr. is, I am sorry to say, doing a sort of "Saturday Night Live" impression of his predecessor Jeffrey Wright. I appreciate the ask here is big, but sadly, not every actor rises fully to the challenge.

If I have one big "nit to pick" in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," it's a problem that affects a lot of adaptations: it over-explains a lot. Because the book is told from Haymitch's point of view, we learn a lot as he infers and gleans; the movie has to painstakingly say all of that. Still, it's a minor quibble.

Before the release of "Sunrise on the Reaping," I saw and heard chatter, anecdotally, that this movie would surpass "The Hunger Games: Catching Fire" in sheer quality. Respectfully, I have to disagree. Not only is "Catching Fire" the best Hunger Games movie by a long shot and just a really great and well-made movie in its own right — Francis Lawrence, thank you again for that incredible aspect ratio change as we enter the arena, and thanks to your cinematographer Jo Willems as well — but "Catching Fire" doesn't have to explain its narrative as intensely as "Sunrise on the Reaping" does. Still, this is simply a quirk of adaptation, and "Catching Fire" being able to narratively coast off of its predecessor is an unfair advantage.

"Sunrise on the Reaping" might not beat "Catching Fire," but it is a truly excellent addition to the Hunger Games film franchise — and it's one of the most thrilling action movies of the year. As this universe continues to expand (that is, if Suzanne Collins decides to write future books), if we keep Lawrence at the helm and keep casting top-notch actors, Hunger Games fans will remain in excellent hands.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" opens in theaters on November 20, 2026.

#3483. Magic: The Gathering’s New Commander Decks Offer Less for the Same Price

The four Commander decks for MTG Nauctis won't feature borderless Commander cards

The four Commander decks for MTG Nauctis won't feature borderless Commander cards

Magic: The Gathering players know it's an expensive hobby. Whether you're trying to keep up with a rapidly changing Standard format or you just want to add a spicy new card to your Commander deck, the hobby has surely gotten progressively more expensive. However, it's one thing to see product prices rise, and a completely different one to see that product lose some of its features while keeping the same price.

During MagicCon: Atlanta 2026, Wizards of the Coast officially presented Magic's latest set in a dedicated showcase, and I'm not talking about Star Trek, which saw its global launch that very weekend. Nauctis: The Sunken Realm is the next in-universe Magic set, scheduled for release on Feb. 5, 2027. Nauctis will introduce a brand-new, underwater world, and the set will feature a variety of products, as usual. This includes four Commander decks, but players have noticed that borderless Commander cards will no longer be included in the product, which is still being sold at a retail price of $49.99.

However, there is still a chance to get those fancy borderless Commander cards. The Premium Edition Commander Decks include one foil borderless face Commander and one foil borderless featured Commander. Plus, the entire deck is foil. However, the retail price for Premium Edition decks is $79.99. This means that players who really like having their borderless Commanders will have to shell out more money than usual, even if that comes with a full foil deck.

That's not the only controversial change that Nauctis will bring to Magic products. Starting with this set, Collector Boosters will drop from 15 cards to 12, while Standard Bundles will no longer feature foil full art lands, and the number of foil basic lands will drop from 15 to 10. Wizards of the Coast explained the reasoning behind some of the changes to make room for various printing experiments like God Packs, but many fans are understandably unhappy.

Nonetheless, the Nauctis Commander Decks at least seem exciting. The Boros (red-white) Seal the Deal has perhaps the best deck name in Magic history. The Bant (white-blue-green) Merfolk Regiment will add more options to one of the most popular typal decks in Magic. Izzet (blue-red) Blood in the Water has sharks. Need I say more? Finally, Sultai (green-blue-black) Terrors of the Abyss looks like the strongest option, if only because its two Commanders, the Ignoble Serpent and Zekes, Acid Rock Fan, have already been inadvertently spoiled on Scryfall.

Terrors of the Abyss's box features the phrases "discard and mill" and "reanimate sea monsters," and that seems to be a strong strategy, based on the deck's Commanders. The Ignoble Serpent costs eight mana (five colorless, one green, one blue, one black) for a 7/9 legendary serpent noble. Its text box reads:

At the beginning of your first upkeep in this game, if The Ignoble Serpent is in your command zone, mill four cards.

At the beginning of your end step, return target sea monster creature card from your graveyard to the battlefield. (Krakens, Leviathans, Octopuses, Serpents, and Whales are sea monsters.)

Commander players know how powerful passive abilities that activate while a Commander is in the Command Zone are, thanks to the infamous Eminence ability. This serpent starts its engine right away on turn one. If you can mill a powerful sea monster in the first four cards of your deck, then as soon as you play The Ignoble Serpent later in the game, that sea monster can hit the battlefield for free. And if you spend most of the game filling up your graveyard with other powerful sea monsters, then Ignoble Serpent's bottom ability makes it fairly easy to overwhelm opponents.

Some of my favorite picks for sea creatures to include in a deck like this would be the classic Simic Sky Swallower (featuring protection and evasion), The Terror of Serpent's Pass, the Unagi of Kiyoshi Island (which provides card draw). I'd be remiss not mentioning the terrific duo of Koma, Cosmos Serpent and Koma, World-Eater, two massive threats that are resilient to removal and also generate a scary number of creature tokens.

However, my favorite option is Sin, Spira's Punishment. When Sin enters or attacks, it makes a copy of another permanent in your graveyard. This means you could get two big monsters on the battlefield for the price of one. Sin can also make copies of lands, and it even draws a card in the process.

With 40 sea monsters in your deck, you have an 89% chance of milling one as part of those first four cards, but since it'll take you awhile to actually get The Ignoble Serpent onto the board, you have time to mill and/or discard sea monsters with cheap effects like Dark Matter Manipulator, Dream Twist, or Mental Note to ensure a big monster hits the battlefield every turn.

Overall, The Ignoble Serpent looks like a hugely powerful Commander, but not necessarily one that's overly game-breaking. Its viability will rely on a careful balance of ramp, mill, discard, and a big pile of nasty sea creatures.

#3482. Does The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Have A Post-Credits Scene? A Spoiler-Free Guide

Get ready for the 50th Hunger Games. This time, it's all about Haymitch Abernathy and the games that turned him into a champion. But is this the last ride for the property? Or might there be more to come?

"Sunrise on the Reaping" offers a thrilling new look at beloved "Hunger Games" characters, but it is a prequel. Much like "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" before it, it's filling in gaps in the timeline of this universe. So, it's not directly setting up sequels like the original run of "Hunger Games" movies. That said, Lionsgate may yet want to lay some seeds for future installments, and in the realm of franchise filmmaking, credits scenes are the best way to do that.

Credit scenes have become expected fare in so many properties. Add that to the fact that Jennifer Lawrence's Katniss and Josh Hutcherson's Peeta are returning in this new "Hunger Games" prequel, and there's even more reason for fans to think there could be something extra during the end credits. So, we're here to offer a spoiler-free guide to the movie's credits scene situation. Seriously, we will not spoil anything meaningful whatsoever. This is merely about giving viewers information to enhance the experience. With that out of the way, let's get to the matter at hand.

No, "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" doesn't have any credits scenes of any kind to speak of. No post-credits scene, no mid-credits scene, nothing at all. "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" revisits the world of Panem and follows young Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) 24 years before the events of "The Hunger Games," starting on the morning of the reaping of the 50th Hunger Games, also known as the Second Quarter Quell.

Francis Lawrence, who directed the emotionally obliterating all-time great Stephen King adaptation "The Long Walk" in addition to several prior entries in this franchise, has returned to the director's chair once more.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" hits theaters on November 20, 2026.

#3481. 7 Most Hopeless War Books of All Time, Ranked

Whether they’re on a screen or on a page, great war stories play a key role in educating the wider public about the horrific realities of armed conflict. Particularly in the 20th and 21st centuries, the lived experiences of the World Wars, the Vietnam War, and more have inspired some brilliant and bleak novels, many of which rank among the greatest works of literature ever written.

These novels span many genres, from tragicomedy to drama to science fiction, but what they all share is a grounded emotional and psychological realism that makes for a truly devastating read. They’re not easy, but they are inventive, intelligent, visceral, and above all honest, which is the quality that you want most of all in a story about humanity’s darkest chapters. So, without further ado, here’s our ranked selection of some of the most hopeless war books of all time.

Joseph Heller’s debut novel, which has been adapted multiple times, Catch-22 is a satirical war story set during World War II. The book uses a non-linear third-person narrative, exploring events from 1942 to 1944 from the perspectives of multiple characters. Primarily, it’s the story of Captain John Yossarian, a U.S. Army Air Forces bombardier based on the Mediterranean island of Pianosa who desperately tries to cling to his sanity while dealing with the relentless absurdities of war and military life.

Primarily a satire of military bureaucracy, Catch-22 derives its title from a bureaucratic fallacy: an insane person should not fly missions, but anyone who asks not to fly on grounds of insanity must be sane enough to fly them. The book explores how this rule, and other equally counterintuitive military reasoning, slowly grind away at a soldier’s sanity. It’s easily one of the most important war novels of all time and a decidedly bleak narrative; the only reason it doesn’t rank higher on this list is that the hopelessness is balanced by Heller’s wit and dark sense of humor.

Written by novelist Tim O'Brien and based on his experiences as a soldier in the Vietnam War, The Things They Carried is a collection of linked short stories revolving around a fictional platoon of American soldiers fighting in the war. A semi-autobiographical work of metafiction, the book explores personal stories of love, loss, and trauma as well as the importance of storytelling, especially when it’s the stories of the people you love. Though fictionalized, the story is inspired by real people and events that O’Brien encountered during the war.

The Things They Carried is a powerful book that blurs the lines of fiction and non-fiction but ultimately delivers a deep truth about life and war. Since the time it was first published in 1990, the collection has received near-universal critical acclaim and become an international bestseller. The book has won several accolades as well and was a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Critics Circle Award.

Kurt Vonnegut’s Slaughterhouse-Five, or, The Children's Crusade: A Duty-Dance with Death is a genre-blending anti-war novel partially inspired by Vonnegut’s own experiences and those of other people he knew who served in World War II. The narrative follows Billy Pilgrim, an American soldier who becomes unstuck in time and experiences his own life in a non-linear fashion after an encounter with fourth-dimensional aliens. Over the course of his life, Billy’s experiences, particularly the trauma of surviving the bombing of Dresden, drive him to adopt a fatalistic worldview as death loses all meaning for him.

One of the most acclaimed war novels and sci-fi books of all time, Slaughterhouse-Five is a highly original book that uses its metafictional narrative to process the author’s personal experiences. Like Billy Pilgrim, Vonnegut also survived the Dresden bombing, and the book is largely his attempt to finally put what he experienced into words. The novel was Vonnegut’s first bestseller when it came out in 1969 and has been highly acclaimed ever since. It’s also been banned in multiple places in the United States as recently as 2024.

Ernest Hemingway’s A Farewell to Arms is a novel set during World War I that follows the story of an American medic, Frederic Henry, who serves in the Italian Army. The book primarily explores Frederic’s romance with English nurse Catherine Barkley, which provides the sole light in his life as the war turns bloodier and more brutal than ever. Eventually, he leaves the army and seeks out Catherine, hoping to start a new life in Switzerland.

A Farewell to Arms is a truly tragic war romance, mainly because, unlike in many war novels, there is some hope to be found in the book: the hope of love and family that Frederic feels thanks to Catherine. However, by the end of the novel, that hope is cruelly taken away, not in a high-stakes battle but in a painfully normal, everyday manner that is all the more heartbreaking for its simplicity. A Farewell to Arms has been widely hailed as one of Hemingway’s greatest novels, and it has been adapted as films, a play, and a TV miniseries. In 2025, the novel entered the public domain and is now freely available online.

Written by Joe Haldeman, The Forever War isn’t a war book in the traditional sense: it’s a military science fiction novel that explores an interstellar war between humans and an alien civilization known as the Taurans. The book follows William Mandella, a physics student drafted into an elite task force to fight in the war using advanced weapons and near-lightspeed technology. Due to the relativistic nature of time, every time William returns to Earth, he finds a world that’s drastically different in its culture, language, and even biology, leading to an ever-increasing sense of alienation.

Published in 1974, The Forever War was highly acclaimed by critics and won multiple accolades, including the Nebula, Hugo, and Locus Awards. Despite its science fiction narrative, the book is inspired by Haldeman’s real experiences serving in the Vietnam War and is arguably more realistic than most historical books. It’s also unique in the sense that, while the story has what you could call a happy ending, it also delivers a bleak message about the inherent meaninglessness and alienation of war. The book was followed by three sequels: 1997’s Forever Peace, 1999’s Forever Free, and the 1999 novella, A Separate War.

A German semi-autobiographical novel by Erich Maria Remarque, All Quiet on the Western Front is one of the most famous war books ever written. The novel follows Paul Bäumer, a young man who, along with his classmates, enthusiastically signs up to fight in World War I. Over the course of the war, Bäumer learns firsthand about the horrors of war, the pain of loss, the alienation from civilian life, and the utter meaninglessness of the patriotic fervor that led him to join military service.

Since its publication in the late 1920s, All Quiet on the Western Front has been widely hailed as the greatest war novel of all time. The book is a bleak, painful, and necessary narrative that exposes the true cost of warfare on the individual psyche and soul — a message that got it banned and burned in Nazi Germany. Today, the novel is universally acknowledged as one of the greatest literary treasures of human civilization, and it has received multiple film adaptations, most recently Edward Berger's 2022 German adaptation, which won four Academy Awards.

Written by Dalton Trumbo, Johnny Got His Gun is a highly influential war novel that isn’t nearly as talked about as it ought to be. Set during World War I, the book is centered on Joe Bonham, a young American soldier who wakes up in a hospital bed and slowly realizes that he has lost all his limbs, eyes, ears, mouth, and nose. Trapped in his own body, his only hope is death, but even that is rendered impossible by military “regulations." All he can do is reminisce about his old life and hard-learned lessons about war.

Despite being an anti-war novel published during wartime, Johnny Got His Gun was quite acclaimed in 1939 and became a popular text among the American left of the time. The book has had a significant influence on American literature, shaping political discourse and literary craft with its stream-of-consciousness critique of war. Trumbo wrote and directed a film adaptation, released in 1971, which became a cult film, and the book has also inspired several other works of cinema and theatre, not to mention the Metallica song “One."

#3480. Lifehacker's Pick for the Best TV to Gift in 2026 Isn't Actually a TV

Welcome to Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, a collaborative multimedia project in which Lifehacker, CNET, ZDNET, and Mashable harness the power of our product testing laboratory and our editors' expertise to offer the best gift-buying recommendations possible. In this episode, we're talking televisions.

I recently did a deep dive into TV development history, checked out what was on shelves for 2026, and I concluded that the best gift TV you can give this year is, actually, a pair of sunglasses. The XBX by XReal video display glasses are basically a TV you can shove in your pocket. Check them out:

I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? More importantly, there's the nature of television itself. Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

Then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a big screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.

#3479. First Reactions To Brad Pitt's Cliff Booth Movie Have Critics United

It's not every day that we get a continuation of one of Quentin Tarantino's most acclaimed movies. Heck, it's not every day we even get a new script at all from the movie-loving auteur. Ever since he debuted "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" in 2019, Tarantino hasn't directed a single feature film — likely a consequence of his self-imposed (and rather silly) rule to limit himself to only directing 10 total movies. But whatever the case may be, he was clearly interested in diving deeper into this alternate-history world with "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth," only this time, he handed over the reins of his script to David Fincher.

Could this unlikely collaboration between Fincher and Tarantino, two very different artists, yield fruit? It sure seems like it has, based on early reactions from the film's Los Angeles premiere. It seems like the entire movie industry has been waiting for this moment, despite the unusual nature of this sequel. Set in 1977, eight years after the events of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," the sequel focuses solely on Brad Pitt's past-his-prime stuntman Cliff Booth long after his harrowing encounter with the Manson family. Gone are his free-wheeling days playing backup to Leonardo DiCaprio's Rick Dalton, replaced by the reality of having to find a new way forward in a much different world. As the film's colorful synopsis puts it, "the fairytale is over."

But not for us! "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" held its premiere screening last night, and social media is positively abuzz with hype from those in attendance. For those looking for a handy roundup of all the first reactions, you've come to the right place.

Is it really possible that we have yet another "Best movie of 2026" contender on our hands this late in the year? If anyone could pull that off, well, we suppose it'd be the dream team of David Fincher and Quentin Tarantino. Starring Brad Pitt, Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Carla Gugino, Matt Groove, JB Tadena, the great Peter Weller, and many more, "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" has plenty of star power going for it. But dare we even hope that Tarantino managed to make lightning strike twice, revisiting this deeply nostalgic world for a second time and somehow living up to the hype?

That seems to be the main takeaway from the critics, journalists, and other lucky fans at the Los Angeles premiere. We'll start with Variety awards pundit Clayton Davis, who described the picture as "a wild, hilarious hangout movie" featuring Pitt's "best performance" since his last time in the role as Cliff Booth. He added, "The cinematography is gorgeous. If the 2019 film was a love letter to L.A., this one is a full-on sonnet [..] Fincher and Tarantino haven't been this much fun in years."

As if that wasn't high praise enough, critic Courtney Howard echoed those sentiments and called the sequel "a pure riot. David Fincher's play at a nostalgic bygone era Quentin Tarantino loves works like gangbusters. Takes time to form, but plays like a LA film noir hangout picture." Meanwhile, Germain Lussier of io9 came out swinging and proclaimed this "my favorite movie of the year and it's not even close. Hilarious, exciting, romantic, you'll never guess what happens next and probably not believe it then anyway. Couldn't love it more if I tried."

Of course, as with any significant Hollywood premiere, some of the more interesting reactions are the ones that go against the grain. While most responses are united in singing the praises of "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth," a select handful note that they may need some time with this movie to fully soak it in. In a world of extremes, reactions that run towards the middle ground are certainly refreshing, at least.

Longtime critic and entertainment journalist Todd Gilchrist suggested that he was still undecided on whether David Fincher and Quentin Tarantino's unique sensibilities are fully a match made in heaven. "I quite liked 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,' but as with all Tarantino projects, I need to see it (at least) twice to properly digest it. I'm not yet convinced QT's shambling, novelistic approach and Fincher's precision are exactly compatible." Erik Anderson of Awards Watch went even further, highlighting that, "Despite some fun and energetic sequences, I found 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth' to be tonally a bit messy [...] It seemed to want a 70s noir style but should have leaned in more."

As always, each viewer's mileage may vary. Luckily, fans won't have to wait much longer. "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" will receive an exclusive two-week window in IMAX theaters starting on November 25, 2026. It will then come to Netflix on December 23, 2026.

#3478. 5 Actresses Who Would Be Perfect James Bond Girls Opposite Robert Pattinson

Who should play the next Bond Girl? We have a few ideas.

It's finally been confirmed that Robert Pattinson will be playing James Bond in the next canonical feature film about Ian Fleming's stalwart British spy. Back in February 2025, Amazon gained creative control of the character, and while we expressed some consternation over the deal, that didn't stop film fans everywhere from speculating what a James Bond movie might look like in the 2020s. Fast-forward to 2026, and there were several finalists for the role of the new Bond himself, among them Nicholas Hoult, Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O'Connor, and the ultimate winner, i.e. Pattinson.

Now, of course, we can play further speculation games. With 007 in place, fans will now have a marvelous time pondering who might be playing other notable James Bond supporting figures like Ms. Moneypenny, M, Q, Blofeld, Felix Leiter, etc.

And, as is a long (and perhaps sexist) tradition in James Bond lore, he must always be paired with a "Bond Girl" or two in every movie. Bond will inevitably meet and seduce an attractive woman, and the woman will typically prove to be an invaluable ally, a secret enemy, or a doomed innocent who is killed to move the action forward. Some models and actors have even elevated their "Bond Girl" roles into fascinating new characters.

I'd have loved to see O'Connor play a gender-flipped version of a Bond Girl, as we haven't yet had any "Bond Boys," and their time has definitely come. Pattinson could easily seduce men and women equally, and depicting O'Connor in bed with Pattinson would be a fantastic "second place" prize for the actor.

Who should play a Bond Girl opposite Pattinson? We think the following performers would do well.

Florence Pugh may be the most obvious choice for the next James Bond movie. Pugh already has spy-movie-adjacent experience playing Black Widow Yelena in several films and TV shows in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, including 2026's ultra-hit "Spider-Man: Brand New Day," so she could likely slip into the role of a slinky espionage expert with ease. Indeed, she kind of played a Bond Girl-like role in "Brand New Day," anyway, appearing nude in a hot tub as Yelena and offering some vital exposition to the movie's hero. But it doesn't take too much imagination to envision Pugh slithering through a casino or fancy-dress ball, wearing an expensive, Met Gala-worthy gown, snarling at Bond and talking to him with power and confidence.

Pugh is a forceful and talented actor, and it seems to me that she would be able to bite into a Bond Girl role with enthusiasm. Robert Pattinson is also quite versatile and, in the right roles, intense and zany. I suspect that Pugh would be able to match Pattinson's hidden livewire energy, allowing the two to crackle. Additionally, Pugh has previously worked with Denis Villeneuve, the director of the next Bond flick, having played Princess Irulan in Villeneuve's "Dune: Part Two" and the upcoming "Dune: Part Three."

So, the question now arises: would Pugh's Bond Girl be a helpful ally, a doomed innocent, or a secret enemy? Every instinct in my body dictates that she'd end up being the third type, holding a gun on 007 while they both wear nothing but a bedsheet.

Katy O'Brian's breakout role was playing the itinerant queer bodybuilder Jackie in Rose Glass' amazing 2024 crime flick "Love Lies Bleeding," which I thought was one of the best movies of its year. What's more, it's clear from her performance in that film that O'Brian is destined to be a star. She possesses a forceful energy and a lot of screen presence, able to balance the intensity from her co-star, Kristen Stewart.

Some might also recognize O'Brian for her supporting role as Jentorra in 2023's overpriced Marvel actioner "Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania." The actor has since appeared in the blockbuster films "Twisters" and "Mission: Impossible — The Final Reckoning" and had a supporting role on the "Star Wars" TV series "The Mandalorian," so she's clearly comfortable with giant productions and would not feel out-of-place in a James Bond movie.

O'Brian has experience in a wide variety of other films, too, having played the lead in the drag queen-themed 2025 zombie movie "Queens of the Dead" and appeared in the biopic "Christy" opposite Sydney Sweeney. Most recently, she appeared in Edgar Wright's "The Running Man" adaptation.

I can picture a scene wherein 007 travels to a bar somewhere and trades barbs with O'Brian, whose biceps are bigger than his. They can then admire the other women in the joint together, sharing a drink and a seeming flirtation, along with some secret information. Then, once something goes wrong and bad guys begin extracting weapons, Pattinson and O'Brian could stand back-to-back and kick a little butt. She has a black belt in hapkido, after all.

Danai Gurira's first major screen credit came in 2004 when she appeared in an episode of "Law & Order: Criminal Intent." From there, she continued to plug away at her career, appearing in episodes of shows like "Life on Mars," "Lie to Me," and "Treme." However, her real big break came when she began appearing on the hit zombie series "The Walking Dead" as Michonne, a character who's become so recognizable that her likeness has shown up in non-"Walking Dead" video games like 2026's "World War Z."

Her career only continued to swing upward when she co-starred in the 2018 MCU blockbuster "Black Panther" as Okoye, the leader of the Wakandan royal guard. And none of this even scrapes her amazing theater career, with Gurira having authored several plays and scored a Pulitzer nomination for her play "In the Continuum."

When James Bond steps into a room, he usually fills it with his charisma and poise. The women he meets, then, should be able to match one of those qualities, and Gurira could do that in abundance. And here's the thing: She's capable of playing either a poised spy contact in a gown or a rough-and-tumble underground figure with equal skill. No doubt, she could swish across a ballroom, dancing with 007 as Strauss plays on the soundtrack, or she could welcome 007 into a dingy basement to flirt while she smokes a cigarette, only to start swinging her baseball bat at the rival spies who would inevitably infiltrate the area.

Most folks wouldn't recognize Arden Cho's face, but they would definitely recognize her voice, as she played the lead character Rumi in Netflix's super-hit animated film "KPop Demon Hunters." But even if that movie somehow passed you by, Cho has been racking up screen credits for decades, appearing in TV shows like "CSI: NY" and in low-rent movies like "Mega Python vs. Gatoroid." Her most prominent live-action TV roles include her turns as Kira on the "Teen Wolf" series, Emily on "Chicago Med," and Ingrid in "Partner Track."

Cho is also a pop star in her own right, having released her first single back in 2011, a song titled "I'm Just a Girl." (A quick note: Despite the actor being a fantastic singer, Rumi's singing voice in "KPop Demon Hunters" was provided by singer EJAE.) Cho is a professional model as well, having worked on campaigns for Nike and Apple, so she would be wholly comfortable in dazzling gowns and sporting high-end makeup. Her profile is certainly rising thanks to the popularity of "KPop Demon Hunters," and she is slated to appear in the upcoming K-Pop-themed feature film "Perfect Girl."

It's hard to say what kind of chemistry Cho would have with Robert Pattinson, although she certainly seems more down-to-earth and relatable. Pattinson, meanwhile, comes across as relatively aloof. As such, one can envision Cho playing a smoky, clever figure who's able to crack wise with 007 without him being quick enough to notice.

Hunter Schafer's filmography isn't terribly large, but her profile in popular culture is enormous. She rose to fame playing the role of Jules in the HBO series "Euphoria," and her movies and TV shows since have all been either fascinating art pictures or high-profile franchise entertainments. Case in point: Schafer appeared as Tigris in "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" in 2023 and played the lead role in the zany Dan Stevens horror film "Cuckoo" in 2024. That same year, she also had a small role in Yorgos Lanthimos' "Kinds of Kindness," which is maybe the most Yorgos Lanthimos movie that ever Lanthimosed. Then, in 2026, she briefly appeared in David Lowery's sapphic pop diva drama "Mother Mary" and will soon appear in the sci-fi series "Blade Runner 2099."

Schafer is dazzling on screen, bringing both sophistication and naivete to her roles, often simultaneously. She looks like an elven princess, and it's almost a pity she was not cast as Princess Zelda in the upcoming "The Legend of Zelda" movie (with the role instead going to Bo Bragason).

I don't know if Schafer has any fight or stunt training, but one can easily imagine her in a lovely dress dancing with, and kissing, James Bond. No doubt, she could serve as a gentle counterpoint to a relatively gruff Bond, and she would only be the second trans actor to appear in a James Bond movie after Caroline Cossey in "For Your Eyes Only." Schafer, however, could — and should — play a much larger role. I can see her kicking glutes and smirking while doing it.

#3477. A Classic Justice League Hero Is Officially Replacing Darkseid In Two Months

DC reveals which unexpected character becomes Darkseid's replacement as the Justice League's next biggest villain. Darkseid wasn't originally devised as a Justice League villain, but his immense power and his obsession with destruction has made him one of the biggest threats to the DC Universe and therefore a recurring JLA antagonist. Besides, the ruler of Apokolips is a multiversal constant, present across all the DC multiverse as a permanent apocalypse looming over every reality. Even when Earth’s greatest heroes destroy his physical body, Darkseid still exists somewhere out there.

Several cosmic tyrants rival or even surpass Darkseid in destructive power, but they ultimately pose smaller threats to the DC Universe. Beings like the Anti-Monitor, Perpetua, Nekron, Barbatos, Mandrakk, and the Empty Hand have each come close to unmaking reality itself, while Brainiac and Lex Luthor match or exceed Darkseid’s intellect on Earth. However, most of these villains usually pop up once every decade for a crossover event before vanishing back into dormancy, while earthly geniuses like Luthor lack Darkseid’s divine army of Parademons. Darkseid strikes repeatedly across generations, constantly corrupting worlds, hunting the Anti-Life Equation, and even reshaping entire timelines like the Absolute Universe.

No other character embodies the total eradication of free will like Darkseid does, but some DC figures make remarkable attempts.

Justice League Unlimited #27 presents one of the most dramatic heel turns in JLA history. On the cover, Michael Holt sits triumphantly on a throne shaped like an upside-down Omega symbol while a shrunken Atom perches on his shoulder. Having previously lost his cherished sense of "fair play" to Charon in the underworld and watched the Atom grow increasingly disillusioned with the League’s villain-amnesty policies, Michael Holt finds an unlikely partner who shares his frustration with the status quo. The solicitation for Justice League Unlimited #27 confirms his new antagonistic role, teasing, "ONCE A MAN, NOW A NEW GOD. MR. TERRIFIC ASCENDS!"

ONCE A MAN, NOW A NEW GOD. MR. TERRIFIC ASCENDS! Mr. Terrific was once the third-smartest man on Earth. Now his amplified genius is about to span the cosmos as he prepares to ascend to godhood — and only the Justice League can hold him back!

Back in Justice League Unlimited #22, Mister Terrific absorbs the Justice League’s collective powers and arrives at the conclusion that he alone can fix a broken universe with his new combination of unmatched intellect and the Justice League's complete collection of superpowers, which he acquires when he gets his hands on the Power Bank holding them all within a single object. Feeling superior to the entire Justice League, Mister Terrific has started to understand Darkseid's ideology, and he now has everything he needs to prove himself the villain's equal and overpower all his former teammates.

Mister Terrific possesses one of the sharpest minds in the DC Universe, but once he absorbs the Justice League’s collective powers, pure logic convinces him that authoritarian control is the most efficient way to fix the universe. Without a selfless heart to temper his calculations, Michael Holt’s brilliance turns clinical and ruthless, echoing the exact same hubris that makes Darkseid impossible to bargain with. Batman, one of the only two DC humans brighter than Mister Terrific, tempers his obsessive strategic mind with compassion, which allows him to understand that efficiency without humanity inevitably becomes oppression.

Bruce Wayne isn’t the only Batman in the DC multiverse. Discover 45 versions of the Caped Crusader and which one is the most powerful of all.

Batman has proven this restraint virtually every time he has gained similar upgrades, and he has always used those temporary boosts strictly to save lives before he willingly gives them up. Bruce Wayne has sat upon the omniscient Mobius Chair, wielded a Yellow and Green Power Ring, and has temporarily acquired Kryptonian-like physiology, yet he has never let godhood seduce him into believing he should rule or reshape the world. The belief that "absolute power corrupts absolutely" is ultimately the difference between Batman's legendary heroism and Mister Terrific's tragic transformation into a Darkseid-like supervillain.

What do you think about Mister Terrific's heel turn?

Justice League Unlimited #27 is available January 27 from DC Comics

Across decades of DC stories, the team's roster repeatedly changes as its members confront alien warlords, ancient demons, powerful sorcerers, and Darkseid.

For all intents and purposes, Black Friday sales are already here. There are plenty of deals out already, even though we're weeks away from the actual event. Early Black Friday Deals and Doorbusters: The official start of early Black Friday deals on Nov. 6. New deals will drop every Friday.

Cyber Sunday and Monday: Best Buy is extending Cyber Monday to five days and says you can find deals going up to 50% off select tech.

You don't need to be any kind of member to shop Best Buy's Black Friday in July sale; however, it is free to sign up for a My Best Buy membership, which will get you free shipping. Target has some week-long deals and a Deal of the Day. Walmart will have three Black Friday and Cyber Monday shopping events. Nowadays, large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026.

#3475. Robert Pattinson Wasn't The First Choice For James Bond — But The Original Favorite Dropped Out

Not to give Amazon any free ideas, but the behind-the-scenes drama swirling around the biggest casting call of the year sounds like it could've been a reality TV series in its own right. The fateful search for who would don their most finely-tailored suit and their trusty Walther PPK came to an abrupt end this week, as Robert Pattinson was officially announced as our newest James Bond. But amid all the hoopla and hype, details have already begun trickling in concerning how this high-stakes round of musical chairs came to a close.

As it turns out, Pattinson may have won the highly-coveted role ... but he wasn't the first choice. To be fair, that seems evident enough from the fact that neither his name nor Nicholas Hoult's appeared in most reports identifying the finalists until late in this lengthy process. The intrigue goes much deeper than that, however.

There's a lot more that goes into casting decisions for James Bond than simply who looks best in a suit. The role is notorious for singlehandedly changing the lives of each and every performer practically overnight, especially in light of the usual Bond tradition of picking (relative) unknowns for the title role. There's life before Bond and life after Bond — and not everybody is cut out for all the fame and pressure and (occasionally) backlash that inevitably come with it.

It'll always be to Josh O'Connor's enduring credit that, according to this Puck report, he recognized these factors ahead of time and decided that it simply wasn't worth it for him. For the rest of us mere mortals, it may be tempting to look at nothing but the popularity and wealth and prestige associated with playing England's most defining fictional spy. If so, well, look no further than the toll this clearly took on our previous Bond. Not only did Daniel Craig have to overcome some seriously nasty comments about his physical appearance in the early going, but certain provocative comments late in his run also revealed the arduous nature of these big-budget productions and the many, many off-screen responsibilities associated with it.

Still, as excited as we are to see Robert Pattinson as Bond (and as someone who survived the "Twilight" phenomenon, he may be uniquely prepared for this in a way nobody else ever has), we'll always wonder what O'Connor could've done with the part. Villeneuve obviously saw that potential himself, and the "Dune" filmmaker is certainly no slouch when it comes to casting. Whatever comes next, we'll be seated for O'Connor's next big performance.

#3474. Lord of the Rings Returns to Theaters Next Week to Reveal an Iconic Moment

See the forging of the One Ring on the big screen

On Nov. 25, Prime Video will release the final two episodes of Lord of the Rings: Rings of Power's third season. The penultimate episode is already confirmed to depict one of the most important moments in Middle-earth's history, the forging of the One Ring. To give that moment the respect it deserves, the episode is getting a theatrical release.

The show's official X account announced this on Nov. 16, sharing a link where fans can find local theaters with screenings. As an added bonus, the cinematic event will actually be an early release of season 3's episode 7, as the screenings will take place on Nov. 23 and 24.

This isn't the first time Amazon has brought one of its original Prime Video series to the big screen, as The Boys' finale also received the treatment earlier this year. As for the actual conclusion to season 3, fans will have to be satisfied seeing that on their TV, phones, or tablets.

Since the start of season 3, audiences have been waiting for Sauron to forge the One Ring. The season, which began with a five-year time jump that serves as a soft reboot of the show, has heavily focused on the villain's attempts to finally create his all-powerful weapon. His failure to do so up to this point has largely been due to the lack of help from the Elven smith Celebrimbor, who forged the rings of power for the dwarves, men, and elves.

The One Ring is arguably the most important object in all of Middle-earth, as it features in Tolkien's novel The Hobbit as well as being the main McGuffin of the original Lord of the Rings trilogy. While we've caught glimpses of its forging in Peter Jackson's films, Rings of Power will be the first time we've seen the entire process in all its glory. If you don't mind the changes the show made to the source material, then this will surely be a moment worth seeing on the biggest screen you can find.

#3473. 10 Google Privacy Hacks Everyone Should Know

Your Gmail account doesn't just have one email address. In fact, it has unlimited addresses, but you need a hack to utilize them. When you're signing up for a new service, you can add another word to your email address, as well as the "+" symbol, to create an alias. For example, if your email is "[email protected]," and you're signing up for an Amazon account, you can use "[email protected]" as your email address. The email will still end up in your main inbox, as if you simply used [email protected]. Not only can this trick turn one Gmail address into an unlimited number of addresses, but it also helps you identify who sold your email address to spammers, because those emails will have the alias in the "To" field.

Gmail's web view has a crucial security feature that lets you view session logs. This feature is inexplicably buried at the bottom of the inbox, and the font size is tiny, so it's easy to miss. To find it, log in to Gmail on the web, and scroll to the bottom of your inbox. Click the Details button in the bottom-right corner, below "Last account activity." This will show you a pop-up that lists the devices, apps, and locations you've recently logged in from. This makes it easy to see if there's been any suspicious activity in your Google account, and you can click the Security Checkup link in the pop-up to review this data. Just note that if you use a VPN or a service like iCloud Private Relay, you might not recognize your own device's location. To check if unwanted apps have access to your Google account, you can visit this settings page.

Google wants to show you personalized search results, which initially feels very helpful, but it also ends up trapping you in an algorithmic bubble. The best way to break out of your search bubble is to periodically use other search engines, but if you wish to stick to Google, you can disable personalized search recommendations in Google Search and the Play Store on Android. Go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized Recommendations and Play Personalization.

Google tracks your web and app activity by default, which includes your search history, voice data (if you use the speak-to-search feature), and activity from sites, apps, and devices that use Google services. However, associated information, such as your location data, is also saved to your Google profile, which you might not assume gets included in "Web & app activity." Fortunately, you can disable this tracking by going to this settings page, scrolling down to "Web & App Activity," and turning off all options in this section.

Google's Timeline feature saves your location in Google Maps to create a map of places you've visited. This is useful if you want to keep track of your recent stops; however, Google can use Timeline data to help businesses see how effective their ads were, or how likely you are to visit nearby stores. Its confirmation page confirms this: "Depending on your settings, activity saved as history in your Google Account, including ad interactions, may also be connected to Timeline data to help nearby businesses estimate the likelihood that people will visit their stores. No personal information is shared with businesses."

Timeline isn't enabled by default, but in case you enabled it a while ago, and are no longer using it, you can turn it off by going to this settings page. Click Turn off, and delete your activity to remove Timeline data from your Google account.

You can't fully escape Google's ads or tracking, but you can disable personalized ads to stop the company from using your account data to show ads. To do this, go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized ads.

While Google claims that it isn't using your emails to train AI, the company does offer AI features that make your emails feel more robotic than human. One of these is "Smart Reply," which offers email reply suggestions such as "Got it. See you soon." I can type that on my own, and I feel uncomfortable with Gmail analyzing the contents of my emails and replies to offer suggestions that I wouldn't use anyway. You can disable this by going to Gmail Settings > General, or by visiting this settings page. Scroll down to "Smart features," and turn off the checkbox next to it. This will disable Smart Compose, Smart Reply, suggestions for pending replies and follow-ups, spelling, grammar, and autocorrect.

A physical security key is a great security upgrade. It's a physical barrier that prevents most ways to hack into your account remotely. Even if someone discovers your email ID and password, and has access to your two-factor authentication code, they won't get in without physical access to that key. You can check out Google's support page for physical security keys for more information on compatibility and setting up your security keys.

Google uses data from Gmail and Google Drive to target ads, which means that your emails, files, and photos could be used for monetization. To stop this, you'll need to disable Personal Intelligence. To turn it off, visit this settings page, and click Turn off Personal Intelligence.
