#3472. BritBox’s Masterpiece Detective Thriller Gets Major Season 3 Update From EP

Greer Riddell is a London-based film and television journalist writing about comedy, streaming and the evolving media industry in the UK and USA. She works at Collider, covering the latest in film, television and entertainment through interviews, features, reviews and industry coverage.

Her recent brand collaborations include HBO, Warner Bros., Netflix, Hulu, Sky, Disney+ and DC Studios. She has covered titles including Saturday Night Live UK, Rivals, Scrubs, Stuart Fails to Save the Universe, Ludwig, Supergirl and Stranger Things.

Her recent interviews include Florence Pugh, Mike Faist and Christopher Abbott for Netflix's East of Eden, Taika Waititi and Jenna Ortega for Klara and the Sun.

Editor's note: The below interview contains minor spoilers for Ludwig Season 2.

David Mitchell's breakout role as Mark Corrigan in Peep Show saw him play a neurotic overthinker who could turn even the most mundane interaction into an existential crisis. Now, in Ludwig, he takes on another socially awkward, semi-reclusive character, but John Taylor has a much more productive way of putting his obsession to use. Under the pseudonym Ludwig, John is an acclaimed puzzle setter whose methodical mind and extraordinary ability to recognize patterns also happen to make him excellent at solving murders.

That talent might have remained undiscovered if it weren't for his sister-in-law Lucy (Anna Maxwell Martin), who forces the reluctant John into impersonating his twin brother, a DCI in the local police force, after he mysteriously disappears. The mystery surrounding James' whereabouts continues into Season 2, but John no longer has to hide behind his brother's identity in this “soft murder” take on The Parent Trap. Instead, the Cambridge Police Authority has brought him in as a "Crime Consultant".

With the second season having just finished its run on BritBox, Ludwig executive producer Kenton Allen joins Collider to discuss the series' success, the challenges of continuing the same story with a new dynamic, and why comedy actors seem so well suited to murder mysteries. He also discusses whether Ludwig could become a long-running detective franchise, teases the series' Christmas special featuring Poirot himself, David Suchet, and shares what audiences can expect from Rabbit, the U.S. adaptation currently being developed by Humphrey Ker (Welcome to Wrexham) and Megan Ganz (It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia).

COLLIDER: When I was doing my research for Season 2, I watched a couple of podcast appearances by you, and something that I thought was really interesting is that David Mitchell actually said he'd be interested in playing a detective, and he fits so well with that! Now, when I watch Ludwig, it's like, well, why was he doing anything else? What do you think it is about David and his performance that makes him such a good Ludwig?

ALLEN: I think it's a number of things, really. I think that you are correct when you say he fits it really well because it was written for him. I don't know whether you know the story, but a few years ago we were shooting another show. Do you know the story?

ALLEN: So he rang me and said, "I've got a secret I need to tell you." I'm slightly worrying what that secret might be. And his secret was he wanted to play a TV detective. And then I spoke to Mark Brotherhood, and that began Ludwig ultimately. So it was written for David, and Mark Brotherhood is sort of a bit like David but from the North of England.

I suppose that David, I sort of have this firm belief that the really great actors, particularly in this sort of genre, have come through half-hour comedy. And so if you look at British TV and you think of things like Cracker — Robbie Coltrane, I know Cracker wasn't a detective, but he sort of was — and you think of Alan Davies and Jonathan Creek, and Alan Davies came through 30-minute TV, and you think of David Jason and A Touch of Frost, and there's a great lineage of comedy half-hour sitcom actors stepping up into one hour. Some people call them “cozy crime,” a phrase I don't like. We prefer “soft murder.”

ALLEN: Yeah. Well, you need an actor that can play that, you know, that can do the serious business of investigating murders, but can also bring the charm and the wit and the irreverence to it. And I think that David brings that to Ludwig, and he has a light element to David in his real life, which I tease him about regularly.

I think he sort of embodies who Ludwig is, which is an outsider, a loner, somebody who prefers his own company to the company of other people, somebody who's very clever but is also quite shy, et cetera, et cetera.

I was intrigued by that connection between comedy and drama. So you mentioned the example of Alan Davies, David Jason, and there's also been a lot of talk around, perhaps this year especially — I went to the Edinburgh TV Festival, and they were all talking about how comedy, British comedy, has this huge resurgence. Is that comedy side of things one of the reasons why Ludwig has done so well, that tone, and what do you think comedy brings as an advantage to the mystery genre?

ALLEN: I don't think it's comedy, really, that brings something to the genre, but I think that in these sort of shows, these sort of murder-of-the-week shows, I think that in a world which is increasingly confusing and upsetting and there doesn't seem to be any answers to anything, I think spending an hour with somebody who is clever and entertaining and fallible and has all sorts of issues, but is capable of sorting out a whodunnit in 60 minutes, is rather reassuring.

There is some order in the world. Puzzles do get solved. Bad people do get caught. I think it's to do with that. I think the comedy, I think people, I think there's a bit of weariness about very hard murder shows. Some American television executive once described to me, "dead women in the trunk of a car" show, which is not a genre of television.

ALLEN: Isn't it? What a charming phrase. But I think there is a weariness of that very graphic, very violent, often women or children being kidnapped or murdered. I think people have had their fill of that. Particularly in a world which is, the news headlines are particularly unpleasant and disturbing and upsetting. I think escaping into a world where problems get solved, but we don't focus too much on the grisliness of the murder and focus more on the how was it done and who did it, I think there's some comfort in that. So, I think there is some comfort viewing in it.

The same there is in Traitors, when you're watching them get murdered, but they're not actually getting murdered. It's just reassuring, I think, to know that despite the chaos outside your living room or wherever you happen to be watching, that there is some north star, which is problems can still be fixed.

That first season, we had that added tension of John impersonating James and when was everybody going to find out, and then everybody found that out at the end of the first season.

So, you've got to come back to Ludwig in a sort of new dynamic in a different way. How can he still be involved with the police investigations in this new season? How did you ensure that this second series maintained that same level of suspense, and how did it keep audiences just as gripped?

ALLEN: Yeah. Well, I think the plan was always, from day one of developing the show, that Ludwig could only pretend to be his brother for one season because I think it stretches credibility to think that he could get away with that for more than a couple of weeks. So we always imagined that he would become, he'd be so good at solving murders and his clear-up rate would be so good and make Cambridge's CID look so good that they want to keep him on as a consultant.

So he becomes a consultant in the second season. But we still don't know where his brother is, why his brother's disappeared, and the evolving mystery about what is going on with Joanne Kempner (Sian Clifford). What is this greater conspiracy? Is his brother involved in it? Is the Kempner family really a decade-long, multiple-decade murdering dynasty? What is that all about?

I think that's the thing that keeps pulling you through the show. As much as John, Ludwig being a really good detective, he's still got an ulterior motive, which is what the hell is going on with his missing brother?

And also, he's got this developing relationship with Lucy and this sort of surrogate family with Lucy and Henry, which is evolving as well. The more time they spend together, the more time they realize that they're sort of codependent.

I really liked Anna Maxwell-Martin's character being perhaps a bit more involved in this season. She's doing her own detective work now at the newspaper. What has having Lucy more involved allowed you to explore that was not possible in Season 1?

ALLEN: Well, it's allowed us to explore what a brilliant actress Anna Maxwell Martin is more. If you've got Anna Maxwell Martin, give her something to do. That's from a producing point of view, but from a story point of view, it enables them to become a kind of investigating duo, Ludwig and Lucy, I guess, and it enables her to follow up leads on the bigger, the wider conspiracy and the mystery of her husband's disappearance, while Ludwig is pulled into various murders.

And I think it just gives a bit more urgency to the show, and I think it raises the stakes that Lucy is no longer the passive — we never wanted her to be a kind of passive wife who'd been abandoned by her husband, was just sort of slightly sad and... Just sort of a typical abandoned wife. The character was not that, and Anna Maxwell Martin certainly didn't play her like that. So she's obviously going to want to get involved. Her husband's missing. That is true. She's not going to sit around and ask Ludwig every week, every day, "Anything else happened in the investigation of my missing husband?" You know, she's going to get amongst it.

ALLEN: Yeah, and her photojournalism comes out of her day job, which is a photographer. So she goes for it, like any modern woman would, don't they? They wouldn't — you wouldn't sit around and go, "Oh, I don't know. I'm just going to sit here and make tea and wait for somebody to tell me where my husband is." She's not going to wait for permission to get involved, I think.

With Lucy, as you said, there's a bit of surrogate family there, but John and Lucy almost act a bit like an old married couple, and there seems to be a bit of history between them. Do you think it's fair to say that John sees Lucy as the one that got away and then perhaps married the wrong brother?

ALLEN: Yeah. I think so. I don't think Lucy thinks that. I think Lucy picked James and obviously married him and has a family with him. I think that Ludwig, though he probably never says it out loud to her in this season, feels that there was something else there, and if only he'd been less on the back foot, maybe he and Lucy could have been together.

But it's obviously the thing that dare not speak its name because she's married to his brother! I think that's in the Bible. You don't go out with your brother's wife. So it's completely forbidden fruit, and obviously neither of them can go there, whatever they're feeling. There's a son, Henry, in the mix, and there's a marriage, and there's all sorts of other things that are in the way of them ever truly saying how they may or may not feel about each other.

Well, it's interesting to watch any way, that sort of there's a devotion there, but perhaps in the past.

ALLEN: It's interesting growing up with identical twins and falling in love with one or both of them, and then we know they're not Mormons. No, she had to pick a brother, and she picked James.

What I really like about Ludwig is that there is obviously the overarching mystery, but then we also have the murder-of-the-week. How do you actually balance keeping those murder-of-the-week stories self-contained and interesting throughout, but also work out how much to feed into each episode of that central mystery that keeps us watching every episode week by week?

ALLEN: You work with a brilliant writer called Mark Brotherhood! And then, one of the answers to that question is a bit technical, but it's sort of true, which is our show is made principally for the BBC, and a BBC show is 59 minutes long, and typically a network show that has commercials in it, they're typically about 44 minutes long. So just in the maths of it, we have 15 more minutes of airtime to play with than you would on a normal commercial procedural. And often when you look at a sort of non-commercial procedural television, you'll see that they have to have more story in them because you've got this other screen time to fill, and you can't have eight more suspects. That doesn't work and is a bit boring. So, I think the nature of making it for the BBC originally means that there's naturally some time there to devote to the bigger conspiracy.

You could make the show at 45 minutes, but I think you'd find that the — and in fact, we're making, we're going to make a pilot for ABC, which we announced a couple of weeks ago. So that'll be very interesting about compressing both the story of the week and the conspiracy into a shorter running time. And the fact that a murder mystery, a story of the week, can sustain so much entertaining screen time. You can see shows where that aren't very entertaining, where it's all they've got, and that can become a little one-note. So I think it's just balancing what we're interested in, and you're led by Ludwig as well, and what is going on in his sort of quasi-professional life and his domestic life and how those two things are balanced out.

Britain has a history of such long-running murder mystery series and detective series. Do you see Ludwig becoming a long-running series, or is that overarching mystery with James' disappearance sort of giving it a natural limit to the story?

ALLEN: We've just wrapped the first three episodes of Season 3. We start shooting the second three episodes on Monday. We shall see.

Okay, I will come back to that at some point then, when I've watched the third season.

ALLEN: Yeah, I mean, you would need to ask that question at the end of the third season. I would say that people don't stop getting murdered.

Yes, there's not going to be many people left in Cambridge. I do keep thinking that.

ALLEN: Well, there's lots of people moving around all the time, but I don't think we'll have found all the murderers in Cambridge by the end of Season 3.

You brought up the fact that there's going to be a pilot made for ABC based on Ludwig, called Rabbit. It has a good audience. People are enjoying it. What was it about the American adaptation that you wanted to explore a bit differently from the original series?

ALLEN: I can't really talk too much about it. For obvious reasons, but I would say that if we get it right, Rabbit will be a brilliant cousin to Ludwig. Just in terms of where it's set and what the attitude is towards crime and crime prevention in North America as opposed to Cambridge, there's some big differences. Our police don't carry guns.

ALLEN: American police do carry guns. There's lots of cultural differences that I think will make it an interesting companion piece to Ludwig. I don't think it will be — it's a bit like the American Office, I guess, in that, you know, the American Office started off relatively like the British Office, but it took on a life of its own quite quickly. And I think that's what we're hoping to do with Rabbit, which is why it's called Rabbit and not American Ludwig.

So, watch this space, but I think there's plenty of cultural differences just between the two settings that give the show its own distinctiveness. And then I think there is a writer, obviously Megan Ganz, working with Humphrey Ker and Jon Steinberg and Dan Shotz myself. So it's seeing the fundamental setup through a different lens.

I'm looking forward to seeing what that becomes.

ALLEN: Yeah. Particularly the creators, Mark Brotherhood, myself, David Mitchell, nobody wants to make a facsimile of a show that we're making and is on air. So it has to have some reason to exist. And I think that Megan Ganz and us have found a very cute, smart way of making a cousin rather than a copy.

So fans of Ludwig will start watching Rabbit as well, and then they've got both shows to enjoy. You brought up the "cozy crime," or what we're going to call "soft murder."

ALLEN: Cozy crime is dead. Soft murder lives!

So it's become quite a significant British export to North America through BritBox.

Well, there's a whole page on BritBox as a category. Detective stories have become a thing. From your experience, why do you think international audiences respond so strongly to these sort of British murder mysteries?

ALLEN: I think that I don't think it's exclusively British because I think there are some examples in the States now of this, and our inspiration for Ludwig, a lot of it came from shows like Columbo and Monk, which were sort of murder-of-the-week shows. I think that international audiences enjoy seeing less grisly forms of ways to kill people, as we've discussed.

We very deliberately set the show in Cambridge, England, because it gives you a great mix of ancient and modern and hasn't been photographed very much in contemporary television. And I think that feels fresh, like Inspector Morse and Oxford felt fresh 30 years ago. Hopefully audiences are enjoying seeing a different slice of British life.

And obviously we're brilliant. We have brilliant actors, brilliant writers. Our on-camera and off-camera talent is world-class. So I think we're, you know, we've always been brilliant storytellers, and we have brilliant actors and brilliant directors and brilliant designers and brilliant everything. I just think hopefully it's an elevated form of a very familiar genre.

The world is not short of shows where people get murdered, but I think there's a lot of shows where people get murdered in a very unpleasant way. And we don't really feature the unpleasantness. We don't really, we don't ever revel in it, really, and we don't deal with it — we rarely deal with the impact on relatives and all of that. I mean, it is a slight fantasy career. Murder is very serious and devastating, obviously, but we use it for entertainment.

David Mitchell's 6-part crime series returns.

I was very happy to see that Ludwig is coming for a Christmas special because, obviously, we get to see more Ludwig, but I really do love Christmas specials and I think more shows should do them. I also saw that David Suchet is going to be a part of that, which is very exciting. People who love murder mysteries will absolutely love that. Is there anything you can tease?

ALLEN: Well, it's, it's rather wonderful, really, because we all, David in particular, are huge fans of Poirot, who is probably the greatest detective of all time. A fantastic Agatha Christie creation, and David Suchet's interpretation of that character is, we think, probably the best detective on screen there has ever been. So obviously David Suchet does not play Poirot in Ludwig, but we have got Poirot meets Ludwig in the show.

ALLEN: It's Christmassy. It is a special to me. It's the highest accolade any television show can ever have, which is to have a Christmas special. It'll be scheduled around Christmas in the UK, and I think on BritBox. We're still working that out. There's snow, there's mince pies, there's Christmas crackers, there's murder!

Ludwig Season 1 and Season 2 are both streaming now on BritBox.

#3471. Why Casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond Is a High-Risk, High-Reward Gamble for Denis Villeneuve

Throughout his 64 years in movies, James Bond, the hard-living superspy, has been the star of the 007 franchise. But by granting Robert Pattinson a license to kill, the producers of the next Bond film are making a bet that one of the most famous men on the planet can slide into a role shaped by the likes of Sean Connery, Daniel Craig, Roger Moore, and Pierce Brosnan without bringing any Edward Cullen-sized baggage.

It’s quite a gamble. After all, Connery, Craig, Timothy Dalton, and poor, delusional George Lazenby were relative unknowns when they were tapped to play the secret agent, and Brosnan and Moore were TV-famous but unproven as film stars. That’s not the case with Pattinson, who has been one of the most recognizable people on the planet for two decades, and who is currently anchoring another massive franchise in “Batman.” So why did director Denis Villeneuve, producers David Heyman and Amy Pascal, and Amazon MGM Studios decide to hand over the keys to the Aston Martin to such a prominent and expensive candidate? Related Stories ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ First Reactions: Quentin Tarantino and David Fincher Deliver a ‘Pure Riot’ of a Hangout Movie ‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier

Well, some of it has to do with Villeneuve’s comfort level. He’s worked with Pattinson on “Dune: Part Three” and knows what the mercurial star can bring to a role. Clearly, he wants to build a darker, brooding Bond. Then, there’s also the need to have insurance. Amazon is launching a new iteration of 007 into a world that looks very different than it did in 2019 when the last chapter, “No Time to Die,” was conceived and shot (it wouldn’t be released until 2021 thanks to COVID). We’ve lived through #MeToo, a pandemic, wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, the fraying of the Western World and, with it, the “special relationship” Bond has sworn to protect. From the start, Amazon was interested in picking a higher-profile actor to outfit in one of Bond’s signature tuxedos. Before the search began in earnest last May, executives were high on the idea of Jacob Elordi.

Plus, some of the other finalists, a group that included Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, and Nicholas Hoult, lacked the kind of sex appeal and danger that the part required. Hoult apparently impressed executives with his audition, but came up short, as he did when he was in contention for Batman (losing out to Pattinson) and Superman (getting Lex Luthor as a consolation prize). He remains very well liked in the industry. With a salary estimated at roughly $2.5 million, Hoult would have been a cheaper option than Pattinson, who one industry source speculated would cost north of $10 million to hire.

But the higher price tag may be worth it. This isn’t just the first Bond to be released under Amazon’s ownership — it’s the first to be produced without the Broccoli family at the helm. The keepers of the 007 flame sold their creative control to Amazon in 2025, leaving the series without a guiding force. Both Heyman and Pascal are old hands, having overseen the casting of the Harry Potter and Spider-Man franchises, respectively, but those are still big shoes to fill.

What’s in it for Pattinson? Well, a chance to put his stamp on an iconic role, as well as an opportunity to reunite with Villeneuve, one of the hottest directors in Hollywood. His commercial bona fides have also, arguably, never been higher. Not only has he shown he can anchor a superhero film with “The Batman” and its upcoming sequel, but he’s also opened more idiosyncratic fare, such as the recent A24 hits “The Drama” and “Primetime.” Clearly, he can bring in the younger audiences driving the box office turnaround while retaining a kind of indie cool that could take Bond in a new and exciting direction. Will he be our perviest 007?

Plus, the recent shake-up at DC Studios, with James Gunn and Peter Safran replaced by former Marvel executive Jeremy Latcham, may spell trouble for Matt Reeves’ “The Batman” series. Although it was conceived as a trilogy, the sequel was delayed multiple times as Reeves dealt with personal matters, forcing him to leave production last month, with Steven Soderbergh stepping in to finish shooting. DC may not want to wait as long to make another installment, and there’s a sense that Latcham may want something brighter and more mainstream than Reeves’ moody, hard PG-13 take on The Dark Knight.

But Pattinson better get ready for a lot more scrutiny than the questions that greeted his casting as Bruce Wayne. “With Batman, there’s a mask to hide behind,” said one industry source. “With Bond, your face is front and center.”

Even Craig, widely considered to be the best Bond since Connery, faced fierce blowback when his casting was announced. He was too blonde, too unconventionally handsome. A website, CraigNotBond, sprang up where fans vented their displeasure.

But when “Casino Royale” debuted in 2006, and Craig showed that he was perfectly capable of kicking ass and ordering his martini shaken, not stirred, the haters were quickly silenced. Will Pattinson be able to pull off the same stunt? It’s a high-risk, high-reward gamble. Just the kind of bet James Bond lives to make.

#3470. 'Game Of Thrones Meets Outlander' Fantasy Series Reveals New Title & 2027 Release Date

Game of Thrones fans looking for a new fantasy series with the same political intrigue may have found the perfect replacement, with an exciting new update on the next entry in the saga.

It's been over 15 years since the most recent entry in the A Song of Ice and Fire series, with A Dance with Dragons arriving back in 2011. While George R.R. Martin continues working on the long-awaited The Winds of Winter, there's still no official release date in sight. HBO has kept Westeros alive through its expanding slate of television adaptations, but readers hoping for another sprawling fantasy epic that scratches the same itch have had to look elsewhere.

One such alternative has been a major hit among fantasy readers, and the New York Times #1 best-selling adventure features "the page-turning politics of Game of Thrones [and] the worlds-spanning romance of Outlander," according to the author's official website, with a brand-new release just announced for 2027.

Ilona Andrews' Maggie the Undying series is officially returning in 2027, with the bestselling author revealing some exciting new details about the next installment in the fantasy saga.

On November 10, 2026, Ilona Andrews officially announced that the second book will be titled This Crown Will Not Rule Me, with a confirmed release date of September 21, 2027. The announcement also included a first look at the novel's cover artwork by Helena Elias, alongside a new story synopsis, which you can check out below.

For those unfamiliar, Ilona Andrews is actually the pen name of husband-and-wife writing duo Ilona and Gordon Andrews, who are best known for their bestselling Kate Daniels, Hidden Legacy, and Innkeeper Chronicles fantasy series.

Their latest series, Maggie the Undying, is a planned trilogy that began with This Kingdom Will Not Kill Me in March 2026. It follows Maggie, a devoted fantasy reader who unexpectedly finds herself transported into the world of her favorite unfinished book series.

The newly revealed description for This Crown Will Not Rule Me teases a dangerous new adventure:

The kingdom of Rellas is safe—but for how long? Having averted a fateful attack on the capital, Maggie must now keep its people safe from an even deadlier struggle for the crown. Unfortunately, her allies keep getting in her way: Everard, who is ever the more insistent on making Maggie his duchess; the knight Arvel, who is determined to uncover her secrets; and a mysterious religious sect that continues to pester her for unknown reasons. If that’s not enough, the plot is no longer as Maggie remembers.

Beyond the political intrigue, the sequel introduces a dangerous "monster extermination" known as the Culling, which is arriving a year earlier than expected with "thrice as many nests." With Maggie's knowledge of the original story becoming increasingly unreliable, her apparent immortality may not be enough to save everyone she cares about.

You can pre-order This Crown Will Not Rule Me via Amazon here.

The first book in the series has already proven enormously successful, becoming a New York Times and USA Today bestseller and earning a nomination for Readers' Favorite Fantasy in the 2026 Goodreads Choice Awards. With that kind of momentum behind it, Maggie the Undying is quickly establishing itself as an exciting alternative for fantasy readers looking for their next Game of Thrones fix.

#3469. The Stop-Motion Tool That’s a Constant in This Crazy, AI-Mixed-Up World

A lot is happening in front of the camera in “Wildwood” — the general Millennial chaos of Portland, Oregon, swarms of baby-napping crows, an army of wolves with cannons and trebuchets — and just as much behind the camera in Laika Studios’ latest stop-motion epic. But for all the innovation and blending of CG and stop-motion required to tell the story of Prue McKeel’s (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) impossible quest into the impassable woods, some key tools have stayed the same for Laika since “Coraline.”

One such tool is Dragonframe, the frame-grabbing software developed by Jamie and Dyami Caliri in 2008, and essential to helping Laika animators craft the naturalistic performances that “Wildwood” director Travis Knight wanted to create. Related Stories Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Edward Said: Between Worlds’ About Palestinian-American Author Lands at Kino Lorber Why Casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond Is a High-Risk, High-Reward Gamble for Denis Villeneuve

“Back in the old days, like the Ray Harryhausen days — it was still the same as how we do it: You have a puppet; you have an object; you move it a tiny bit; you take a picture; you move it a little more; you take another picture. But you had no way of knowing exactly what the frame that you just took looked like and how it related to the frame that you’re about to take,” Knight explained on an episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast. “You had these gauges where you could try to approximate the distance something moved, but it was this act of faith. You didn’t really know; you had to wait until you developed the film to see how it moved. And that’s why a lot of early animation has that kind of herky-jerky quality.”

Dragonframe and other frame-grabbing software systems take a lot of the guesswork, if not quite all of the faith, out of that process. Laika animators can check what they’ve just done on a computer, moving between the most recent frames taken and the one that an animator is currently on. This allows animators to ensure that whatever motion they’re puppeting, be it walking, running, flying, or the unfathomable wrath of nature flowing out through a giant tower of living vines exploding forth from the Earth, flows together.

“Whether it’s a 20-frame shot or a 1000-frame shot, you can look at all the frames that precede it to make sure that the object or the puppet is moving the way it should,” Knight told IndieWire.

Laika has used Dragonframe on every one of its films, but just because a tool is that useful and reliable doesn’t take the artistry and effort of animating out of the equation, or lower the particular stakes of stop-motion.

“2D animation, CG animation, they’re iterative. You can set key frames. You do your breakdowns. You do your in-betweens. You can go back and refine and keep going and reworking things until you get the perfect performance. With stop-motion, it’s progressive. You start on frame one, and the animator, coaxing life with their hands into this puppet, is working their way through a frame at a time. You don’t get to go back and change it.”

That lack of take-backs permanence, though, also helps stop-motion animators be intentional and certain in their choices. “You’re contorting your body into all these positions to get these puppets to move properly. It’s mentally very draining because you have to do all this three-dimensional chess as you’re trying to figure things out, because it is technical, but it always has to feel organic,” Knight said. “ It’s human ingenuity, it’s human creativity, it’s devotion, it’s care, it’s time.”

All that care and time goes into pulling off the magic trick of making steel, silicon, and fabric objects feel fully alive. That’s been the game for stop-motion since Ray Harryhausen. Whenever Laika develops new processes or sticks with tried-and-true tools, it’s to give animators the ability to do that. “[We don’t want] to get in the way of seeing this puppet as a person. The finest stop-motion animators can do all that with their hands. But we’ve developed different techniques and tools where some of the less experienced animators can actually get to that same level,” Knight said.

#3468. Garmin Cyclists Can Now Make Themselves Appear on Waze in Real Time

Cyclists who ride with Garmin gear can now appear as live, moving icons on the Waze driving app, and nearby drivers will receive an alert to slow down and watch for them on the road.

For riders already using Garmin devices, opting in costs nothing and adds a new layer of safety, particularly on roads where drivers may not expect cyclists. The feature is rolling out now, but you should be aware of its limitations.

Riders can simply opt in once through Garmin Connect. After that, sharing starts automatically when an outdoor cycling activity begins and stops when the ride ends. While a ride is underway, Waze users near the cyclist see a cyclist icon move along the road and receive a Live Cycling Alert reminding them to slow down and stay aware.

The feature runs on LiveTrack, Garmin's existing live location-sharing tool, which lets friends and family follow a rider's real-time location, speed, course, and more. Garmin says this collaboration extends that peace of mind to motorists, giving them greater awareness of their surroundings.

Garmin notes its location sharing is temporary and session-based. The rider's name, identity, and route are hidden, and no personal information is shared or displayed in Waze. Drivers see only an anonymous icon and the alert.

You'll need a few things to get this feature up and running:

A compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin watch

A phone running Garmin Connect with a data connection

An outdoor cycling activity (the feature doesn't apply to indoor rides)

The good news is using the feature is free: LiveTrack costs nothing on compatible Garmin bike computers and watches, and Waze is free for drivers.

This new feature is a great safety perk, but there are real-world caveats worth considering:

This feature is for Waze only. Alerts reach drivers only when Waze is open on their phone. Google Maps, which has far more users, is excluded, so a large portion of the drivers you share the road with won't see you this way.

It depends on your phone's signal. Your position travels from the Garmin to your phone, then to Garmin's servers, then to Waze, and finally to the driver's phone. On a patchy rural signal, a few seconds of lag could put the icon on the wrong side of a bend from where you actually are. A rider who leaves their phone at home or whose phone loses signal simply won't show up on a Waze map, as a ride without a data connection is invisible to Waze.

Finally, remember to treat this safety feature as an extra perk, not a guarantee. At the end of the day, it isn't a replacement for bike lights, bright clothing, and defensive riding.

#3467. Magic: The Gathering Designer Says Commander’s Most Divisive Staple Isn’t Going Anywhere

Commander’s “foundational, iconic heart” is here to stay

The two best T-shirts I saw at MagicCon: Atlanta 2026 were easy to choose in a sea of delightfully nerdy references and imagery. One was black with a wall of white text spelling out the lengthy definition of Banding, a notoriously confusing Magic: The Gathering mechanic that’s now 33 years old. The other was a white shirt featuring a picture of a Sol Ring card crossed out by a red circle and slash. “BAN SOL RING,” it read.

The first shirt provides a public service and a punchline about ancient Magic history. Based on an interview conducted at MagicCon, the second is a bold demand that Magic principal designer Gavin Verhey has no interest in entertaining.

“Sol Ring is the foundational, iconic heart of the format,” Verhey tells Polygon.

Commander’s most ubiquitous artifact, Sol Ring, costs one colorless mana and taps to produce two colorless mana. There are few Commander experiences more satisfying than drawing one to start the game, allowing you to drop it on the first turn (and maybe even follow that up with an Arcane Signet). Suddenly, your deck’s strategy accelerates. If you have a four-cost Commander, they’re out on turn two. But no matter the cost of your Commander or what your deck wants to do, Sol Ring is going to help it all happen sooner.

I never want to see another turn-one Sol Ring again

That ruthless efficiency is also a reason to ban it. An early Sol Ring can give one player a major advantage, forcing everyone else to either catch up or collectively deal with the person who drew it. Its near-universal usefulness also eats up a slot that could otherwise go toward something more directly tied to a distinctive strategy. Verhey recognizes the card’s power. He just sees its place in Commander differently.

“It’s been in basically every single Commander precon we’ve ever made,” he says. “It’s in almost every Commander deck players build. People love it, and they love their unique variations of Sol Ring.”

There are 146 individual printings of the card, with 75 unique pieces of artwork. One features Garfield the cat dancing with his beloved Arlene. Another depicts Dogmeat from the Fallout franchise staring at his reflection in a bowl of water. Many, including the oldest, show a bright ring of light in the midst of a blazing inferno.

In a casual, four-player format, Verhey argues, the possibility of someone getting an explosive start thanks to a Sol Ring can help make individual games feel different. In a 100-card singleton format like Commander, you have a 7.46% chance of drawing one, so that is actually quite rare. Everyone has access to the same card, but who draws it — and what the rest of the table does about it — changes from game to game.

“I think it actually creates dynamic Commander games a lot of the time,” Verhey says. “You played Sol Ring on turn one. We all see that threat, right? We all know who the enemy is.”

For Sol Ring’s critics, the early advantage and ensuing dogpile are part of the problem. For Verhey, they can be part of the fun: an immediate complication that gives three other players something to respond to.

“Is it incredibly strong? Absolutely,” he says. “Is it necessarily the poster child I would have chosen if I was creating Commander from scratch? Probably not.”

But Commander already exists, and Sol Ring is deeply embedded in it. Verhey doesn’t foresee challenging that status “at any point.”

Still, it has at least been considered in the past. When the former Commander Rules Committee banned Mana Crypt, Jeweled Lotus, and Dockside Extortionist in September 2024, it explicitly acknowledged that Sol Ring met its criteria for a ban. The committee nevertheless made an exception because removing the card would fundamentally change the format’s identity.

There’s room to disagree about whether that distinction makes a turn-one Sol Ring an enjoyable gameplay experience. But preserving variety in Commander doesn’t mean eliminating every staple just because everybody uses it. For now, and probably forever, if you’re the type of person who’s going to show up at MagicCon with a “Ban Sol Ring” shirt, then you’re just going to have to ban it within your pod.

#3466. Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Edward Said: Between Worlds’ About Palestinian-American Author Lands at Kino Lorber

This year’s TIFF and Venice were quieter in terms of breakout sales, especially when compared to last year’s splash for “Obsession,” and several awards contenders were scooped up before they even premiered at the festival. But other smaller buyers have emerged in recent weeks to release some of the more critically acclaimed titles that didn’t land major sales ahead of time.

The festivals are long done, but we’re still tracking every sale that happens, so check back frequently.

Distributor: Kino LorberDirector: Maiken BairdFestival: TIFF DocsBuzz: This documentary about Palestinian-American author and intellectual Edward Said earned strong reaction in its premiere at TIFF and festivals like NYFF and IDFA, in part because though he’s been dead for over 20 years, his writing and his views have been far more relevant in a post-October 7 landscape. IndieWire’s review out of TIFF praised the construction of the documentary and how it manages to be decades-spanning and comprehensive in a manageable running time. And Anne Thompson spoke with the filmmakers about the challenges of making the documentary and the fear that it being about Palestine would pose barriers to a distributor stepping up to buy it. Thankfully, Kino Lorber did just that, and it will be planning a theatrical release for 2027. Distributor: Cohen Media GroupDirector: May el-ToukhyFestival: Venice CompetitionBuzz: Venice’s top prize winner of the Golden Lion has found a U.S. deal, this one made out of AFM with Cohen Media Group. Not only did el-Toukhy (“Queen of Hearts,” “The Crown”) movie win the Golden Lion this year, star Mathilde Arcel also won the Volpi Cup for Best Actress. The Danish film, also Denmark’s official Oscar selection, is a period drama set after World War II about a former housekeeper now set to be married to the household’s wealthy patriarch. But as she plans an extravagant dinner party to celebrate the occasion, hidden aspects of her past begin to resurface. Namely, it has to do with Danish witch hunts of those associated with Nazis after the war, and our positive review called it an “angry, despairing film” with a “Haneke-level bleakness in its assessment of human nature.” Cohen Media Group also recently bought an Isabelle Huppert comedy called “All About Corinne” that played at TIFF and premiered at Locarno.

Distributor: Sony Pictures ClassicsDirector: Niki ByrneFestival: TIFF Special PresentationsBuzz: Sony Pictures Classics have acquired all rights in the United States, Benelux, Switzerland, Italy, Scandinavia, Spain, United Kingdom, Eastern Europe (excluding Poland), Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Israel and Asia (excluding Singapore) to “The Julia Set,” written and directed by Niki Byrne. The film had its world premiere at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival and follows a gifted young math prodigy (“One Battle After Another” breakout Chase Infiniti) who is “recruited into an elite prep course culminating in the most punishing exam in mathematics, while at the same time falling into a romantic relationship with her charismatic teaching assistant, Pascal (Christopher Briney).”

Distributor: Strand ReleasingDirector: Hanaël El YousfiFestival: TIFF DiscoveryBuzz: This directorial debut follows two friends, one Muslim and one Jewish, spending a carefree summer in Marseille, only to see the expectations and tensions between their traditional families start to get in the way of their friendship and leads them to take hold of their own destinies. It had its international premiere at TIFF, but it actually had a small bow at a French festival called the Angoulême Francophone Film Festival, where it won an Audience Award and a Special Prize for its cast. “The Daughters of Abraham” first opens in France on December 30. But Strand, a Culver City-based distributor behind recent releases like Mexico’s Oscar submission “On the Road,” “In a Whisper,” and the 4K restoration of Gregg Araki’s “Mysterious Skin,” will release it in North America in 2027.

#3465. 10 Movies Like ‘Interstellar’ You Should Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Christopher Nolan’s 2014 megahit Interstellar has it all: big sci-fi ideas, cool robots, ugly crying, and a Matt Damon character in need of rescuing. Grounded in the intensity of the human experience, this story of humanity’s potential extinction and the sacrifice of one man to save it doesn’t just deliver exotic planets and thrilling spaceship maneuvers; it also provides all the feels as Joseph Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) sacrifices everything he has in an effort to save the entire human race. It’s one of the best science fiction films ever made, with Nolan’s signature complexity, time manipulations, and emotional wallop. If you love this movie, here are ten more that offer a similar viewing experience.

If you loved both the special effects in Interstellar that make space travel feel viscerally thrilling (and terrifying) and the mind-blowing concepts, this is the film for you. Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 epic (written by sci-fi master Arthur C. Clarke) traces humanity’s development from mildly smart apes to spacefaring capitalists who discover a mysterious obelisk on the Moon that sparks a mission to Jupiter. While it operates in a colder emotional key than Nolan’s film, 2001: A Space Odyssey absolutely delivers on the epic side of things (and the cool—if slightly deranged and deadly—artificial intelligences). Stream 2001: A Space Odyssey on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for more existential missions with somewhat reluctant heroes in space, Project Hail Mary is your next stop. When the Sun begins to dim due to the interference of an alien entity, scientists identify the one nearby star that isn’t being similarly affected. Brilliant molecular biologist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) winds up forced to go on what is assumed to be a fatal, one-way mission into deep space to try to find a way to save humanity, unexpectedly assisted by a charming alien he names Rocky. It’s got the same emotional volume and big ideas as Interstellar, and fans of Nolan’s film will love it. Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+ or Philo, or rent it on Prime Video.

Part of what makes Interstellar so compelling is the stakes: The human race is slowly dying, and a handful of people must make incredible sacrifices to save it. That’s the vibe of Sunshine, set in a future where the Sun is dimming and a spacecraft is dispatched to deliver an enormous bomb designed to reignite the Sun’s fusion cycle. But the mission is the second attempt after the first ship vanished mysteriously seven years earlier, and when the new crew stumbles on the derelict wreck of the first mission, things quickly descend into violence and madness—but the crew remains determined to save the world, no matter the cost. Rent Sunshine on Prime Video.

Interstellar works in large part because of the emotional dynamics at play. McConaughey’s character leaves his children behind and is forced to witness them growing up without him, missing out on their lives and saddled with the knowledge that they resent him despite the necessity of his mission. Arrival is a First Contact story focused on language—linguist Louise Banks (Amy Adams) is drafted into an effort to understand the strange, complex language of the aliens. As she slowly builds to an understanding of how the aliens communicate and perceive time itself, her own heartbreak and loss come into play, giving this film a similarly devastating emotional punch. Stream Arrival on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Family dynamics and the toll of lonely space missions fuel Ad Astra, a film with the same emotional core as Interstellar. Twenty-nine years ago, famed astronaut Clifford McBride (Tommy Lee Jones) led the Lima Project, a space station around Neptune searching for intelligent life. Thirteen years ago, Earth lost contact with him. When bursts of energy emanating from Neptune threaten to end life on Earth, his son, Roy (Brad Pitt), is dispatched to try to make contact with his father. It’s an epic journey with a powerful climax that will satisfy fans of Interstellar in every way. Stream Ad Astra on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

Ridley Scott’s prequel to Alien has its flaws, but if you’re looking for a sense of epic spacefaring adventure in the same key as Interstellar, it’s perfect. When two scientists discover a star map apparently left behind by ancient aliens, they secure funding from the Wayland Corporation to organize a space expedition to the indicated planet. Accompanied by a colorful crew and the android David, they discover an apparently abandoned outpost of the species dubbed the Engineers. The story wrestles with questions about humanity’s origins, purpose, and potential—but this being an Alien film, things quickly turn horrifying. Rent Prometheus on Prime Video.

Adapted from Carl Sagan’s 1985 novel, Contact follows astronomer Dr. Ellie Arroway (Jodie Foster), who becomes involved with an effort to decipher a signal originating from the star Vega. The signal turns out to be a set of instructions for constructing a one-person spacecraft of some kind, and Arroway is eventually selected as the candidate to take the journey. There’s a sense of courage in the face of the unknown that’s similar to Interstellar, as well as the thrill of strapping into a spaceship and pressing the ignition. Plus, there’s the added bonus of seeing one of the greatest trick shots in cinematic history. Rent Contact on Prime Video.

Stanislaw Lem’s 1961 novel Solaris explores what Lem saw as the impossibility of ever understanding a truly alien life. The two major adaptations—Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 version and Steven Soderbergh’s 2002 take starring George Clooney—are both worth watching, but Tarkovsky’s film is a masterpiece of psychological horror. The story is set mainly aboard a space station orbiting a planet covered in what appears to be a sentient "ocean" and chronicles the strange haunting and inexplicable experiences of the humans living on the station. If your favorite part of Interstellar is the ending when things get trippy and weird, you’ll probably love Solaris. Stream Solaris on HBO Max, Plex, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

The story of a mission to Jupiter’s moon Europa to search for intelligent life, Europa Report has the same sense of terrifying excitement that accompanies Interstellar’s missions to the different candidate planets. Leaning into the fragility of life in an environment not designed to support it, the mission crew face a steady stream of loss and danger as they work to catch sight of alien life on the frozen, deadly moon, ultimately faced with making terrifying sacrifices in order to provide humanity with the answers that it seeks. Stream Europa Report on Netflix, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

A film based on a 1956 epic science fiction poem written by a Swedish Nobel Laureate might seem like an unlikely match for fans of Interstellar, but it’s actually perfect. As the Earth becomes uninhabitable, humanity begins launching ships to colonize Mars. When one such ship, the Aniara, is damaged and veers irreversibly off course, the passengers and crew are faced with the knowledge that they will sail off into the void without hope of rescue. Within a few years, despair has driven some to suicide and madness, while others cling to the possibility that they might yet find a way back. The film offers a different perspective on the existential crisis of humanity’s extinction, exploring the worst-case scenario to its bitter, bleak end. Stream Aniara on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3464. Prime Video’s 10/10 Fantasy Series Officially Not Returning in 2026

Lade Omotade is a News and Features Author at Collider, covering everything from casting announcements and streaming trends to behind-the-scenes stories and the cultural impact of today's biggest film and TV franchises. Since joining the team in 2024, she has written more than 1,000 news stories, with her work also cited by outlets like AOL and IMDb.

Prime Video's most divisive fantasy release of the year arrived less than a week ago, and its four-episode premiere has already propelled the series to the top of the streaming charts. Set five years after Season 2, The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 explores the height of the war between the Elves and the Dark Lord Sauron. The season is set to run through November 25, making it Prime Video's final fantasy release of the year. As a result, no other original fantasy titles will debut on the streamer this year, including one of its most underrated.

Set in the fantasy universe of The Legend of Vox Machina, this series takes place about 20 years later, though you don't need to watch The Legend of Vox Machina to follow it. Titled The Mighty Nein, it centers on a completely different, independent group of outcasts and morally grey characters, adapted from Critical Role's second tabletop campaign. Now, one year after its memorable Season 1 finale, the animated series has finally gotten a Season 2 premiere date, giving fans plenty to look forward to as they return to Exandria.

Unfortunately, The Mighty Nein won't return this year. According to TV Insider, the award-winning series will officially return for its second season on March 24, 2027, with all eight new episodes dropping at once. The news was announced on November 15, 2026, during TwitchCon and a special actual-play one-shot titled The Rings of Power: A Middle-Earth One-Shot. The event featured Critical Role cast members Sam Riegel, Travis Willingham, and Liam O'Brien, along with Rings of Power cast members Maxim Baldry and Benjamin Walker. O'Brien, the one-shot's game master, announced the Season 2 release date.

The Mighty Nein Season 2 will bring fan-favorite characters exciting new adventures. One is a pirate adventure that takes the group across the high seas, where they continue to grapple with their pasts and relationships. The Beacon remains a threat, of course, and longtime Critters familiar with the original Mighty Nein tabletop campaign can expect appearances from new faces.

As fans recall, at the end of The Mighty Nein Season 1, audiences finally saw the misfit antiheroes together for the first time. This included tiefling Jester Lavorre (Laura Bailey), half-orc warlock Fjord Stone (Willingham), goblin Nott the Brave (Riegel), wizard Caleb (O'Brien), Cobalt Soul monk Beauregard Lionett (Marisha Ray), and tiefling bloodhunter Mollymauk Tealeaf (Taliesin Jaffe), all of whom met up with barbarian/mercenary Yasha Nydoorin (Ashley Johnson).

The Mighty Nein Season 2 premieres in March. Stream past episodes on Prime Video.

#3463. Why Clemenza Didn't Return For The Godfather Part II

The Godfather Part II continued the story of Michael Corleone (Al Pacino) after becoming the new Don of the Corleone family, and while most of the cast from the first movie returned, the character Peter Clemenza was notably absent. Played by Richard S. Castellano, Clemenza was one of Vito’s caporegimes and oldest and most trusted friends, who was instrumental in Michael cementing his power, and his absence was conspicuous.

In 1972, Francis Ford Coppola brought what’s now considered one of the greatest movies of all time and the best in the gangster genre: The Godfather. Based on Mario Puzo’s 1969 novel of the same name, and with a screenplay co-written by Puzo and Coppola, The Godfather was a massive critical and commercial success and made way for one of the greatest movie trilogies of all time.

The Godfather introduced viewers to the Corleone family in New York City, led by Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando). When Vito decided to hand over his empire to his youngest son, Michael, conflict with the rest of the city’s crime families was triggered, putting the lives of Vito’s loved ones in great danger, while Michael was pushed to take the lead despite staying out of the family business his whole life. The Godfather was followed by two sequels, and though most of the cast returned in The Godfather Part II, Castellano’s Clemenza didn’t come back.

Throughout The Godfather, Clemenza was tasked with getting rid of some of the Corleone family’s enemies, most notably Don Victor Stracci during the infamous “baptism killings” and he planted the gun for Michael to use to kill Sollozzo and McCluskey.

The Godfather Part II arrived just two years after The Godfather, and is obviously both a sequel and a prequel, picking up the story of Michael now as the new Don of the family while also going back in time to explore the origin story of Vito. The “present” timeline notably didn’t include Clemenza, which was strange given his strong connection to the Corleone family and his place as one of their most trusted capos.

Coppola said in a DVD documentary (via Mental Floss) that Castellano had declined to return as he wanted more money and dialogue approval. The latter demand came after he ad-libbed the now-famous “take the cannoli” line in the first movie at the urging of his wife, Ardell Sheridan. However, Castellano denied this in an interview in 1981 (via New York Post) and explained he didn’t return in The Godfather Part II as he disagreed with how Clemenza had been written.

According to Castellano, the original script had Clemenza testifying against the Corleone family, which he - quite rightly - claimed was completely off-character. Castellano added that the demands on him were “impossible” as he had settled on a price, and he was required to gain weight after losing 194 pounds to play young Clemenza. He also claimed Coppola promised to tell the press he had turned down the role for artistic reasons, but Coppola ended up saying something entirely different.

Despite Castellano not returning to play Clemenza in the present timeline in The Godfather Part II, Coppola found a way to give him closure and fill in that space. Bruno Kirby was cast as young Clemenza for the flashback scenes to Vito’s backstory, and in the present timeline, Clemenza was killed off-screen, with the betrayal of the Corleone family given to someone else. Fredo mentioned that Clemenza died of a heart attack, but Cicci implied he might have been murdered.

Ultimately, Clemenza was replaced by Frank Pentangeli (Michael V. Gazzo), who was given the storyline of testifying against the Corleone family. It was a smart move: seeing Clemenza betray the Corleone family would have felt like too much of a swerve, even if it also felt strange not seeing him in The Godfather Part II. Pentangeli was, instead, retroactively established as another long-term Corleone capo who had worked with Vito in his early career in the olive oil business.

Having been a key figure under Clemenza's leadership running the Corleone's family operations in New York, Pentangeli inherits the operation, kicking off an almost-immediate set of conflicts as he seeks to consolidate his position, but Michael refuses to allow him to take out his rivals, the Rosato brothers. Because of Michael's keenness to establish strong relations with Hyman Roth (Lee Strasberg), who is aligned with the Rosatos, he refuses, and Pentangeli is incensed by the insult.

Pentangeli quickly becomes the heart of the story as the walls close in on Michael and the Senate hearing investigating organized crime and allegations of his crimes threaten to crumble his empire. Gazzo's performance is great, and earned him a Best Supporting Actor nomination at the Oscars - which he ultimately lost to Robert De Niro for the same movie, understandably. Any other year, he would have had a strong chance of winning.

Even with the Rosato brothers and Roth pulling the strings, it would never have worked for Clemenza to be the one to betray the Corleones: it had to be someone like Pentangeli, who inherited his power, and like Michael, immediately faced a challenge. Those underworld politics were a great foundation for the entire subplot, which ultimately saw Michael using Frank's brother Vincenzo to intimidate him into recanting his Senate statement in fear. It's at this point that Gazzo really earns his plaudits, and his arc subtly reflecting Michael's own precarious position in the first movie only works because of how well he sells it all.

Ultimately, Robert Duvall's Tom Hagen using Frank's knowledge of Roman history and how traitors' families would be spared if they killed themselves is a brilliant, chilling end to his story, and shows both the dark morality of this world and the complex parallel with Ancient Rome. There's also an incredibly compelling mystery left unanswered, which was only explained in the original script: Frank's children were under Vincenzo's protection in Sicily, and his brother turning up was supposed to be a reminder not to betray his blood oath and the Mafia's code of silence, or retribution would be taken on his kids.

It's an unfortunate cut, but the fact that Gazzo's performance so thoroughly convinces of the threat without it ever having to be spelled out is the final testimony to how great he was as Clemenza's replacement. Ultimately, Castellano's unwillingness to sign on for the sequel may have led to the loss of a great character, but it worked out better for The Godfather Part II.

The Godfather Part II is a continuation of the Corleone crime family saga. The film explores Vito Corleone's early life in Sicily and 1910s New York, while Michael Corleone navigates the 1950s, seeking to expand the family's influence into Las Vegas, Hollywood, and Cuba.

#3462. Robert Pattinson as James Bond Proves That IP Is No Longer the New Movie Stars

Every James Bond casting announcement marks the start of a new era. The fictional MI6 agent has been one of pop culture’s few constants over the past seven decades; and each time a new actor steps into the role, it tells us something about the entertainment landscape we currently inhabit. Bonds can be intensely serious or silly and self-deprecating, and actors have entered the franchise at ages ranging from their late twenties to mid-forties. The role always goes to a member of the Commonwealth, but the variation that’s possible within those parameters has turned the franchise into a vertical wine tasting that illustrates what male movie stardom looks like in each decade. Related Stories Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Edward Said: Between Worlds’ About Palestinian-American Author Lands at Kino Lorber The Stop-Motion Tool That’s a Constant in This Crazy, AI-Mixed-Up World

The first Bond of the Amazon MGM era was destined to be even more of a turning point than usual, no matter who landed the role. The next film in the franchise will be the first one ever produced without the involvement of the Broccoli family, who have carefully guarded each iteration of the character since “Dr. No” came out in 1962. It marks the biggest movie investment that Amazon has ever made, as the tech giant spent nearly $10 billion to acquire MGM (of which Bond was the clear crown jewel) and then wrestle full control away from the Broccolis.

With Denis Villeneuve at the helm, it arguably marks the first time that Bond has been rebooted by a true auteur director with a distinct preexisting style and fan base. And it follows a Daniel Craig era that many feel took the idea of a dark, realistic James Bond to its logical endpoint with no obvious direction to go next.

When Robert Pattinson was officially announced as the seventh actor to play 007 on Monday morning, the latest era of the Bond franchise officially took shape. But it also marked the end of a larger Hollywood era in which blue chip legacy characters were seen as infinitely more important than the people playing them. We spent much of the past decade declaring that intellectual property is the new movie star(s). But casting the current Batman actor as James Bond proves that is no longer the case.

That line of thinking began to take shape in the 2010s, an era of Hollywood that will forever be defined by the phrase “cinematic universe.” As moviegoing became less of a consistent consumer habit and more of an event-driven hobby, the industry found that putting an A-list movie star or two in a new film was no longer enough to guarantee a big opening weekend. What did work, though, was slapping a Marvel logo in front of something and watching the box office dollars flow in.

Top-tier franchises were places where you went to build your star power, not cash it in. A new Bond or Spider-Man announcement was often the mainstream world’s introduction to a rising star that would be a household name within a few years. The approach was certainly better for the producers who steward these franchises: it ensured that the real value was contained in the stories and iconography that they controlled, making it relatively easy to bring in massive box office hauls with interchangeable actors who often moved onto bigger things before they became too expensive or demanding.

As that formula becomes less workable, it’s fair to wonder where we’ll start going to find our new stars. If you were casting a new Spider-Man in this environment, you probably wouldn’t pick an obscure theater actor like Tom Holland. We’re already seeing more stars come out of independent genre films, one of the few niches that can still be profitable without star power. “Obsession” gave the world its biggest breakout star of 2026 in Inde Navarette, and now she’s heading to the Marvel Cinematic Universe to help lead the “X-Men” franchise. But legacy franchises were once Hollywood’s most reliable path to minting new stars, and the industry will have to get creative if it doesn’t want the pipeline of bankable stars to fizzle out.

From an artistic standpoint, there’s every reason to believe Pattinson will make an excellent Bond. He has already worked with Villeneuve on the upcoming “Dune: Part Three” and has proven himself to be one of his generation’s most versatile leading men. He’s equally capable of playing brooding heroes and sniveling villains; a 2026 slate that includes “The Drama,” “The Odyssey,” and “Primetime” is evidence of both his range and consistent box office appeal. But from a business standpoint, it’s a decision that you wouldn’t make if you didn’t have to.

His deal reportedly costs more money for less commitment than any of the other finalists who screen tested. You’ll be juggling a production and promotion schedule that also includes “The Batman” franchise and other major films. In the run-up to the movie, more eyes will be on the man himself than the timelessness of the brand. And when the time eventually comes to replace him, expectations for the level of actor you need to land will be higher than ever before. It’s the kind of move you make when you simply cannot afford to fail. Nobody would deny that that’s the exact situation Amazon MGM finds itself in, but the mere fact that something as reliable as a new James Bond movie could place a studio in such a position is notable in and of itself.

It would be reductive to say that the pendulum has entirely swung back towards favoring movie stars. The old model where you could regularly deliver hits by putting George Clooney and Julia Roberts on a poster is certainly nowhere to be found. It might be more accurate to say that we’re in a “more is more” era of Hollywood, where no film is ever guaranteed to become the kind of cultural event that’s required to turn a profit on these massive tentpole budgets. With more competition for audience attention spans than ever before, you need to pair the power of Bond and the power of Pattinson and Villeneuve to feel truly comfortable with your investment.

#3461. Marvel Boss Officially Reveals Why Avengers Switched from Kang to Doctor Doom

Avengers: Doomsday is a month away and will find the Avengers, the New Avengers, and X-Men from the Fox films facing off against Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom. Originally, the fifth Avengers film was titled The Kang Dynasty and would have starred Jonathan Majors as Kang, who appeared in Loki and Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania. Marvel fired him in December 2023 after he was convicted on assault and harassment charges, and retooled The Kang Dynasty into the Doctor Doom-centric Doomsday.

However, according to Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige, the Marvel Cinematic Universe always would have pivoted to Doom replacing Kang as the next Avengers-level threat, regardless of Majors' legal issues and firing.

Speaking with Empire Magazine, Feige revealed the plan to pivot away from Kang began around the release of the third Ant-Man film in early 2023. "Quantumania was not received the way we would have liked," Feige said (via IGN). "There are many elements of that that we're proud of, the Kang performance being one of them. But we were changing [The Kang Dynasty] even at that point. It would still have been called The Kang Dynasty, but it would have been a set-up for Doom, midway through that movie."

Majors' Kang the Conqueror variant was the villain of Quantumania after Kang first appeared as He Who Remains in Loki season 1. Much like how Josh Brolin's Thanos appeared throughout the MCU before going toe-to-toe with the Avengers in Avengers: Infinity War and Endgame, Kang was being established as an overarching antagonist before The Kang Dynasty. In contrast to them, Doom has been haphazardly established in the MCU via post-credits scenes in 2025's The Fantastic Four: First Steps and the recent re-release of Endgame. Setting up Doom in a film titled The Kang Dynasty would have been a bold move.

From the public's point of view, it certainly seemed like Marvel retooled the Avengers films in response to Majors' convictions. However, according to Feige, that wasn't exactly the case. "We didn't want to rush into any rash decisions in terms of employment. People think there was a cause-and-effect with Jonathan's issues, and that certainly accelerated some things. But the Doom of it all was well underway before that."

Marvel is known for deception and trickery, so you're well within your rights to doubt Feige's comments here. However, as next year's Avengers: Secret Wars hasn't had a title change, it makes sense that the plan all along was for Doctor Doom to supersede Kang as the main villain. After all, Secret Wars shares its name with Jonathan Hickman and Esad Ribić's 2010s comic series of the same name. That event featured Doom as God Emperor reigning over a realm patched together from fragments of various Marvel universes and continuities. As Doomsday is all about universes colliding and resulting in Incursions, it seems very likely 2027's Secret Wars film will adapt the comic of the same name.

You won't have to wait long to see Doom, the Avengers, and more on the big screen. Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters on Dec. 18.

#3460. The Apple Watch's New 'Siri Recap' Feature Is Even Creepier Than I Expected

The “Siri Recap” feature that Apple announced in September is finally available in a developer beta, and I’ve spent the last 24 hours with the feature turned on. It’s even more unsettling than the “Live Rewind” feature that launched at the same time. It listens to all my conversations, and produces summaries that are both helpful and deeply creepy.

I have a button in the watch’s Control Center that can turn the recapping abilities off, but if I forget to do so, Siri listens to everything. I’ll get a recap of my entire evening, presented in roughly hour-long chunks, including things I would have completely forgotten I had even heard about.

The recaps somberly mention silly memes my kids were laughing about, and make major bullet points out of offhand remarks from brief conversations. If a conversation sticks to a single topic, I’ll often get a reasonably good summary of it, with specific facts and numbers highlighted; but just as often, Siri will get confused and mix up several topics or completely mishear a name or phrase.

Apple has four features that it considers part of “audio intelligence":

Music recognition, better known as Shazam. We’ve had a version of this on the Apple Watch for a long time now, although it has some improvements and now identifies music automatically.

Sound recognition, which can notify you about doorbells and babies crying. A version of this launched in 2020 as an accessibility feature.

Live Rewind, which gives you an on-wrist transcript of the last 15 seconds of detected speech.

Siri Recaps, which summarizes entire conversations for you to read on your phone.

Live Rewind had the flashiest demo from the Apple event: A server rattled off the day’s specials at a restaurant, and then the Apple Watch-wearing diner checked his watch to see a readout of exactly which dishes had just been mentioned. The utility is both obvious and kind of unnecessary: Why wouldn’t you just ask the server to repeat the list while they’re standing right there?

I haven’t found myself using Live Rewind, except out of curiosity about how the feature works. I discovered that it doesn’t pick up song lyrics very well, and also that by the time I think to check what was just said in a conversation, more than 15 seconds has passed since the part I was unsure about. I haven’t yet found a reason to use it for real.

But Siri Recaps? Those are both useful and unsettling. I enabled the feature, and decided to test it out later. But since it was on, it dutifully listened in as I picked up my son from school and gave him an update on an ailing family member’s health. We stopped by the library, and along the way we chatted about a variety of things: holiday travel plans, library policies, and the possibility of humans living in space in the future. Siri was listening to it all.

At least for now, the feature is only available in a developer beta, so sign up for that now if you want to try it. You'll need an Apple Watch Series 12 (or Ultra 4) and an iPhone 16 or better, excluding the 16e. (I have a 16 Pro, so I'm good.)

After you're updated to 27.3, go into the Watch app, tap Siri, and turn on Siri Recap. You can set a schedule for when it should listen (for example, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., if you want it on for the work day but off for the evening). You'll need to set a passcode on your watch, and you'll be guided through a step to upgrade your audio connection. The control center on the watch will have a button you can use to turn Siri recaps on and off at will. To read your recaps, go to the Siri app on your phone.

But still: I feel weird publishing the contents of these recaps, because they do contain things that people said to me in what they assumed was a private setting. I had the feature on when I attended a choir practice, and Siri recapped the brief chats I had with other choir members before and after practice. (Interestingly, it did not recap any of the quiet conversations I had with fellow sopranos while the tenors were rehearsing their part. I’m not sure if the watch was unable to hear us over the music, or if Siri is programmed not to listen when music is being played.)

Because speakers aren’t identified, it seems Siri doesn’t know what to do when there is a disagreement. A human note-taker would jot down that Person A made a point in favor of something, and person B made a point against. But when my son and I disagreed about how likely space colonization might be in the future, the recap didn’t reflect the separate positions that were put forth. It summarized the conversation as including “debating the feasibility and timeline of human space colonization and asteroid mining,” which isn’t exactly accurate, but close enough.

When it comes to the content of the discussion, the recap notes a bullet point of “skepticism regarding permanent space colonies within the next 100 years.” It didn’t include my reasons for being skeptical, and didn’t mention my son’s opposing viewpoint at all. If I were using this recap to jog my memory of the conversation, it wouldn’t be all that helpful.

Details are sometimes egregiously incorrect. After a discussion about a family member’s health, the recap had notes on the prognosis of “father.” The family member we discussed is not anybody’s father. Names in general seem to be a problem; I recommended a book to my son, and the recap includes notes about the content of the book, but not its title. The book’s author appears in the introduction to the recap (sort of a summary of a summary), but not in the content of the recap itself where the book is mentioned.

I should probably turn Siri recaps off. It seems wrong to let people chat with me without letting them know that their conversation is being ... well, not technically recorded, but basically recorded.

But it’s so tempting to leave it on so that I can review my day. Some of the details in the recaps are useful, like the dates that were discussed as options for a holiday party. The recaps will be deleted in about a week (unless I save them to the notes app), so if I want to remind myself of a conversation a few days ago, I should be able to scroll back through my recaps and find it.

I would be a fool to rely on the recaps, though. The most important points of a conversation are often left out; Siri doesn’t know what’s actually important, and there’s no way to guide it as to what to pay attention to. Specific details can be wrong, as I mentioned. There’s also no way to control when a “conversation” starts or stops, unless you are turning the recap feature on and off from the watch.

And there’s more: Not only are names usually omitted (wait, who did she say I should ask about that project?), the few identifiers that make it into the recap, like names of events, are often wrong. Subjects of discussion are often conflated in really unhelpful ways: My husband mentioned paying for certain course registrations for one of our children, and later I talked to that child about an unrelated exam. The recap got all of these things mixed up with each other and was wrong about pretty much every detail. About all the recap could usefully do is to remind me that something about AP U.S. History was discussed. Reading the recaps can be like reliving your day entirely in the passive voice.
