#3459. Cary Grant, Clint Eastwood, and Christian Bale: The Stars Who Almost Played James Bond

When director Denis Villeneuve selected Robert Pattinson to play secret agent 007 in the next James Bond movie, he broke with tradition by casting an undeniable movie star in the role. Earlier Bonds were either relatively unknown (Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Daniel Craig, Timothy Dalton) or big names in television who hadn’t yet proven themselves on the big screen (Roger Moore, Pierce Brosnan). Yet Villeneuve and producers David Heyman and Amy Pascal’s choice of Pattinson isn’t completely at odds with the franchise’s history. At several points in the last 64 years, some of the box office’s biggest draws have flirted with the role and either turned it down or been rejected by the filmmakers. Related Stories Robert Pattinson as James Bond Proves That IP Is No Longer the New Movie Stars Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Edward Said: Between Worlds’ About Palestinian-American Author Lands at Kino Lorber

Right from the beginning, Bond producers were torn between going after a bankable name and letting the character be the star. Cary Grant was one of the world’s most famous actors when producers Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and Harry Saltzman began pre-production on “Dr. No,” the first feature film to showcase James Bond. (The character had previously been played by “The Shining” hotel manager Barry Nelson in a 1954 TV adaptation of “Casino Royale.”) He was also a close friend of Broccoli’s — so close, in fact, that he was best man at the Broccoli’s wedding.

Alas, that personal relationship wasn’t enough to get Grant to play Bond as Broccoli wanted. Grant was already starting to wind down his career and wanted to leave the public with their impression of him as a dashing young man. By 1966, he was done, so signing a multi-picture contract to star as Bond in 1962 didn’t appeal to the soon-to-be retired actor. Broccoli and Saltzman’s requirement that their Bond sign a long-term contract was also an obstacle for two other famous actors they approached. Both James Mason and Peter Lawford bristled at the idea of being committed to Bond for three or more films.

Rex Harrison and David Niven both wanted the part but were turned down in favor of Sean Connery, whose most prominent role to date was in the Disney movie “Darby O’Gill and the Little People.” “Dr. No” and its sequels made Connery a star, and for many viewers he remains the definitive Bond. By the time the sixth 007 movie, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” rolled around in 1969, however, Connery was tired of the role and stepped away — launching the first major search for a new James Bond.

Given that Connery wasn’t a household name when he made Bond an international icon in “Dr. No,” Broccoli and Saltzman were less inclined to go after a major movie star than they had been during the James Mason and Cary Grant discussions; most of the people seriously considered for “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” weren’t particularly popular at the time, and are even less well known now. (Few modern movie buffs would be able to pick John Richardson or Anthony Rogers out of a lineup, though the more famous Terence Stamp did meet with Broccoli about the role.)

The most popular actor Broccoli and Saltzman pursued was “Batman” star Adam West, who turned the part down because he felt 007 should be British — a response that would be repeated by other actors the next time a new Bond was needed, which turned out to be a lot sooner than Broccoli or Saltzman would have liked. Male model George Lazenby had almost zero acting experience when he secured the coveted role, but he took his good fortune for granted. In one of the great cinematic miscalculations in history, he assumed James Bond’s days were numbered in the age of “Easy Rider,” and declined to return for more 007 adventures.

Back at square one, Broccoli and Saltman decided to reverse course and once again go after big movie stars, including American ones. They offered “Diamonds Are Forever” to Clint Eastwood, who, like West, turned down the role because he felt Bond should be British. He would, however, direct and star in his own Bond-esque spy adventure, “The Eiger Sanction,” a few years later. Burt Reynolds, as famous for the hits he turned down (“Die Hard,” “Pretty Woman”) as for the ones he made, turned down Bond for the same reason.

John Gavin, best known today for his roles in Alfred Hitchcock’s “Psycho” and Douglas Sirk’s “Imitation of Life,” had no such reservations about playing Bond, and was the first American cast in the role. Unfortunately for him, Connery had second thoughts and decided to come back one last time, so Gavin was out, and Connery was in for “Diamonds Are Forever.” Gavin was briefly considered again for the eighth Bond picture, “Live and Let Die,” but by then the producers decided 007 should, in fact, be British and went with television star Roger Moore.

Moore had actually been offered “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” but had to turn it down due to an episodic series commitment. He became one of the longest-running Bonds, starring in seven 007 movies between 1973 and 1985. However, he began grumbling about leaving the series as early as 1979, leading the filmmakers to open discussions with Timothy Dalton (who turned down the role in “For Your Eyes Only” before committing to the series with 1987’s “The Living Daylights”) and James Brolin, whose bags were packed to play what would have been (again) the first American Bond in “Octopussy” when Moore had a change of heart.

The tradition of actors who either turned down or missed out on Bond in earlier films coming back to play the character was a sturdy one: just as Moore and Dalton would play the character in multiple films after initial false starts, Pierce Brosnan lost out on “The Living Daylights” due to a scheduling conflict (with his series “Remington Steele”) before replacing Dalton in 1995’s “GoldenEye.” Before the producers committed to Dalton in “Living Daylights,” a wide range of actors were considered and approached. Brosnan was the frontrunner, but Sam Neill came close, and the studio wanted Mel Gibson, but Broccoli overruled it, once again wanting a Brit (never mind the near-casting of James Brolin).

Although Brosnan was perhaps inevitable as Dalton’s replacement given the producers’ thwarted desire to have him in the 1980s, Hugh Grant, Sean Bean, and Liam Neeson were all considered for “GoldenEye.” Neeson turned the part down, later admitting that his girlfriend (and eventual wife) Natasha Richardson didn’t want him to play it. The producers wanted Bean but were overruled by MGM. Luckily for the actor, he made a strong enough impression to score a role as the picture’s villain.

Brosnan would play Bond four times, from “GoldenEye” through 2002’s “Die Another Day.” After that, the producers decided to make a change (reportedly because Brosnan’s salary demands were getting too high) and reboot the franchise with “Casino Royale.” Several now noteworthy actors were considered before Daniel Craig snared the part and became (after a brief initial flurry of internet outrage) the franchise’s most beloved Bond since Connery; Clive Owen, Sam Worthington, and Matthew Rhys were all in the running, and Henry Cavill was high on director Martin Campbell’s list.

Most intriguingly, Christian Bale turned down the part, which producer Barbara Broccoli said was his for the asking after she saw his stunning turn in Mary Harron’s “American Psycho.” Bale, amusingly, said he didn’t want to play Bond since he had already just played “a serial killer.” He also, according to the book “Christian Bale: The Inside Story of the Darkest Batman,” felt the role played into “despicable” stereotypes. Bale’s loss was Craig’s gain, as he led the Bond franchise into one of its most artistically and commercially successful periods — leaving Robert Pattinson with sizable shoes to fill.

#3458. 10 Hacks Every Reddit User Should Know

If you're looking for discussions, recommendations, or advice online, it's hard to avoid Reddit. From mainstream sports to niche crafts, it does seem that there's some kind of Reddit community for everyone. (And if there's not one, you can make one yourself.) If you're using Reddit, here are 10 hacks you should know about to improve your experience on the site.

Reddit used to let everyone view your post and comment history, but in recent years, you can make your profile private. You can hide your posts, comments, and the subreddits you're a part of. If you want to do this, click your profile icon once you've logged in to Reddit, and go to Settings > Profile. Alternatively, you can follow the direct link to Reddit's profile settings page. Click the drop-down menu next to Content & Activity, and select Hide all. You should also turn off Online Status on the same page to stop people from seeing when you're using Reddit.

Old Reddit lets you use the site's classic design, and I prefer it to the more modern UI. Old Reddit looks dated, but it doesn't have infinite scrolling, distracting animations, and a bunch of features designed to increase the time you spend on the platform. It's no wonder that Reddit is making it harder to access this version of the site. As long as it's around, you should switch to Old Reddit for a cleaner reading experience. You can do that by going to Reddit Settings > Preferences and enabling Default to Old Reddit. You can also visit old.reddit.com, though you'll need to sign in for access

Many subreddits use custom themes that range from beautiful to borderline unusable. If you want a more consistent UI across the site, you should disable these custom subreddit styles. Go to Reddit Settings > Preferences and turn off Use community themes. If you're using Old Reddit, click the preferences button in the top-right corner, and under "display options," disable allow subreddits to show me custom themes.

A multireddit is a feed that shows posts from a customized group of subreddits. You can think of it as a way to break out of Reddit's algorithms, and create your own Reddit feed. I use multireddits to follow all sports-related subs I'm interested in. I even have one for gaming, and one for fountain pens. It's a great way to create interest-specific feeds, and if you make them private, no one else can see them. To create one, click the Create custom feed button in the left pane in new Reddit. In the Old Reddit design, click the Create button in the left pane. Be sure to select the Private button to keep it from showing up for others. You can add as many subreddits as you like to the list, and bookmark the feed to access it whenever you wish to.

Reddit has recently adopted an Instagram-like experience for its feeds. It removed the ability to sort posts by new, controversial, best, etc., and instead offers "For You" and "Following." If you dislike this change, you can bypass it. I use Reddit on mobile Safari, and I recommend an extension called Sink It for Reddit. It can automatically redirect you to Old Reddit, and there's a feature that optimizes it for mobile, which brings back the old sorting options. You can also use third-party apps such as RedReader for Android, or RDX for Reddit on an iPhone or iPad to restore the old sorting options for Reddit posts.

After all these years, Reddit's built-in search still leaves something to be desired—at least, on the surface. To find posts on Reddit faster, use search filters on the site. For instance, adding "title:" to your search will limit the results to post titles, and boolean operators such as AND, OR, and NOT also work for advanced searches on the site.

#3457. ‘Minotaur’ Review: Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Riveting Comeback Remakes Claude Chabrol and ‘Unfaithful’ for a Hopeless Wartime Russia

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 19, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release the film in theaters Friday, November 20.]

Andrey Zvyagintsev nearly died and then came back to life in 2021 amid COVID complications, but unlike another Cannes filmmaker who resurrected from near-death only to make bad art, the Russian auteur’s riveting comeback “Minotaur” is not only a return to form — it’s also exactly the kind of hopeless, coldly gazing, and politically indicting film only the director of “Leviathan” and “Loveless” could ever make.

Based on Claude Chabrol’s 1969 erotic thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” which itself inspired Adrian Lyne’s deliciously lurid adaptation “Unfaithful” with Diane Lane in 2022, “Minotaur” follows a feckless, selfish man down a dark rabbit hole of his own digging amid the news that his wife is having an affair. We’ve seen this story before, and we know where it’s going. But Zvyagintsev, with a camera as still and gimlet-eyed as the Sphinx except when it’s gliding through the saddest rooms in the world like a seeking serpent, delivers an outcome and a movie more hopeless and on-brand than you could’ve dreamed of. His screenplay, co-written by Simon Lyashenko, is as tight as a drum, or as a rug you wrap up a dead body inside. Related Stories Cary Grant, Clint Eastwood, and Christian Bale: The Stars Who Almost Played James Bond Robert Pattinson as James Bond Proves That IP Is No Longer the New Movie Stars

Even without knowing the plot of Chabrol’s or Lyne’s film, you know everybody is doomed to their own resigned lot in life when you’re in a Zvyagintsev picture, the same director who tore an already estranged couple apart with the disappearance of their son in “Loveless,” only for the boy never to be found because, well, that’s life under Mother Russia.

But in the Russia of “Minotaur,” which was actually shot in Latvia because the days of shooting politically trenchant material in Russia are done, Gleb Morozov (Dmitriy Mazurov) is the CEO of a shipping company. He lives in a Russian suburb, ensconced from life’s daily horrors, in a modernist home made of glass, steel, fine wood, and concrete. It’s autumn 2022, and Russia is mobilizing into Ukraine, with the town’s mayor mandating that Gleb assemble a list of his employees to be drafted into service. Videos of bombings, meanwhile, are entering people’s social media feeds.

Life at home for his wife Galina (Iris Lebedeva) is an empty chain of days; she’s an unemployed housewife whose existence revolves around getting their son Seriosha (Boris Kudrin) to school on time. A woman for whom getting the right presents and ordering the right food for his birthday party is a full-time job to fill the vacant space of a day. But as “Minotaur” quite quickly reveals, she’s having an affair with a 33-year-old photographer, Anton (Yuriy Zavalnyouk), whom she visits almost daily under the guise of yet another appointment. It’s something to live for, a thrilling escape from a miserable life of staring into the void, waiting for her husband and son to come home.

Lebedeva, who is astonishing here, feels less like a doomed Chabrol heroine than someone cut out of Antonioni. A forcefield of ennui with an elegant trenchcoat around her, and with the furtive glee that comes with having a secret, she makes her way a few times a week down the road to her assignations with a younger, virile artist in the sort of apartment where a woman as beautiful and rich as this would ordinarily never deign to be.

It’s no secret to the audience that Gleb, who has a history of infidelity and jealousy, is going to find out what she’s up to, nor is it a shock how he reacts. It’s mildly frustrating that Zvyagintsev, for his first film in nine years and after a brush with death, chose material that is very much familiar to his already savvy cinephile audience.

But the thrill of “Minotaur” is in how the filmmaker repositions the inevitable violence wrought from being cuckolded, the stuff we recognize from classic noir movies, into the political context of life in Russia amid its invasion into Ukraine. Imagine a Hitchcock thriller situated in the saddest, crummiest, most totalitarian corners of our times — and with an unfliching camera that offers no reassurance — and you’ll have some idea of just how bleak this unfeeling movie can get.

Mikhail Krichman, cinematographer on all Zvyagintsev’s films, returns on “Minotaur” with a glacial, widescreen gaze that encourages the viewer to examine everything around them. There’s a hypnotizing 360-shot that starts with Galina and Anton day-drinking and then getting into bed, with composers Evgueni and Sacha Galperine’s worrying score pressing upon them, only to come back to the pair in an unchanged, postcoital position. But they can’t stop what’s coming to them, which is nothing good.

Zvyagintsev loves a red herring almost as much as a cosmically depressing visual joke, like the tiny picture of Putin hanging over a boardroom. Or the detectives who eventually show up at Gleb and Galina’s house, only to later look at some serious hard evidence that could solve their wild goose case and instead think, eh, let’s just go to lunch. Or this film’s last shot, which does not leave the viewer in an easy state of mind despite the comforting falsities that its characters embrace as they float above it all.

Zvyagintsev’s latest film, like all of his others from the fraught father-son journey of “The Return” to the slinking, snaky noir of “Elena,” is devoid of easy resolution, least of all hope. It may feel too familiar to those who have followed this filmmaker’s work closely, but “Minotaur” is capable of crushing you with its final suite of images that refuse to let you forget that the world we are living in is hell.

The actors are exquisite, transcending whatever allegorical mouthpieces you might read into them as, like when Lebedeva’s Galina, absolutely wasted after not hearing back from Anton for at least 24 hours and then drinking an entire bottle of wine at a bar, berates her son and husband for ordering the same old shit for dinner every night when she’s not cooking. Margherita pizza, margherita pizza. “Where is me?” she yells at the husband she feels nothing for. The husband who has been instructing their son how to bash in the faces of bullies who come at him at school.

“Minotaur” isn’t the best movie of Zvyagintsev’s career, but the icily exacting power of his filmmaking is undeniable — and it sucks you in like a vortex. Rarely are you so glued to a tale you’ve heard so many times before. Andrey Zvyagintsev, welcome back. We missed, and we need you.

“Minotaur” premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release the film later this year.

#3456. Macaulay Culkin Officially Revives Home Alone With New Sequel

Macaulay Culkin officially revives Home Alone.

Culkin stars in a new sequel to the classic film that comes from one of the most unlikely of places. Culkin's best roles involve a number of TV shows and movies across the board, especially as his career has seen a resurgence in recent years. But his role as Kevin McCallister in the first two Home Alone movies will forever remain a classic part of both his career and cinema history. He's even reprised his role across various ad campaigns, lending his talent to nostalgic approaches to the movie and its cinematic importance.

Now, Collider has confirmed Culkin is back as Kevin McCallister for a McDonald's holiday campaign, advertising a limited-time Home Alone meal. The meal, which arrives in the US on December 1, 2026, consists of either a Sausage, Egg & Cheese McGriddles for breakfast, or a Big Mac for the rest of the day. It comes with movie-inspired Little Nero's Pizza McShaker Fries and a Lovely Cheese Pizza Dipping Sauce, useable for both fries and a customer choice of McNuggets or McCrispy Strips.

In addition to the food, each meal also comes with a collectible sock featuring McDonald's characters pulling inspiration from the Home Alone movies. There's also the Everything Sundae McFlurry, a separate dessert item that comes equipped with Oreos, M&M's, and hot fudge.

As for Culkin's role, he stars as Kevin in an ad wherein he's a McDonald's employee manning an empty restaurant during a snowstorm. The advertisement shows off the food, which he makes for himself in a comedic montage. Check out the full advertisement featuring his return as Kevin below:

In addition to the Home Alone-inspired food and collectible socks, customers in Los Angeles can sign up to participate in the Home Alone challenge pop-up on December 4 and 5, happening from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. PT. The free, first-come, first-serve event requires online registration, with reservations limited to groups of eight people or less. It's an additional element to the food-centered campaign, and one that puts the movie first with plenty of promising surprises.

The Home Alone meal is the second time Culkin has returned as McCallister for an advertisement role. His latest rendition was in a 2018 Google Assistant commercial, where he utilized the technology for a more modern take on the movie. According to the report, Culkin was drawn by the idea of associating McDonald's "comfort food" with the movie, having "no notes" about the meal when it was presented to him.

With the meal only two weeks away, it won't be long until the taste of Little Nero's in fry form, coupled with a cheese pizza sauce, all arrive at McDonald's. The breakfast option coupled with the regular lunch and dinner menu means there will be plenty for customer to enjoy, while the socks add a fun collectible item to the mix. The commercial makes for a fun reprisal of Culkin's Home Alone role, while adding the comfortable mix of McDonald's food to a nostalgic blast from the past.

#3455. Macaulay Culkin Officially Returns as ‘Home Alone’s Kevin McCallister

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Macaulay Culkin gets recognized ten times more between November and January, by his own estimate, something he refers to as having “cornered the fourth quarter market.” Kevin McCallister spent Home Alone trying to get everybody to leave him alone, and now the holidays are when people are most likely to stop Culkin in the street.

Culkin sees it at holiday screenings, too. Adults who grew up watching Kevin take on the Wet Bandits are now bringing kids who have no idea what’s about to happen when Harry grabs that doorknob. Culkin has seen that handoff in his own living room, too. In a new interview with Collider's Hannah Hunt, he expressed that the movie has “taken on its own life,” which goes a long way toward explaining why he’s still game to play Kevin 36 years later.

Macaulay Culkin is officially back as Kevin McCallister for McDonald’s new holiday campaign. The limited-time Home Alone Meal starts rolling out internationally on November 24 and hits participating U.S. restaurants on December 1, while supplies last. Each U.S. meal comes with one of four collectible sock designs inspired by the movie, and the menu runs from a Sausage, Egg & Cheese McGriddles at breakfast to a Big Mac at lunch or dinner.

Little Nero’s may still be the only place Kevin can order a lovely cheese pizza, but McDonald’s is putting that flavor on its fries. The lunch and dinner meals come with Little Nero’s Pizza McShaker Fries, and there’s a Lovely Cheese Pizza Dipping Sauce you can get with McNuggets or McCrispy Strips. The Everything Sundae McFlurry is sold separately and comes with hot fudge, Oreo pieces, and M&M’s. Check out the lineup below. Fans in Los Angeles can also register for the Home Alone Challenge, a pop-up running December 4 and 5 from 5 to 10 p.m. PT. There’s a ball pit, a slingshot challenge, and a free Home Alone Meal for fans who complete the experience.

Culkin’s first thought about bringing Kevin back for McDonald’s was that “it’s about time.” He put the movie and the menu in the same category. You know what the McNuggets are going to taste like, just as you know exactly what’s going to happen when Marv takes his shoes off. You order them and put the movie on anyway. “The actual food and the movie are comfort food, really,” Culkin said. His wife, Brenda Song, was excited about the collaboration, too. “Brenda thinks it’s really cool,” he said. “And that’s really what matters most.”

Culkin had “no notes” when he saw the meal, and he decided to unbox the collectible socks right there on the call. He gave Grimace his due as “the most famous McDonald’s character of all” before holding up a pair with his own face on them. “If you ever wanted to walk on my face,” he joked, “you can just go to McDonald’s, go get yourself some socks.”

As for what Kevin would be like as a grown-up, Culkin figures he’d still get a kick out of “defying authority," which is part of why the movie works so well on kids in the first place. They spend all day being told what they can and can’t do, and here’s somebody their size who gets to tell two grown men exactly where they can step. Culkin thinks the fantasy holds up when you’re old enough to pay for your own pizza, too. “You always have a boss,” he said.

At Culkin’s house, one kid has taken that identification with Kevin a little further. Neither of Culkin’s sons knows their dad played Kevin McCallister, even though they’ve watched Home Alone with him. “They don’t know it’s me,” he told Collider. His oldest, Dakota, has his own explanation. “He thinks he is Kevin.” He looks so much like Culkin did at that age that even a cousin saw the poster while scrolling through a menu and asked why Dakota was in the movie.

The boys ask plenty of other questions while they watch, but Culkin can see Dakota only now starting to put that particular one together. He’s already guessed how the news will break: some kid on the playground, probably named Lenny or Nino, will tell Dakota before he gets the chance. Culkin figures he’ll sit him down afterward and have what he calls a “Beaver Cleaver” moment. Until then, Culkin is happy to let Dakota watch Home Alone and see himself in it, comparing the whole thing to letting his kids believe in Santa Claus:

“You want to keep that magic as long as possible."

For now, there’s still time for another Christmas where Dakota gets to be Kevin and his dad gets to sit beside him and watch. The Home Alone Meal comes to McDonald’s in the U.S. on December 1. The movies are available to stream on Disney+.

#3454. 10 Hacks Every Hulu User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you don't like the content Hulu is suggesting for you, you have several options to curate your recommendations. "Disliking" a show or movie removes it from your Home view and You May Also Like entirely, so the only way you'll see that content is if you search for it. You can dislike on the Details page if you're watching on your TV or use the thumbs down on mobile or web. (The "Like" button will obviously influence your algorithm in the opposite way). If your "Continue Watching" queue is cluttered with shows you started but didn't like enough to finish, you can remove them from your watch history as well as the My Stuff list. This, too, will allow content to remain searchable but not suggested in other areas of the app.

If PIN protection is enabled, users must enter a four-digit PIN when switching between profiles on a single account. This is intended as a parental control feature, since it's available on non-Kids profiles and can keep children from accessing more mature content on an adult's profile. However, you can also enable this feature to keep other users from seeing your viewing history and preferences or influencing your algorithm by watching their content under your profile (accidentally or on purpose). To set up a PIN, log into your account on Hulu's website, select your profile, and go to Manage Profiles > Parental Controls. You'll have to choose a PIN and enter your password to confirm the changes.

Another approach to protecting your profile and algorithm is to set up separate profiles for specific use cases, such as when you have guests or if you host watch parties for certain shows. This keeps content from influencing your recommendations and prevents other viewers from seeing what's in your watch history or saved content (especially if there are things you want to keep private).

If you find that subtitles and captions are too bold—or not visible enough—you can change the font, color, size, and style from the default so they enhance your viewing experience rather than detracting from it. Hulu allows you to adjust the color and opacity of the font, background, and window so you get the right contrast, and you can also select the specific font and font scaling. On your streaming device, go to Settings > Subtitles & Captions, then hit the back button on your remote to save your preferences. You can update these settings on mobile and desktop as well.

If you have a long list of shows and films to watch but can't decide what to start next, look for the "Expiring Soon" badge to see which titles are leaving the service in the next two weeks. Badges display the number of days remaining, so you can determine what to prioritize and whether it's worth diving in based on how much time you have to finish before the expiration date. Go to "My Stuff" to monitor saved titles that are expiring soon.

If you've been watching Hulu under an account shared with family or friends and need to switch to your own subscription, you can transfer your profile to keep your watch history and settings intact instead of starting from scratch. You can initiate a profile transfer on a TV-connected device. Note that account holders have to approve transfer requests within seven days, and once expired, transfer requests cannot be resubmitted—so be sure to let the primary user know that you've made the request.

If you've shared your Hulu login information with friends or activated your account on devices you don't own, you may want to regularly audit where your account is being used and remove any that don't need access. This includes TVs in Airbnbs and hotels. If you stay logged in, unauthorized users may have access to your Hulu account and personal data. You can see activated devices (and their activation date) under Your Account > Watch Hulu on Your Devices > Manage Devices. Click Remove next to old or unrecognized devices.

Hulu has an offline mode that allows you to download shows and movies to watch when you don't have a network connection. This is useful for traveling or when you know your wifi or cell service will be limited. Downloads are only available on supported iOS and Android devices, which means you may have to consider how much space your content takes up. You can select High for video quality if you want maximum resolution, but you may want to choose Standard if you are short on storage. This option is available under Downloads > Settings > Video Quality on iOS and Account > Settings > Downloads > Video Quality on Android. Note that once you click play on downloaded content, you have 48 hours to watch it before it expires—so don't start it unless you are ready.

If you have a Hulu + Live TV subscription, you must designate a "Home" network, which determines the local channels included in your plan. You can update your location up to four times within a 12-month period, but this limitation is meant to prevent viewers outside a household from sharing a subscription. Hulu does allow you to stream live TV on mobile when you're away from your home network (within the U.S.) as long as you access your account on that network every 30 days. If you travel often, check in with your mobile device frequently to avoid being locked out when you're away. Note that you can still watch streaming content with no restrictions.

#3453. ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Returning to Theaters with a New Rosario Dawson Cameo — and Box Office Records and Oscar Noms in Mind

Usually this is the time of year when early-year and summer awards contenders come back to theaters (see: “The Odyssey”). But even though it only left theaters not long ago, Sony is re-releasing “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” which is now the biggest domestic release of all time.

The studio is bringing the film back to theaters on December 4, with tickets going on sale November 19. And the new version will be an extended cut of the film (cheekily titled “Spider-Man: [Brand New] Brand New Day”) that will feature one deleted scene in which Rosario Dawson stars as a character called The Night Nurse. Director Daniel Destin Cretton had previously told press that she shot a scene for the film that was cut. Related Stories ‘Minotaur’ Review: Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Riveting Comeback Remakes Claude Chabrol and ‘Unfaithful’ for a Hopeless Wartime Russia Cary Grant, Clint Eastwood, and Christian Bale: The Stars Who Almost Played James Bond

The real reason “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” is coming back to theaters is because it gives the film yet another chance to add on to its record box office haul. Maybe it surpasses $1 billion domestic? It’s only $41 million shy, and the re-release of “Avengers Endgame: Encore” managed to gross $40 million domestic, so there’s a real chance of that. It also turns out that Sony really does view the film as an awards contender and thinks it deserves to be back top of mind. SPE chief Tom Rothman recently told Deadline that the studio was launching an FYC campaign for the film and believed “Brand New Day” worthy of a Best Picture nomination.

“If there aren’t people thinking about it, we’re gonna do what we can just to make people think about it,” Rothman said. “I think it’s also incumbent upon studios who make these kinds of quality commercial films to get people to think about it, and here’s what I ask people when I walk around: ‘Are you telling me that there are 10 films this year that are better than this film?’”

The only other new studio wide release on December 4 is “Violent Night 2,” so it’s a relatively light weekend in what figures to be an incredibly crowded Christmas box office, one that even includes Sony’s own “Jumanji: Open World” and of course “Avengers: Doomsday” the weekend prior.

#3452. ‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier

A very successful “values-based entertainment” company that was begat — in the parlance of its biblical heritage — from a film-filtering service that illegally edited “objectionable content” out of major Hollywood movies, Angel Studios has since become the world’s foremost purveyor of megachurch-approved multiplex content. The bigger they got (on the strength of projects like “The Chosen” and the QAnon cause célèbre “Sound of Freedom,” the latter of which pioneered a questionable ticketing model that continues today), the more that Angel removed from the films they released. Not just sex and swear words, but also anything that even vaguely resembled a soul. Related Stories ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Returning to Theaters with a New Rosario Dawson Cameo — and Box Office Records and Oscar Noms in Mind ‘Minotaur’ Review: Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Riveting Comeback Remakes Claude Chabrol and ‘Unfaithful’ for a Hopeless Wartime Russia

With “Hershey,” a decidedly vanilla biopic about the most famous chocolatier who’s ever lived, the studio has taken its socio-religious project to its logical conclusion: They’ve made a movie that’s been stripped of any flavor whatsoever. It’s the cinematic equivalent of carob powder. It’s what Ned Flanders will force his kids to watch next Halloween.

Somehow unimaginatively bland and Splenda-sweet all at once, this godforsaken affront to good storytelling may not have benefited from any of the material that its distributor has deemed amoral, but “Hershey” is so mind-numbingly absent the most basic friction of the human experience that I wanted to fall to my knees and thank the lord that a few errant Kisses made it past The Angel Promise on a technicality. It’s too bad Milton S. Hershey never used his platform to baselessly sow doubt in a foreign election, because at least one of Angel Studios’ co-founders would clearly have been cool with including that (ecocidal fascism is fine, just don’t say “fuck” while you’re razing the Amazon, as that would offend Jesus).

As you may have gathered by now, I am probably not the target audience for this unrepentant godslop.

Not because I’m agnostic (“Hershey” is as secular as Angel Studios’ output gets, its overt religiosity limited to a brief scene in which the movie’s namesake pleads for help from an unspecified higher power), but rather because I stubbornly, blasphemously insist that a womb-to-tomb biopic should bear at least some faint resemblance to the stuff of real life. I couldn’t possibly care less about the facts (though I struggle to believe that Hershey and his wife literally danced with joy after learning that a twist of fate had spared them from being aboard the Titanic), but there isn’t a single moment in this film that feels like it was written by a real person, let alone lived by one.

Let’s back up a beat. To be clear, Angel Studios didn’t technically make this movie — that distinction belongs to the spiritually aligned production company Dandelion Media, who partnered with Hershey Entities for a fully authorized feature-length commercial meant to “bring [the chocolate brand’s] story into culture in a more immersive way.” The success of that marketing spend remains to be seen, but it can’t hurt to highlight Mr. Hershey’s ostensible purity at a time when the company that bears his name has been under fire for diluting its products with compound coatings in order to save money. And so we have a punishingly straightforward film that paints the Pennsylvania icon as a square-jawed, sweet-toothed wife guy who loved candy, orphans, and sitting way too close to the edge of the massive water tower that overlooks the town he remade in his own image.

Directed by Mark Waters, but absent any trace of the poppy confidence he once brought to the likes of “Mean Girls” and “Freaky Friday,” “Hershey” opens with its first and only stylistic flourish as a match cut transforms an immaculate chocolate Kiss into a small lump of coal — Milton Hershey’s life would turn out to be sweet, but it sure didn’t start that way. The film that follows sadly feels less like “Lawrence of Arabia” than it does an AI-generated adaptation of Hershey’s Wikipedia page, its algorithmic sense of human interaction rendered all the more uncanny by its ecclesiastical approach to conflict (and also by its blown out cinematography, which suggests a very literal interpretation of Angel Studios’ promise to produce “movies and shows that amplify light.”)

Adhering to the prosaic structure and candied morality that the Erwin brothers have made endemic to the world of faith-based biopics and their immediate kin, the film sees Hershey’s life as a blessed march towards his eternal reward — one that’s only slowed down by the litany of speed bumps that pop up along his path to heaven.

Young Milton’s very serious Mennonite mom is a major bummer, but she lets him out of the house to work for a local printer. The JRPG-like town where he grows up in the 1860s seems inhospitable to dreams, but its muddy roads make it appear as though the streets are paved with chocolate. His dad (Alan Ruck, a long way from “Succession”) abandons him pretty fast, but not before bending down to the kid like Zooey Deschanel in “Almost Famous” and telling him: “You’re a Hershey, and that means when you follow your dream, you don’t let anyone get in your way.” Apparently his dad’s dream was to not live with his family anymore, but so be it. A good example is a good example.

Every stumbling block is immediately followed by a burst of divine providence, as Sharon Paul and Timothy Michael Hayes’ script adheres to the grindset mindset of the prosperity gospel while Rolfe Kent’s saccharine score blends everything together into a tasteless slurry of unrefined sugar. The film insists that a little sweetness goes a long way, as an orgasmic taste of rock candy is all that Milton needs to make it through the day, but it doesn’t heed its own advice. Milton’s passion leads him to a job working for a saintly confectioner named Joseph Royer (a beneficent Richard Kind, as close to a live-action Bing Bong as he’s ever been), who just smiles it off when the kid forgets to turn off the peanut roaster and nearly burns down the whole shop.

Later, after sprouting into Finn Wittrock and starting his own caramel company, Milton is miraculously spared from ruin several times over by virtue of his non-denominational faith in himself and the universe. One low moment is redeemed by a massive order from overseas. Another resolves with a traveling salesman busting into the Lancaster Caramel Company with an offer to invest in chocolate — the future of snacking! “This chocolate,” Milton sniffs, “it could be good if it wasn’t so bad.” I know the feeling. The next time disaster strikes, he inadvertently stumbles upon the Hershey Kiss in the very next scene. The plotting is schematic enough to make “Bohemian Rhapsody” seem like “Last Days” by comparison.

Somewhere in there Milton enjoys a meet-cute with a woman named Kitty Sweeney (Alexandria Daddario), a grinning beauty who credits caramels with curing her shyness. Her job as Milton’s wife is to be his biggest cheerleader, and then — as the years melt away — to collapse in undiagnosed pain whenever he leaves the room. At one point it is implied that she and Milton have sexual intercourse, but only so the movie can leverage the couple’s inability to conceive a child into a robust philanthropic regime that allowed them to house and educate any number of white male orphans.

Of course, expecting this movie to acknowledge the Milton Hershey School’s history of racial and social discrimination would be as delusional as thinking its third act might address the labor disputes that unsettled Hershey’s chocolate factory in the late 1930s. Such things are simply not sweet enough to befit a story about how some vague belief and a little stick-it-to-em are all a man needs to prosper in this great land — even if a warts-and-all version of that same story would still be a model of American success.

Considerably less textured than the chocolate bars that have become synonymous with its title character, Waters’ film is so determined to launder one man’s dreams into reality that it comes to assume its own kind of dream logic in return — one divorced from the basic relationship between cause-and-effect or an event and its meaning.

In what might be the single most deranged movie scene of the year, Milton and his ailing wife Kitty literally dance for joy on the bow of a ship after learning that a twist of fate has spared them from being aboard the Titanic, even though upwards of 1,400 other people went to a watery grave that night. I’m not sure that qualifies as bringing the brand’s “story into the culture in a more immersive way,” but it’s definitely what I’m going to be thinking about the next time I bite into a milky and delicious Hershey Bar. After watching this perversely chalky film about the company’s founder, it’s a wonder that I can still remember what their signature product even tastes like.

Angel Studios will release “Hershey” in theaters on Wednesday, November 25.

#3450. ABC Officially Confirms Devastating Grey's Anatomy News After Spinoff's Major Delay

An upsetting revelation about Grey’s Anatomy season 23 follows its spinoff’s already discouraging delay. Returning for a record 23rd season as part of ABC’s Fall 2026 lineup, Grey’s Anatomy was supposed to be replaced by its Texas-based spinoff during midseason, as the TV series would have had to take over Grey’s Anatomy’s Thursday night timeslot. However, massive delays made such a plan unfeasible, pushing back the Grey’s Anatomy spinoff from a 2026-2027 premiere to a 2027-2028 one. ABC nevertheless revealed even more dismal news regarding the long-running medical drama.

Grey’s Anatomy’s third spinoff is set to be based in rural West Texas and follow doctors at a medical center in the last town for miles. Such a setting pushes the Grey’s Anatomy spinoff to be completely different from the parent series, not only for the setting, but also for the type of storylines and traumas that reach the medical center in question.

Every Grey’s Anatomy spinoff that ever existed had been filmed in Los Angeles, which prompted Shonda Rhimes and Meg Marinis’s new brainchild to attempt to secure a tax credit so that it could do the same. However, California refused to award Grey’s Anatomy’s spinoff a tax credit twice, resulting in the production having to be moved to Albuquerque, New Mexico.

This inevitably delayed production enough that the Grey’s Anatomy spinoff couldn’t debut during the 2026-2027 midseason. However, another update regarding the popular medical drama is also upsetting, as Grey’s Anatomy season 23 will air its winter finale this week.

After airing only five episodes of Grey’s Anatomy season 23, the medical drama is set to have its winter finale on Thursday, November 19, 2026. It is the first ABC TV show to do so, accompanied only by 911: Nashville, as all the other TV series that were part of ABC’s Fall 2026 lineup are set to return after a small hiatus, before taking another one for the end-of-the-year holidays.

Grey’s Anatomy season 23 already having a winter finale date set up makes the current time particularly difficult for the medical drama, especially given that its Texas-based spinoff will be delayed for at least half a year if not more. Grey’s Anatomy season 23, episode 6’s trailer nevertheless promises an action-packed episode of medical chaos, hierarchical issues, and personal ones too, as Richard Webber’s wish to move the patient overflow to the VIP floor seemingly puts him at odds with both Grey Sloan Memorial’s new chief, Seth Norton, and his own wife, Catherine Fox.

While the news of Grey’s Anatomy season 23 already having a midseason finale is undoubtedly disappointing, its return has also been set up, and it’s the best possible outcome for the ABC medical drama. Unlike Grey’s Anatomy season 21, which had its midseason finale during the third week of November only to return in early March, season 23 will come back sooner.

Grey’s Anatomy season 23’s winter premiere is set for Thursday, January 7, 2027. This means the hiatus is only seven weeks long, which isn’t short per se, but it cannot be considered a long one either. Such a schedule mirrors Grey’s Anatomy season 22’s one from last year, when the ABC medical drama aired its midseason finale in mid-November only to return in January 2026.

Grey's Anatomy has made way for three spin-off series, though not all of them have been set in a hospital. Here's what they're about.

Grey’s Anatomy season 23’s return schedule would have inevitably looked differently had its Texas-based spinoff begun production earlier. However, the disappointment of a longer break for the record-breaking show would have been offset by another medical drama coming from the same minds that made Grey’s Anatomy the compelling drama that it is.

With the Texas-based Grey’s Anatomy spinoff’s debut delayed, having Grey’s Anatomy return in early 2027 is the best possible news for fans of the medical drama, particularly considering how Grey’s Anatomy alternated its return date between January and March consistently in the past ten years.

#3448. How to Make Sure an 'Onion' Site on the Dark Web Is Legitimate

Thankfully, Tor Browser already has a cryptography-backed feature that can verify the authenticity of an onion site, by confirming whether it has end-to-end encryption and extended validation certificates. Here's how this feature works, where it falters, as well as what other red flags you should look for.

While phishing on the dark web works as it does on the clear web, scammers have a few unique advantages due to the secretive nature of the environment. Most importantly, you can’t just glance at an onion link to tell if the site is genuine. Normal website URLs tend to be short and memorable, while onion links are 56-character strings of alphanumeric text that look mostly like gibberish.

When you try to connect, Tor Browser verifies the URL against the originating website’s cryptographic key, which is how you know nobody has hijacked the address or tampered with it midway. But since this has the unwanted effect of making domains harder to recall, scammers have a much easier time generating lookalike addresses or creating website clones.

For example, many popular websites use “vanity prefixes” to make their onion addresses more easily identifiable or to add some branding appeal. That means their 56-character onion link starts with something like “facebook,” “bbcnews,” or “ciadotgov.” But scammers can use a free tool like mkp224o to generate lookalike addresses with the same vanity prefix as the legitimate website, which gives users a false sense of security.

Of course, most dark web users don’t type addresses directly into Tor Browser; they use dark web directories like the Hidden Wiki to find useful onion sites relevant to their search. Scammers will create fake search engines or link directories to point users to their fake websites, like when the Ahmia search engine discovered that a copy of its platform was directing users to 255 cloned services back in 2015.

Of course, it’s possible to orchestrate phishing attempts that don’t involve cloning sites at all. Researchers at Freie Universität Berlin describe a sophisticated technique where attackers serve the real website through their own reverse proxy, which lets them manipulate parts of the site or log your online activity without your awareness. In 2019, ESET even found a trojanized version of Tor Browser that replaced Bitcoin addresses on websites to direct payments to hackers. So both genuine websites and your browser itself are also vulnerable to manipulation if you download or access them from an unverified source.

There are a few best practices to avoid phishing attacks when using the dark web. None of them are foolproof on their own, but together, they considerably lower the risk of ending up on a fake or manipulated website.

On the desktop version of Tor Browser, you can access an onion site using a shortened version of its URL called an Onion Name. For now, this feature only works with SecureDrop, so newsrooms can establish tip lines with addresses like mysitename.securedrop.tor.onion, which would then redirect to the 56-character original onion address. This feature is in active development, so more platforms might support it in the future.

When you load up an onion site using the Tor Browser, you’ll see an onion icon on the address bar, which confirms that your connection is end-to-end encrypted. But you can also click on the onion icon to check if the site has an Extended Validation (EV) certificate, which tells you that its authenticity has been verified by a trusted certificate authority like DigiCert. While not every legitimate onion site will have an EV certificate, famous ones like Facebook tend to.

On the other hand, if you see a caution sign next to the onion icon, that means the site is using a self-signed or expired certificate that isn’t guaranteed by a trusted authority. It may also imply that the site is being served over an insecure URL. This doesn’t definitely tell you it’s a phishing site, but it’s a red flag to watch out for nevertheless.

Don’t rely on search engines, link directories, Reddit threads, or Telegram channels too heavily on the dark web. Once you’re sure you’ve found the onion address for a genuine site, bookmark it so you can access it directly the next time you want to visit.

If you realized that you’ve been the victim of a phishing attempt, the first step is to close the browser window with the fake site and access the real onion address to reset any account passwords you may have accidentally divulged.

Also, generally try to enable two-factor authentication and PGP logins on any dark web account that supports it for added security. And if you downloaded Tor Browser from anywhere other than the official Tor Project site, uninstall it now and grab a fresh copy from the official address.

#3447. 10 HBO Miniseries That Are Perfect From Start to Finish

Justine Kraemer is a Senior List Writer at Collider and a freelance writer based in Ontario, Canada. She is passionate about finding new angles on the latest movies and TV shows. With over five years of industry experience, her goal is to highlight lesser-known and interesting elements of pop culture projects.

HBO has featured some of the greatest miniseries of all time. While the streaming service has no shortage of compelling movies and TV shows for viewers to get attached to, the miniseries stand out. For years, HBO has provided viewers with miniseries that have remained topical and have stood the test of time. While there are many miniseries to choose from, there are several that stand out and can be revisited again and again.

Some HBO miniseries are based on literary works and adapt stories that speak to the human experience. Other series dramatize real events and highlight characters based on real people who had to witness some of the most remarkable moments in history. All of these series feature deeply human stories that provide new perspectives for viewers. The best HBO series are memorable dramas that tackle complex themes and introduce characters who face extraordinary circumstances.

Mare of Easttown is a crime drama that follows Mare Sheehan (Kate Winslet), a weary and emotionally scarred detective in a small Pennsylvania town, as she investigates the murder of a teenage girl while grappling with her own personal traumas. These include the death of her son by suicide and a custody battle for her grandson. Mare of Easttown follows the investigation as it unfolds, and long-buried secrets and tensions in the close-knit community are brought to light.

Mare of Easttown is one of HBO's best miniseries of all time since it captures the atmosphere of a working-class Pennsylvania town with striking authenticity. The characters, locations, and dialogue feel lived-in and genuine, which grounds the story​​​​​. Every character in the series is given a compelling backstory that makes them easy to invest in. While Mare of Easttown is a slow burn, the mystery at the heart of the series is well-crafted, full of twists and emotional stakes.

Olive Kitteridge is based on the 2008 Pulitzer Prize-winning novel of the same name by Elizabeth Strout. The series stars Frances McDormand as the titular character, who's a sharp-tongued, retired schoolteacher who lives in the fictional seaside town of Crosby, Maine. As Olive grapples with her strained marriage, her distant relationship with her son, and her own inner turmoil, the series paints a portrait of a woman who is more than her gruff exterior. The series follows her daily struggles to come to terms with where she is in life.

Olive Kitteridge stands out among HBO's miniseries because of McDormand's haunting and devastating performance. In lesser hands, this character would be far from sympathetic. Instead, McDormand leans into Olive's humanity and shows how emotionally complex she is. Rather than relying on sensationalism or drama, Olive Kitteridge tells a deeply human story about how messy life can be, and what ultimately makes life worth living.

Generation Kill is based on journalist Evan Wright's (Lee Tergesen) experiences being embedded with the Second Platoon of the First Reconnaissance Battalion's Bravo Company during the American invasion of Iraq in 2003. The series follows a group of young Marines as they navigate the chaos, confusion, and contradictions of modern warfare, as they struggle with the tension that exists between their idealism and sense of duty and the brutal reality of combat.

Unlike many war series that dramatize or mythologize combat, Generation Kill presents the Iraq War with documentary-like precision. The series doesn’t rely on clichés or hero archetypes. Instead, it gives viewers a diverse cast of fully realized Marines, some of whom are idealistic, others who are disillusioned, all of whom are flawed. Generation Kill is one of HBO's best miniseries because it asks difficult questions about a war many viewers remember without ever presenting easy answers.

​​​​​​​Watchmen is a sequel to the original 1986 graphic novel by Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons. Like the graphic novel, the series is set in an alternate-history United States where masked vigilantes are treated as outlaws. Watchmen specifically focuses on Angela Abar (Regina King), a masked detective known as Sister Night. The story unravels a complex conspiracy tied to the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre and the legacy of the original Watchmen.

In a media landscape that has no shortage of superhero stories for viewers to choose from, Watchmen stands out as one of the best. The series succeeds in being a spiritual sequel to the graphic novel while creating new stories that new fans can invest in. Watchmen is intricately plotted and full of twists, symbolism, and philosophical depth. Ultimately, Watchmen stands out as one of HBO's best miniseries because it is daring, intelligent, and makes viewers think.

Mildred Pierce is based on James M. Cain’s 1941 novel of the same name. Kate Winslet stars as the series' titular character, a determined, working-class woman in Depression-era Los Angeles who builds a successful restaurant business while grappling with her complex relationship with her daughter Veda (Evan Rachel Wood). Throughout the series, she does her best to gain her daughter's love and respect.

Mildred Pierce stands out as one of HBO's best miniseries of all time because it succeeds as a literary adaptation and a period piece. The series stays true to Cain’s original novel, since it uses a slow and deliberate pace that allows for deeper character exploration. At its core, Mildred Pierce is a devastating portrait of a mother-daughter relationship marked by love, obsession, pride, and betrayal, which is a dynamic many people can relate to.

Tanner '88 is a political mockumentary that originally aired on HBO during the 1988 U.S. presidential campaign. The series follows fictional Democratic candidate Jack Tanner (Michael Murphy) as he runs for president, blending scripted drama with real political events and figures. By inserting its fictional characters into real campaign settings and interactions, Tanner '88 satirizes the political process, media manipulation, and the intricacies of campaigning in America.

Tanner '88 remains one of the best HBO miniseries of all time because it was wildly ahead of its time. The series seamlessly merged fiction with real-life political events, creating a pseudo-documentary style that blurred the line between reality and satire. Tanner '88 offers a biting look at the reality of America's electoral system that remains timeless. The series holds a mirror up to the American electoral process, which remains an object of fascination to those in America and beyond.

The Pacific is a war-drama miniseries that follows the real-life experiences of U.S. Marines during World War II’s Pacific Theater. The series specifically focuses on three main characters, Robert Leckie (James Badge Dale), Eugene Sledge (Joseph Mazzello), and John Basilone (Jon Seda). The Pacific highlights some of the most brutal battles of World War II's Pacific Theater, including Guadalcanal, Peleliu, Iwo Jima, and Okinawa.

The Pacific is one of HBO's best miniseries because it delivers a harrowingly realistic look at some of the most brutal battles of World War II. Unlike typical war dramas that focus only on action, The Pacific deeply explores the psychological toll of combat. The series shows how prolonged exposure to violence and trauma affects anyone who experiences war. In short, The Pacific stands out for its brutal honesty, cinematic scale, and emotional depth.

Chernobyl dramatizes the events surrounding the catastrophic 1986 nuclear disaster at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in Ukraine. The series follows key figures such as scientist Valery Legasov (Jared Harris), government official Boris Shcherbina (Stellan Skarsgård), and fictional composite character Ulana Khomyuk (Emily Watson) as they uncover the truth behind the explosion, battle government denial and secrecy, and risk their lives to prevent further devastation.

Chernobyl succeeds in meticulously reconstructing the events of the 1986 nuclear disaster while balancing dramatic storytelling and factual detail. Rather than sensationalizing this tragedy, the series highlights the systemic failures that led to it and emphasizes the fact that ordinary people had their lives destroyed. Ultimately, Chernobyl plays like a thriller and presents characters who have to fight to survive.

Band of Brothers is a drama that follows the true story of Easy Company, a unit of the 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment of the 101st Airborne Division in World War II. The series follows Easy Company as they experience some of the most pivotal moments of the war, beginning with the D-Day invasion of Normandy, continuing through the Battle of the Bulge, and ending with the capture of Hitler’s Eagle’s Nest. Band of Brothers mainly follows Major Richard "Dick" Winters (Damian Lewis), who does his best to lead his men.

Band of Brothers' attention to detail makes it stand out as one of the best HBO miniseries of all time. The series is more than a war drama. Instead, it's a character study of some of the men who experienced World War II firsthand. Band of Brothers is another example of a series that could have glorified war, but instead provides an honest look at the cost of victory. The series succeeds in highlighting the heroism and sacrifice America's soldiers had to embody to win the war.

Angels in America is a groundbreaking miniseries based on Tony Kushner’s Pulitzer Prize-winning play of the same name. The series is set in mid-1980s New York during the height of the AIDS crisis. Angels in America interweaves the lives of several characters, including Prior Walter (Justin Kirk), a gay man diagnosed with AIDS, and Roy Cohn (Al Pacino), a closeted, powerful lawyer also battling the illness. As their lives unravel, the story blends harsh political and social realities with surreal, fantastical elements.

Angels in America is HBO's greatest miniseries because it's a fearless exploration of the AIDS crisis and the homophobia that enabled it to grow unchecked. The series' unapologetic approach gave visibility and dignity to LGBTQ+ experiences during a time when many were still being ignored and stigmatized. Angels in America uses dream sequences, angels, ghosts, and hallucinations not as gimmicks, but as metaphors for deeper psychological and cultural truths.

#3446. ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: They Shoot Franchises, Don’t They?

A grimmer, gloomier “Hunger Games” is on the horizon with “Sunrise on the Reaping,” adapted from Suzanne Collins’ prequel novel about the origin story of the hardened alcoholic Haymitch Abernathy. Here, the teenage version of Woody Harrelson’s character in the original films is played by Australian actor Joseph Zada, the blond, ringletted Adonis who also starred as the moody Cal Trask in the recent “East of Eden” series.

Franchise fans might be riveted by Francis Lawrence’s latest installment — points for consistency, as he’s directed all the films dating back to 2013’s “Catching Fire” — but those audiences not already invested in the dystopian material and tales of tributes will find themselves left out in the cold by an overlong (it’s 158 minutes, so get comfortable), visually soupy, and narratively morose reprisal. But no matter, as this new slice of bankable I.P. is likely to rake in a hysterical amount of money, and perhaps launch Zada’s career as a face of new Hollywood stardom. Related Stories ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ First Reactions: Quentin Tarantino and David Fincher Deliver a ‘Pure Riot’ of a Hangout Movie ‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier

The film is set during the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell. Only 16 years old, Haymitch is thrust into games that are rigged from the start — and whose broadcasting is ultimately edited and deepfaked to look like pro-Capitol propaganda. (The film nudges a little bit toward the ethics of state surveillance and how footage can be manipulated or even fabricated for political ends.) His pastoral, if impoverished, life in District 12 is small but happy, with girlfriend Lenore (Whitney Peak) and a mother and younger brother (Kara Tointon and Smylie Bradwell) with whom he shares close affinity, plus a best friend we’ll eventually find out will become the father of Katniss Everdeen (Lawrence) in the later films.

After a reaping (refresher: that’s when tributes are selected ceremonial-style, here as by a grotesquely pulled-tight-in-the-face Glenn Close as Drusilla Sickle) turns bloody, long-shot Haymitch ends up being selected at only 16. Violence follows him everywhere, as during the subsequent Tribute Parade, tragedy strikes Haymitch’s childhood friend (Molly McCann) during a horse-drawn Tribute chariot ride. Sequences meant to be thrilling often lack connective tissue to the rest of the material, or are devised in such a maelstrom of CGI (as goopy and cacophonous as a Marvel battle) that it’s difficult to feel engaged. It’s also unhelpful that most of the supporting cast is so wildly over the top, especially Capitol residents played by Close and a smarmy and mannered Kieran Culkin. Jesse Plemons as a Hunger Games camera operator brings a shade of moral dimension to the proceedings, but as with his “Digger” role, the actor feels woefully underused. Ralph Fiennes as Capitol president Snow, meanwhile, is given but scraps of material to work with.

The by-the-book script by Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie appears to stick faithfully to Collins’ 2025 novel, with plenty of potential for visual appeal that goes largely unrealized. The Hunger Games arena Haymitch is thrust into is rife with hidden dangers: poisonous streams, a deadly force field, and other trippy flora and fauna that vibe like a dark mirror version of “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory,” but again, “Sunrise on the Reaping” trips up on the CGI fakery.

The movie’s stacked young cast of tributes and mentors (those victors of previous Hunger Games tournaments) includes Mckenna Grace as a District 12 tribute who’s not to be trusted, the endearingly wily Ben Wang (recently excellent in the SXSW film “Brian”), plus a gravely underused Maya Hawke as the winner of the 49th Hunger Games, Kelvin Harrison Jr. as victor of the 34th, and the great Lili Taylor as a legacy tribute played previously by Lynn Cohen (aka Magda on “Sex and the City”) in the second film. These characters mostly exist to introduce themselves to Haymitch, be established as good or evil or helpful or unhelpful, and then be shuffled out of the scene. Elle Fanning is rather amusing, however, as the Capitol stylist Effie Trinket, styled and nearly drowned out by extremely outré fashions. Glenn Close also (with a visage channeling Katherine Helmond as Ida Lowry in “Brazil”) could’ve been used to better effect.

The specter of death looming over the film should not be confused for much in the way of actual depth, and while Zada’s performance is charming enough, his character lacks the gravitational charisma or arc that, say, Jennifer Lawrence brought to the original films. He feels like a cog or a function to get this prequel to line up with the prior films — and isn’t that what he is? Which makes the movie, and ergo probably the book, feel a little bit like a cold cash grab rather than a necessary deepening of the series’ lore. When Haymitch comes home from Second Quarter Quell and descends into depression and alcoholism, that’s when the movie gets most interesting. Not a great sign when your film’s tepid coda is also its best moment.

And equally worrying is a series of cameos tacked onto the film’s end that smack of depressing fan service. These movies seem to be mostly critic-proof and hugely appealing to their core audience, but “Sunrise on the Reaping” is a dreary slog, another death-march “They Shoot Horses, Don’t They?” riff with a pretty Gen Z cast, and one that mistakes new layers of darkness (and trauma!) for the sort of profundity that its filmmakers hope will burnish a creatively withering property.

“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” opens in theaters on Friday, November 20.

#3443. Desire, Death, and a Breakthrough Year for Queer Cinema

A willingness to die for sex is a familiar bargain for queer people. Born in the twentieth century at the wrong place and time? Beware of Nazis, AIDS, and other mortal dangers. Hollywood has at times depicted these threats in ways that emphasize the humanity of LGBTQ+ people, as when Tom Hanks played a lawyer dying of AIDS in “Philadelphia,” during the height of the epidemic in 1993. The industry also has a history of finding ever more creative ways to kill off and scapegoat queer characters, a trope that as recently as 10 years ago seemed to be running amok.

But a more twisted and nervy dance between desire and death has unfolded in this year’s spate of particularly macabre queer films. After years of what felt like permanent advances in rights and representation, LGBTQ+ people have been stung by backlash, including attacks on gender-affirming care, legal threats to marriage equality, and cuts to suicide prevention. Amid a reduced perception of safety, anxieties about the possibilities and consequences of nonnormative desire are spilling out onscreen like so much fake blood. Even so, their formulation is evidence of social and creative progress. Related Stories ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: They Shoot Franchises, Don’t They? ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ First Reactions: Quentin Tarantino and David Fincher Deliver a ‘Pure Riot’ of a Hangout Movie

This alarm has played out, perhaps most obviously, in horror films. In Adrian Chiarella’s “Leviticus” and Jane Schoenbrun’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” same-sex attraction engenders extreme and potentially deadly terror, be it from detractors or the people it consumes. Both films explore not the evils of queerness — an argument that belongs to the tradition of queer-coded villains — but the horrors of having one’s desires villainized.

The year’s queer history films also subvert conventional narratives around sexuality and deadly fates. In Andrew Scott’s awards-season vehicle “Elsinore,” Ian Charleson’s dying wish to play Hamlet is one many actors would share; the film doesn’t focus on how or why he has AIDS, but what he wants to do before it kills him. The Spanish epic “La Bola Negra” depicts forbidden romance, but desire isn’t what dooms its multiple generations of queer men. The fact that they’re swept up in the currents of history, just like everyone else, is part of the film’s revolutionary power.

The era for combatting the notion that being gay is a no good, very bad thing in a straightforward way finally seems to have passed. Usually such sermons were preaching to the choir anyway. Gone is the teary earnestness of a conversion therapy drama like “Boy Erased,” from 2018, in which much of the trauma wrought on Lucas Hedges’ character derives from the church but is carried out by earthly messengers. In “Leviticus,” when a healer tries to pray the gay away from a pair of lovesick adolescents, he conjures supernatural and murderous doppelgangers.

After rituals of deliverance are performed over the convulsing bodies of a pair of schoolmates (played by Joe Bird and Stacy Clausen), each one is haunted by an illusion of the other that tries to kill them. The concept of “Leviticus,” named for the Old Testament book that forbids man to lie with man, partly functions as a wry play on the idea that you never get over your first crush. It also takes the fear that so many queer people know well — that what you desire most will be your downfall — to literal and horrifying extremes. Imagining the bigotry of organized religion as a senselessly violent supernatural force is a radical reversal. The boys aren’t the problem; the boogeymen that torment them spring from the so-called good book.

Schoenbrun’s meta queer fantasia “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” likewise performs a canonical revision. The nonbinary killer in the campy franchise within the film were themselves killed and sunk to the bottom of a lake by their comically gender-panicked peers. A victim seeking revenge, the TV-headed slasher is called Little Death, a nod to a French term for orgasm, la petite mort. Hannah Einbinder’s millennial filmmaker is on a quest to reboot the franchise, but more significantly, to achieve her own “little death.” In order to grow more comfortable with sex, and give into her own desires, her fear of intimacy — one that, again, many queer people know well — needs to be killed.

The movie ultimately intertwines fear of death with the fear of intimacy in a way that demonstrates the stakes — how you can feel so afraid of getting close to someone you could just die. But what must be slaughtered in this case is fear itself — so that same-sex desire, which has so often been pathologized and villainized, can flourish. (The trail of straight people extravagantly dispatched along the way, like so many gays before them, is one of the film’s many deranged and delightful flourishes.)

There is a potent realignment evident in the year’s period films as well, which center the desires and fates of queer characters on their own terms, rather than taking their oppression or disease as subjects unto themselves. “Elsinore” leans a bit heavily on obvious sentiment while leaving much of the thematic richness of “Hamlet” on the table. But Charleson’s determination to play the part before he dies is what drives the film, while the indignities of succumbing to AIDS are mostly a secondary plot.

Contrast that with recent period dramas on TV, like “It’s a Sin” (2021) about young people facing the AIDS crisis in London, or “Fellow Travelers” (2023) about the Lavender Scare in the U.S., and focusing on Charleson’s dream itself rather than the injustice of what threatens it marks a distinct shift.

The broad sweep of the canvas in “La Bola Negra” heralds another major turn of the page. The play of the same name by Federico García Lorca that partly inspires the movie, and appears in one of its several timelines, is about a young man denied access to an elite social club because he’s presumed to be gay. But homophobia isn’t the primary struggle (or a harbinger of death) for the film’s other gay characters. It certainly doesn’t help two doe-eyed young men (played by Miguel Bernardeau and Guitarricadelafuente) brought together and kept apart by the Spanish Civil War. But the forbiddenness of their infatuation is just one current swirling around them, the most pressing of which is, well, the Spanish Civil War.

Weaving the fates of queer characters into the broader scope of history, and suggesting a lineage of ancestry and shared desire, as “La Bola Negra” so marvelously does, feels like a kind of imaginative reparations. And it marks a bolder, more robust tactic in humanizing queer lives; the film traces generational ties and uncovers untold histories, rather than contending with acute crises like religious doctrine or deadly disease.

There is a stranger and more expansive creative palette evidenced in these films, one that suggests the unnerving climate for queer people in the real world is only furthering the reaches of the imagination. In carrying forward the legacy of queer cinema, it seems the gays presumed buried by the trope are finally rising up.
