#3442. 10 Best Boxing Movies To Watch If You Love The Greatest, Ranked

Muhammad Ali could win a fight before throwing a punch. Opponents had to contend with his footwork, his mouth, and the unnerving confidence of a man who seemed to know the outcome. Often, he did. Yet the self-proclaimed greatest became a polarizing public figure, risking his career rather than compromise his convictions.

Prime Video's The Greatest, starring Jaalen Best, brings that complicated life to television. The authorized series explores the relationships and personal consequences behind Ali's victories. For viewers who finish the show wanting more, boxing cinema offers rich stories about people who discover that the toughest fight is often waiting outside the ring.

Some follow real champions. Others invent fighters whose struggles feel familiar, even when their records do not. Rocky and Creed offer underdogs worth cheering for, while Raging Bull makes rooting for its protagonist considerably harder. Even Million Dollar Baby, one of Clint Eastwood's best films of the last 30 years, has more on its mind than the final score.

These 10 films are ranked by their filmmaking, performances, lasting influence, and relevance to the themes of The Greatest. A great sports movie needs more than a convincing final bout. The best ones understand the person who has to climb into the ring, and what remains of that person when the crowd goes home.

There is an irresistible novelty to watching Muhammad Ali play Muhammad Ali. Released in 1977 and based on his autobiography, The Greatest follows the champion from his early career as Cassius Clay through his conversion to Islam, opposition to the Vietnam War, and historic return to heavyweight glory. Nobody could accuse the casting department of getting the leading man wrong.

Ali's charisma survives the awkward dramatic beats, although a great boxer playing himself does not automatically make a great actor. Director Tom Gries delivers a conventional biography of a thoroughly unconventional man. That limitation puts it last, yet it remains fascinating alongside the new series: here is Ali trying to tell his own story while he is still living it.

Denzel Washington received an Academy Award nomination for his portrayal of Rubin "Hurricane" Carter, the middleweight boxer whose career was derailed by a murder conviction. Norman Jewison's The Hurricane spends more time on Carter's imprisonment and struggle for freedom than on his actual fights, making it an unconventional addition to a boxing list. Its punches, however, still land hard.

The connection to Ali is compelling. Both were prominent Black athletes shaped by racial tensions, although their circumstances differed. Washington brings anger and dignity to a screenplay that simplifies disputed aspects of Carter's case. For fans of The Greatest, it broadens the conversation beyond athletic achievement to the consequences of becoming a public figure in a divided country.

James J. Braddock was hardly anyone's idea of a future heavyweight champion during the Great Depression. Injuries and poverty had pushed him toward the docks when an unlikely comeback turned him into a national sensation. Ron Howard tells the story with an old-fashioned Hollywood conviction that makes audiences forget they already know the outcome.

Russell Crowe gives Braddock bruised decency, while Paul Giamatti brings grit as manager Joe Gould. Cinderella Man is more traditional than the films ranked above it, and its inspirational machinery is occasionally visible. Nevertheless, the boxing is forceful. Its portrait of a fighter providing for his family contrasts with Ali, whose public battles were fought on a different stage.

Some boxing movies feature an opponent easier to handle than the fighter's family. David O. Russell's The Fighter follows Micky Ward (Mark Wahlberg), a Massachusetts boxer building a career while his half brother and trainer, Dicky Eklund (Christian Bale), struggles with addiction. Their family is loving, suffocating, and occasionally impossible to watch without wanting to intervene.

Bale and Melissa Leo won Oscars, but the film's real achievement is making Micky's independence feel as thrilling as any title bout. Its humor gives the material breathing room. Ali also had advisers convinced they knew what was best for him. The Fighter understands how hard it is to own a career when your family believes it owns a piece.

Choose the movie with the higher Rotten Tomatoes score.

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

Ryan Coogler faced an unenviable assignment: bring Rocky into a new era without making the original hero look like a museum exhibit. He gave the spotlight to Adonis Johnson (Michael B. Jordan), Apollo Creed's son, who wants a boxing identity independent of his father's reputation. Sylvester Stallone's aging Rocky becomes the trainer rather than the attraction.

The fight choreography feels immediate, and Stallone delivers one of his most affecting performances. There's a direct link to the Prime Video series: Jordan's production company, Outlier Society, helped bring The Greatest to television. Creed ranks below the more accomplished films here, but its understanding of how athletes inherit and resist expectations makes it rewarding after spending time with Ali.

Clint Eastwood's Million Dollar Baby begins with familiar sporting ingredients: a stubborn trainer and a determined outsider everyone underestimates. Hilary Swank plays Maggie Fitzgerald, a waitress desperate to box professionally, while Eastwood is Frankie Dunn, the reluctant coach who eventually agrees to teach her. Their prickly relationship gradually becomes the film's emotional center.

What follows is darker than the usual underdog story. That turn earned debate, along with Best Picture and acting Oscars for Swank and Morgan Freeman. Among Clint Eastwood's greatest movies outside the Western genre, it's one of the most affecting. It ranks fifth because Ali's story takes a different emotional path, although few boxing dramas are better acted.

Will Smith had a difficult assignment in Michael Mann's Ali: persuade audiences to accept another actor inhabiting one of the 20th century's most recognizable personalities. He commits completely, reproducing Ali's physical swagger while finding the uncertainty beneath it. Smith received his first Best Actor Oscar nomination, and the performance remains one of the strongest arguments for his dramatic range.

Mann concentrates on the decade between Ali's first heavyweight title and his 1974 victory over George Foreman, covering events dramatized in The Greatest. The film shows how sporting achievement and political conviction became inseparable. The series has more room for relationships; Mann's film has a muscular visual style and Smith's transformation. They offer different routes into the same complicated life.

Some people admire Jake LaMotta as a boxer; others would cross the street to avoid him. Martin Scorsese's Raging Bull has little interest in reconciling those opinions. Robert De Niro plays LaMotta as a man whose aggression brings success in the ring and ruins nearly everything outside it. The performance won De Niro his second Oscar, deservedly so.

Scorsese's black-and-white photography makes the fights brutal, almost dreamlike spectacles. Yet the scenes that linger are confrontations in cramped apartments. LaMotta's story is the inverse of Ali's: a boxer unable to communicate what is happening inside him, however loudly he shouts. On filmmaking alone, Raging Bull could take first place. The two films ahead connect more directly to The Greatest.

50 years after its release, Rocky remains astonishingly good at making a small victory feel enormous. Sylvester Stallone wrote and starred in the story of Rocky Balboa, a Philadelphia club fighter handed an unlikely shot at heavyweight champion Apollo Creed. The setup is almost a fable, but the film understands the ordinary indignities of being underestimated.

John G. Avildsen's film won Best Picture, influencing nearly every boxing drama that followed. Rocky's relationship with Adrian (Talia Shire) matters as much as training. The ending makes a point most imitators missed: earning respect can matter more than winning on the scorecards. Rocky is the definitive fictional boxing underdog, but first place belongs to Ali himself.

No actor has ever reproduced Muhammad Ali quite like Muhammad Ali. Leon Gast's Oscar-winning documentary When We Were Kings takes viewers to Zaire in 1974 for the "Rumble in the Jungle" against George Foreman. The footage reveals a fighter who can command a crowd with a grin, needle his opponent, and make a political statement without waiting for permission.

Amid 1996 movies that still feel untouchable, When We Were Kings stands apart. Gast captures the event's historical significance and the personalities gathered around it. The music gives the occasion a cultural charge, while the boxing remains thrilling even when its outcome is familiar. It's a documentary with a thriller's momentum, powered by Ali himself.

When We Were Kings earns first place because it offers what a dramatization, however accomplished, cannot: the real Ali in all his magnetism and contradictions. Watch it after The Greatest and the astonishing part is how little exaggeration the series needed. Ali really was that much larger than life.

#3439. Movie Theaters Are Back, but the Rest of Hollywood Seems to Be Crumbling

Movie theater owners have been through hell.

The pandemic forced many of them to shut their doors for months. When they could finally turn their marquees back on, Omicron and other variants made audiences skittish about returning to cinemas. Then the writers’ and actors’ strikes upended production, leaving them with fewer movies to screen. A promised moviegoing revival kept getting delayed or disrupted, often by circumstances outside of the exhibition industry’s control.

At long last, things are finally changing. Domestic ticket sales are up 20 percent year over year, and with potential blockbusters like “Dune: Part Three,” “Avengers: Doomsday,” and “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” on the horizon, analysts expect revenues to easily eclipse $10 billion for the first time since COVID. Grosses in North America currently sit at $8.76 billion through November 15, fueled by franchise fare such as “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “Toy Story 5,” but also by unconventional hits ranging from “Project Hail Mary” and “The Odyssey” to “Obsession” and “You Can See Everything.” Related Stories Desire, Death, and a Breakthrough Year for Queer Cinema ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: They Shoot Franchises, Don’t They?

Audiences are showing up for superhero movies and three-hour documentaries about a convicted felon. And media companies, which treated the theatrical business as the sick man of the entertainment industry, are finally seeing the value in cinemas, with the likes of Amazon MGM Studios and Skydance committing to making more movies for the big screen than most major studios did over the last decade. Better yet, younger viewers are driving the comeback, with studies showing that Gen Z members are the most frequent moviegoers.

That’s the good news. Elsewhere, Hollywood seems to be crumbling. Netflix, which has done more to reshape the entertainment industry this century than arguably any other company, is teetering, having jettisoned both chief content officer Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin in a brutal purge. Ted Sarandos, who is clearly feeling the heat after the company’s stock has fallen 35.6 percent year-to-date, has brought in Peter Rice, a well-regarded former Fox and Disney exec whose calm demeanor and unthreatening good looks are out of c-suite central casting, to steady the ship.

As Hollywood has stumbled around trying to develop a better business model, the solution that many companies have landed on is to get bigger, fast. Thus, Fox sold to Disney, MGM was auctioned off to Amazon, and David Ellison’s Skydance bought Paramount and then quickly merged it with Warner Bros. Others, such as Comcast, spun off assets to make themselves more digestible. Has it worked? That’s the $80 billion question at Skydance, where executives have pledged to make 30 movies a year and turn a combined Paramount+ and HBOMax into a true Netflix challenger. Yet Ellison must pull this off while paying down a massive amount of debt.

So far, their early moves haven’t inspired much confidence. Executives like CBS News chief Bari Weiss have embraced the Silicon Valley ethos of “move fast and break things,” but what they’ve built instead, such as a simulacrum of “60 Minutes,” doesn’t seem better than what they’ve replaced. And if, as a recent Variety story about Skydance’s post-merger strategy suggests, part of their cost savings involves making sure executives don’t send out for “sandwiches and green juices” from Erewhon, they’re in for a world of pain. They can have Jimmy John’s cater lunch, and it won’t make a dent in their debt.

Skydance has already laid off most of Warners’ leadership and offered buyouts to the rank-and-file. Another wave of layoffs is expected at the company any day now. And across town, those types of cuts are the default move, with everyone from Disney and NBCUniversal to Amazon and Sony slashing hundreds of jobs. Are some of these layoffs in anticipation of what a leaner, AI-assisted future might bring? Probably. But with many of these companies’ share prices flatlining or falling, they aren’t being enacted out of foresight or a position of strength.

“I can’t remember a time when things have felt so scary,” an entertainment executive confessed to me recently.

And they’re right. It’s always popular to say the movie business is dying or the television industry is collapsing, and those doomsayers have been proven wrong time and time again. People want to be entertained. It’s just that making money entertaining them has never been harder for Hollywood.

Dynamite had announced in July 2025 that it had acquired the comic-book rights to Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Angel. Then things got much more concrete about resurrecting the IP in 2026 because Buffy got a release date for July 2026, and Angel was supposed to follow in August 2026. But then July came and went with no new Buffy ​​​​​​release.

It was also announced that Kelly Thompson, who is actively working on Absolute Wonder Woman, was attached to Buffy the Vampire Slayer as a writer, with Stephen Byrne as the artist. Thompson is now finally clearing the air about the delays and confusion, and recently went on the Off Panel podcast to unveil the actual reason behind the delays. Not to mention that Angel #1 was supposed to debut on August 19, 2026, and Dynamite Entertainment cancelled all initial retailer orders for this other Thompson series in late August 2026, too. This naturally made some fans wonder whether Dynamite had killed the projects entirely, especially considering that Absolute Wonder Woman kept moving forward.

It hadn’t, and Thompson at the time had clarified that the books had to be re-solicited, so the existing ones had to be cancelled first. During her chat with David Harper, however, Thompson went on to reveal that while “some of the delay was [her] own fault,” there were other legal factors at play. She went on to add: “Part of the reason I haven’t been doing a great job at that is that, for reasons I can’t discuss, that are complicated.” And then Thompson’s clearest possible answer perhaps came out while she expressed her sentiments about the delayed release in the following words:

“Especially with complicated IP and the legal side of things, whatever, there were some things that had to be worked out, and here we are. I’m very excited. We’re finally getting started. If people don’t know, March 2027 is the date. Buffy comes first, and then Angel.”

The contrast with Absolute Wonder Woman explains Thompson’s scheduling problem. Buffy #1 and Angel #1 were both pulled from their schedules and eventually shifted to March 2027 amid creative, publishing, and undisclosed legal complications. Meanwhile, Thompson and Hayden Sherman’s DC series simply kept moving. Absolute Wonder Woman #23 arrived August 26, #24 on September 23, and #25 on October 28, with Absolute Wonder Woman #26 scheduled for November 25. Thompson says Sherman works quickly enough that she has to keep feeding the book scripts. So while the other two faced delays, she had active work available for Absolute Wonder Woman that required her immediate attention, which is probably what she was hinting at while taking responsibility for some of the delays as her own.

#3435. Grand Canyon Small Plane Crash Kills 3

A missing plane that vanished near the Grand Canyon has been found wrecked ... with all three people aboard confirmed dead.

According to the National Park Service, crews located the missing Piper Comanche aircraft and a debris field around 10:15 AM Monday in the Basin area of Grand Canyon National Park's North Rim.

The plane was first reported missing around 11:30 PM Sunday, prompting an extensive search operation ... it was last known to be in the vicinity of the Basin area with three people said to be on board.

Authorities launched an aerial search early Monday morning, with the Arizona Department of Public Safety using forward-looking infrared technology and night vision to try to locate the aircraft, according to NPS. The search effort also included Coconino County Search and Rescue, Kane County Search and Rescue and the Air Force Rescue Coordination Center.

The National Transportation Safety Board says they will investigate the crash, with assistance from the National Park Service, however it's still unclear what caused the plane to go down at this time.

The identities of the passengers have not yet been released.

#3431. 10 Shows Like 'The Traitors' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What started as De Verraders way back in 2021 has become a global reality phenomenon: Peacock in the U.S. hosts the American version with the sartorially supreme Alan Cumming, and also the earlier UK take as well as iterations from Australia, Canada, and New Zealand—but there are spin-offs in France, India, Germany, Ireland, Turkey, and more. Basically, throw a dart at a map and you're likely to hit a country with its own take on The Traitors. And yet! The addictive nature of reality TV means that we can't really ever get enough. In that spirit, here's more backbiting reality TV, and a couple of dramas that offer up similarly duplicitous thrills.

A reality show with a complex history as relates to The Traitors, the premise being so similar that it may well have served as an inspiration. Here, players participate in collaborative missions in order to build a prize fund. But it's not all fun and games: There's a secret double agent among the group (the mole, obviously) whose sole task is to undermine the ability of the rest of the group to earn money. Eliminations are done via quiz: The group is grilled on the information they've collected about the mole, and whoever knows the least gets the boot. Originally airing in the aughts, Netflix brought it back for a couple of seasons more recently, with the potential for more to come. Stream the most recent seasons of The Mole on Netflix.

If there were a prize for dramatic title (and set design), you could do a lot worse than this one. In this South Korean reality show, 12 celebrity contestants are challenged to build a prize pot through strategy games. Sometimes they're collaborative, sometimes entirely competitive, and sometimes a blend, but prizes come in the form of "Pieces" that can be won or lost (and that eventually combine to create their own final puzzle). Anyone who finds themselves without a single Piece is out. Pieces can be spent to buy advantages, and also traded, so the show turns on players forming alliances in order to build the prize pot and survive as long as possible. Stream The Devil's Plan on Netflix.

Here, a bunch of strangers are holed up in an apartment building, cut off from the outside world—and each other. Players can only interact via a custom app, and, thus, can portray themselves however they want, whether that means being 100% genuine (unlikely!) or creating a whole new persona. Players judge the competition based on their interactions, determining the "Influencers" who will get to decide on the eliminations. The show ran for seven seasons on Netflix, and is moving to Hulu for the forthcoming eighth. Stream The Circle on Hulu.

You show up at a fancy hotel, and someone hands you a suitcase containing one million dollars. It's yours to keep—as long as you can keep it a secret. In this one, all the contestants get a suitcase, and only one contains the money. Much as with The Traitors, the goal is to figure out who's keeping the secret, with challenges designed to help flush that person out. If the truth is discovered via a vote, that former millionaire is ousted and the money is concealed in another suitcase until the final contestants are given the opportunity to swap bags with someone who they think has the money. Easy come, easy go, I guess. Stream Million Dollar Secret on Netflix.

I'm a little more into the normies on Traitors myself, but there's no question that a big part of the appeal (for most seasons) is watching reality-show celebs go at it with cash on the line. So it is with House of Villains, a Big Brother-style competition with Joel McHale as ringmaster. The core premise is pretty simple: villains (Richard Hatch, Tom Sandoval, Jonny Fairplay, one-time Trump bestie Omarosa Newman, etc.) compete in challenges for rewards and for safety from the inevitable banishment. It's all mostly an excuse to watch some of TV's biggest personalities go for each other's jugulars. Stream House of Villains on Peacock.

This is not a reality show, but rather a drama about a reality show that may well slake your thirst for treachery while offering up consequences a bit more dramatic than the bruised egos and hurt feelings of The Traitors. Here, eight strangers are selected to compete in a game in which they're locked together in a building and sequestered on different floors each night. They earn money for each minute they last in the game, but all their provisions must be purchased with money they've won, at an extreme markup. At first, the contestants pool their resources so that everyone gets more money—until they learn that people on higher floors are getting more. Then things get nasty Stream The 8 Show on Netflix.

This one plays a bit like The Traitors in reverse: A $250,000 prize pot is, right off the bat, allocated to all 11 contestants who get to hang out in a luxurious villa. So the game isn't about winning money so much as it is about how much you'll keep and how much you're willing to share. Eliminations offer the opportunity to remove those who the others don't want to share with—though contestants don't have to actually ever vote anyone out. They can just keep their portion of the money and hang out, something that obviously does not happen. Challenges along the way force contestants to reveal embarrassing and sometimes ugly truths about themselves that may well put them on the outs with the others. There's only one season at present, though there's potential for more. Stream The Trust on Netflix.

Blending the Big Brother-esque social aspects of Traitors with Survivor's love of the great outdoors, this one drops four teams of four into the Alaskan wilderness (moving to Panama for season three). The contestants are all, by inclination, loners, but the game has only one core rule: Only a team (of at least two) can win, so while the game has the typical reality show eliminations, these wilderness enthusiasts must work together in order to take the money. In the same way that The Traitors creates a tension between competition and cooperation via its communal prize pot, Outlast sees its contestants forced to maintain relationships whether they like it or not. Stream Outlast on Netflix.

The tasks on Traitors aren't typically the most thrilling part of the show, which makes this James Bond-branded competition a solid match if you want more complicated and better developed challenges. In this one, nine teams of two visit exotic locations in each episode and compete in spy-themed activities with the ultimate goal of winning £1 million by making it to the end. It leaves out the bits where people sit around a castle strategizing, but it includes, like Traitors, a dapper Scotsman not afraid to camp it up—in this case, Brian Cox, serving as the spymaster who directs the teams in their missions. Stream 007: Road to a Million on Prime Video.

Squid Game: The Challenge would probably be a more reasonable choice for this list—given that it's a proper reality show and not a blood-chilling thriller. But I'm sticking with the original drama here since, as perfectly entertaining as that spin-off is, it feels like it misses the point. In the original (surprise smash hit) drama, 454 needy contestants are recruited for a new reality competition in which they're tasked to play rather simple children's games—with deadly consequences that are cheered on by the wealthy financiers who are willing to pay good money to watch both the poors go at each other, as people turn on each other to survive and to win the rather shockingly large prize. A bit like The Traitors if all of Alan's murder schtick were literally true. Stream Squid Game on Netflix.

#3430. Google’s new Android XR glasses work with iOS, Made for iPhone certified

Google today announced Android XR audio glasses called Intelligent Eyewear that notably support iOS with Made for iPhone certification.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

Intelligent Eyewear is made by Samsung with frame designs from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker. There are 30 unique designs in total, and the frames weigh 40-44 grams with a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera.

Google’s Glasses companion client for iOS handles compute, including HDR processing, and saves images and videos (up to 90 seconds) to Apple Photos. The Made for iPhone certification comes into play for Wi-Fi Aware connectivity that allows for fast media transfers.

Gemini commands that use the camera, like visual search or translation, don’t trigger the light because those photos or videos are not saved anywhere, including Gemini History. Before that media reaches the cloud, Google redacts faces from video feeds and filters out bystander voices. This processing is done by the companion app. Additionally, that media isn’t used to train AI models or target ads.

Other key specifications include four microphones and two open-ear speakers. Besides voice commands with the “Hey Gemini” hotword, there is a touchpad that accepts taps and swipes. A physical on/off switch lets you wear Intelligent Eyewear as regular glasses.

On iOS, Gemini can make calls, send 1:1 messages (including via iMessage), and receive notifications.

Battery life is rated at nine hours on a single charge, while there’s a charging case that stores seven charges. Features include turn-by-turn Google Maps directions and real-time translation. On the streaming front, there’s support for Apple Music, Spotify, YouTube Music, and Audible.

Google’s Android XR glasses require an iPhone 13 Pro or newer.

Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear is available in three frame designs, starting at $395 for optical and sun styles. Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear is available in the US and South Korea from $449.

Pre-orders open today with retail availability on December 10.

#3428. ‘The Rings of Power’ Is Officially Being Review-Bombed on Rotten Tomatoes

He has covered everything from Marvel to the Oscars, and Marvel at the Oscars. He also writes obsessively about the box office, charting the many hits and misses that are released weekly, and how their commercial performance shapes public perception. In his time at Collider, he has also helped drive diversity by writing stories about the multiple Indian film industries, with a goal of introducing audiences to a whole new world of cinema.

There's a chasm between critics and audiences that occasionally becomes wider and more noticeable. For instance, several of Dwayne Johnson's recent movies — Red One, Black Adam, and even the Moana live-action remake — have all earned solid audience scores on Rotten Tomatoes despite having been poorly reviewed. The reverse of this phenomenon is equally prevalent. Just as a star can get their army of fans to rally behind a critically panned film, fans can also organize a mob to take down any film or show that goes against their values and beliefs.

This act of targeted hate designed to affect a film or show's popularity rating on an aggregator website has come to be known as review bombing. Typically, such campaigns are orchestrated by disgruntled fans who object to the most basic progressive ideas, such as inclusivity and diversity. This is one of the reasons why titles that have been most affected by review-bombing tend to feature actors or filmmakers from minority groups. Take, for example, Star Wars: Episode VIII — The Last Jedi, the series The Acolyte, and HBO's The Last of Us.

One of the biggest examples of audiences outright rejecting a major new project and making their dislike felt online is The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power. The mega-budget streaming series recently returned with a third season on Prime Video, and while the reviews have been mostly solid, the fan reaction has been predictably unpleasant.

The Rings of Power premiered in 2022 amid reports that Prime Video invested $250 million before the show's release and committed $1 billion over five seasons. The first season of the show clocked 150 million views, according to Amazon, but reports suggested that the series struggled to retain audiences for the duration of its eight-episode run. The second season saw similar issues. The third season is getting an unusual rollout, beginning with four episodes out of the gate, with two more the next week and the final two the week after that.

The Rings of Power holds an overall 83% critics' score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, but its audience score is languishing at 53%. The first season was most affected, with a 38% audience score based on more than 25,000 ratings. The third season, on the other hand, holds a 68% audience score. Viewers have been comparing the show to Peter Jackson's landmark film series, while also questioning some of the creative decisions and casting choices. You can watch The Rings of Power on Prime Video and make up your own mind. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3427. Five Things I Wish I'd Known Before Getting a Foldable Phone

The iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first. Personally, I’ve had my eye on the Google variant, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold—and recently I finally took the plunge. I thought I’d done my research to know how different having a foldable phone would be, but I still had a bit to learn. Here are some of the things I wish I’ve learned along the way after making the jump to foldables.

One of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed. And there’s a good reason for that: The larger screen while open has exactly the same 1.41:1 aspect ratio as the smaller screen while closed. This has a ripple effect on how every app you use looks and feels—and whether you like Apple’s approach is largely a matter of personal preference.

Compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open. On the outer screen, apps are a little less wide than on my old phone, but there’s plenty of space for reading books or articles on the inner screen.

I like the tall, thin display personally because it feels easier to reach buttons with my thumb, and the wider display is better for reading. However, this approach can occasionally result in some odd app layouts. Not every app is designed for tablets, especially on Android, and shifting the aspect ratio between the inner and outer display sometimes means re-rendering or even restarting an app entirely to load properly.

The iPhone Duo has a more consistent aspect ratio and general feel between the inner and outer display, but it comes at the cost of a really wide phone. Neither approach is better or worse on its own, but it might be worth going to a local store to get your hands on the phone you’re thinking about before buying.

For years, the screens on most smartphones have been made of increasingly tough and scratch-resistant glass. So tough that you might not even need a screen protector anymore. On a foldable phone, that can be true of the outside display, but it’s very much not when it comes to the inner, foldable display.

Screens might be foldable, but the strong, durable glass that makes your phone so scratch-resistant isn’t. No matter what foldable phone you use, the covering on the inner display will be more flexible, and thus softer. Apple uses a nano-texture polymer film that can be replaced, but the film on most foldable phones cannot. That means if they get damaged or scratched, those marks will be there for the life of your phone.

If you (like me) haven’t considered a screen protector in a while, it might be time to try one again, at least for the inner display. It’s also worth keeping in mind how rough you plan to be with your phone. Construction sites or factories might not be the best home for a foldable phone you plan to open a lot, but an office job should be a bit safer.

Similar to the screen protector issue, cases can be more of a headache. Most rigid cases will come in two pieces, and the piece that covers the outer display can be shockingly minimal—barely more than a frame, for some of the cases I looked at. A poorly made case can be brittle or pop off more easily, so it’s more important to get a high-quality one.

If you like to use your phone case as your wallet, it’s also important to be wary of cases that aren’t specifically designed for your model of phone (and maybe some that are). A lot of wallet cases are built to unfold to reveal your phone’s screen on one side, and your cards and ID on the other. But depending on how your foldable phone unfolds, it could be awkward to reach the inner screen.

The hinge also introduces more spaces for dust and debris to get into your phone. Despite the extra moving parts and gaps, most foldable phones still offer the now-standard IP68 dust and water resistance rating. That mainly applies to what can get inside and damage the components inside your phone. It’s still possible for hair and dirt to get gummed up in any pinchable spaces, so look out for any case that might provide even more nooks for dust to collect in.

I’ve set up most of my apps how I like them by now, but when I first got my foldable phone, I had to revisit some settings I thought I was done messing with. One of the most notable examples was my ebook apps: I was previously using a single-column, medium-font layout, but it looked ridiculous on the inner display. After switching to a two-column layout, it not only felt more natural, but a lot like reading a regular book.

Similarly, there were some uses for my calendar app that got a whole lot more useful. I’ve never really been able to use anything other than either the one-day or Schedule view if I want to make out anything, but on the inner screen, I can finally look at my week at a glance. But that meant tweaking some things—like showing reminders, which fit naturally amid my events in Schedule view, but become a cluttered mess when I saw 14 different reminders to take my meds at once in the Week view.

Most apps do a decent job of automatically adjusting to different screen sizes, but I found a few outliers that I had to figure out myself. As an example, Google Docs would default to a view with extremely tiny text when I first started using it. It took me a bit to figure out that this was due to a “Print layout” toggle in the document’s settings. This is, for some reason, enabled by default when opening a document on the larger inner screen. It can take some time to learn the eccentricities of all your apps, but it’s worth poking around when you can.

I know, it sounds so obvious, right? The outer screen is the one you’ll use most often, so how could you forget about it? But when you unfold the inner screen, the outer one is still useful in some surprising ways that I hadn’t even considered until I went poking around in some of my apps.

One of the most adorable examples is the Made You Look feature in the Pixel’s Camera app. When unfolded, you can take a picture using the rear camera and see a preview like normal, while the outer screen shows silly animations to capture the attention of a baby or toddler that you want to look into the camera. Admittedly, this is an older feature, but it’s a clever one. For adults, you can also use the outer display to get a selfie preview while using the rear-facing camera.

The outer screen is also just better for some things. YouTube is one of the few apps that has a unique layout designed for a partially folded screen, with the video playing on the tilted-up portion of the screen, and video controls on the bottom portion.

However, in my experience, it was a lot nicer to watch a YouTube video by just propping up the outer screen by unfolding the phone a bit, like a kickstand. My Pixel even detected when YouTube was in full-screen mode on the outer display and would be more forgiving of unfolding the phone without switching to the inner screen. The phone anticipated I might just want to prop up the smaller screen, which I thought was a nice touch.

#3425. Netflix's Epic Sci-Fi Series Is Officially Not Returning In 2026

Netflix's epic science fiction TV series is not going to be returning to the streamer in 2026, and viewers are going to have to wait until 2027 for the next season. We thankfully seem to have moved past the years of Netflix canceling shows at the drop of a hat. Now, if you see a show you like, you don't have to worry it's going to be canceled before it really gets going.

Still, Netflix faces the same production issues as other streaming services. There will always be delays and shows moved from one year to the next. Netflix might have gotten its act together in terms of giving its original series longer leashes, but that doesn't mean you should expect a new season every year.

3 Body Problem is a good example. The hit sci-fi series premiered in 2024, and fans have been waiting for season 2 ever since. Unfortunately, it's not arriving anytime before the end of the year. Based on Liu Cixin's novel series, Remembrance of Earth's Past, 3 Body Problem adapts the first book in the trilogy.

The series brings together a group of scientists, engineers, and thinkers from China and London who are all attempting to make contact with aliens at the height of the Cold War. What they find could alter humanity's future forever. This is the third adaptation of the story, but the first to be made primarily in English.

The series premiered in March 2024 and went on to earn a 78% on Rotten Tomatoes and garnered an Emmy nomination. Two months later, the series was renewed for a second and third season, ostensibly to cover the next two books in the series, but fans are going to have to wait a little longer.

3 Body Problem is set to return for season 2 in January 2027, so those hoping for the next installment of the series before New Year's Eve may be annoyed, but can also be glad the show at least has an official release date, and one that is not all that far away, considering how long they've been waiting.

The series is set to premiere on January 14, 2026, with all eight episodes dropping simultaneously. Artwork for season 2 suggests that the extraterrestrials at the center of the show are making their arrival to Earth. Hopefully, the nearly three-year wait for season 3 doesn't suggest another three-year wait for season 3.

3 Body Problem was a big success for Netflix when it aired. It was nominated for Best Drama at the Emmys, losing to Shōgun, and also nabbed several nominations at the Creative Arts Emmys. It was an ambitious task to take on 3 Body Problem considering its complex story and that it was originally written in Chinese.

It seems to have paid off for Netflix, however, and it's one of the streamer's best sci-fi TV shows. David Benioff, D. B. Weiss, and Alexander Woo managed to take the nerdy, complex story that Woo wrote (he's a former computer engineer) and make it palatable for the masses without dumbing everything down.

The series takes its time setting the stage, and it's only towards the latter half of the season that you begin to understand where the story is going. 3 Body Problem season 2 won't have that problem, and now that the place-setting is done, the series can get right into the thick of things.

#3424. The Unexpected History of 'Black Friday'

Since the 1950s, Black Friday—once simply known as "the day after Thanksgiving"—has grown into a quasi-holiday in the United States marked by steep discounts, ceaseless shopping, and occasional violence. But more recently, Black Friday has also metastasized. It's not a day anymore. It's a week, a month, a veritable state of mind. (Speaking of which, check out Lifehacker's Black Friday coverage. We got all the deals, baby!)

While pre-dawn trips to the mall are waning as online shopping grows, in-person shopping on Black Friday is still a big deal in the U.S.—it’s estimated that around 80 million Americans visited a brick-and-mortar store on Black Friday in 2025. But how did Black Friday come about, and what does it all mean?

“Black Friday” in the United States originally referred to the start of the Panic of 1869, when the collapse of the price of gold devastated the national economy. “Black Friday” as a description of the day after Thanksgiving dates back to 1951; the term first appeared in the journal Factory Management and Maintenance, where it referred to the number of employees who skipped work on the day after Thanksgiving. Around the same time, the police in Philadelphia and Rochester started informally using “Black Friday” to describe the traffic and crowds that appeared in their cities as shoppers hit the stores on the day after Thanksgiving. The phrase gradually caught on. It was picked up by national press in 1975 when the New York Times used "Black Friday" specifically to describe the day after Thanksgiving and the shopping and sales it brings.

But even before it had a name, Black Friday was a thing. The day after Thanksgiving has been known by merchants as the start of the shopping season since the late 1800s. By the early 20th century, retailers sponsored Thanksgiving Day parades that traditionally ended with an appearance by Santa Claus, as if to say, “Now it’s time to shop for Christmas.” By unspoken agreement among retailers, Christmas-themed advertisements rarely appeared before Thanksgiving in our grandparents’ day. This informal bargain obviously no longer applies.

Referring to a day as “black” traditionally denotes a period of calamity or tragedy, leading some to suggest different names for the day. In the early 1960s, Philadelphia merchants suggested “Big Friday,” a name which did not catch on, leaving retailers with the weak explanation that the “black” in Black Friday refers to the black ink denoting profits in a ledger. Oft-repeated lore suggests that retailers are "in the red" all year, and only start making an annual profit at the end of the year, but big retail chains generally make money all year long.

A more modern issue with the name is that Black Friday sales now last for days or even weeks, beginning in early to mid-November and bleeding over into the following Saturday, Sunday, “Cyber Monday,” Tuesday, and beyond, leading people to say things like, “Do you want to go Black Friday shopping this Sunday?” So far, alternative names like “Five-Day Frenzy” and “The day I get to trample someone to save $8 on a Nespresso” haven’t caught on. But here’s hoping.

Beginning around 2010, an insatiable thirst for profits led many retailers to push the start of Black Friday shopping to Thursday (aka Thanksgiving Day). Kmart opened Thanksgiving morning. Toys R Us opened that night. By 2011, Walmart was opening its doors at 10 p.m. on Thursday. The trend led to widespread backlash, with many Americans appalled that employees were forced to work on Thanksgiving or angry that consumerism was encroaching upon a holiday meant to celebrate colonialism. By 2021, most major retailers had relented and elected to remain closed on Thanksgiving.

The term “Cyber Monday” describes the boost in online retail sales on the Monday after Thanksgiving, sparked by workers returning to the office and getting right to online shopping. The term first appeared on Nov. 28, 2005, in a Shop.org press release entitled “'Cyber Monday’ Quickly Becoming One of the Biggest Online Shopping Days of the Year," which may be the most influential press release ever written. Since its early 2000s birth, Cyber Monday has become the biggest online shopping day of the year. Americans spent $14.25 billion online on Cyber Monday 2025, according to Adobe Analytics. So is Cyber Monday bigger than Black Friday? Retailers really don't care: Analysts now tend to mash everything into the category of "Black Friday–Cyber Monday" (or even "Cyber Week").

If all this naked consumerism makes you a little squeamish, you're not alone. Anti-consumerists have named the day after Thanksgiving “Buy Nothing Day,” which you can celebrate by doing charity work, cutting up your credit cards, or simply not purchasing anything. Pioneered by artist Ted Dave and popularized by Adbusters magazine, the first Buy Nothing Day was celebrated in Canada in 1992.

It’s hard to measure the success of the alternative holiday. Both online and brick-and-mortar retail sales have increased sharply since 1992, suggesting Buy Nothing Day’s effect is negligible. On the other hand, maybe big retailers are losing millions because someone on Bluesky reminded you not to shop. Sure.

Depending on how you measure it, Black Friday has resulted in between one and 17 deaths. Jdimytai Damour is the only person killed directly due to a Black Friday sale: The 34-year-old worker was trampled to death by a surging crowd at a Long Island Walmart on Black Friday in 2008. If you include car accidents, shootings, retail worker suicides, and fatal heart attacks, Black Friday’s death toll balloons to 17, with 128 reported injuries.

Black Friday violence has even inspired a horror flick: Eli Roth's 2023 holiday-themed slasher Thanksgiving opens with a hilariously brutal Black Friday riot at a big box store, setting off a chain of events that involve a lot of people being murdered by a dude in a Pilgrim mask.

I mean, yeah, of course. Critics of Black Friday point out that there are arguably better times to buy a new TV (like the week before the Super Bowl), not to mention plenty of other goods. Savings from Black Friday shopping are often illusory—big-ticket “doorbuster” items generally sell out quickly, leaving behind goods that are, by and large, priced the same as they would be at any other time of year. Some retailers even mark up products ahead of Black Friday so the discounts look bigger. If you're buying online, your browser history, location, and cart contents can tweak the prices you see on Black Friday, as they can on any other day.

Yet despite protest holidays, the unpleasantness of shopping when stores are overcrowded, and the frustration of hunting for bargains that often aren't that great to begin with, Black Friday stubbornly remains an unofficial holiday, celebrated by over 100 million Americans in one way or another. What that says about our country's relationship with capitalism is unclear, but personally, I’m going to continue my own day-after-Thanksgiving tradition of eating pie for breakfast and thinking about going for a walk, but then watching The Quick and the Dead instead. I'm not protesting anything; I just don't need the hassle.

#3420. Walmart’s 2026 Black Friday and Cyber Monday Sales Are Now Live

If you're thinking of picking up any big-ticket items—whether for yourself or as a gift for someone on your list— I would advise you not to sleep on Walmart's sale. Walmart is the first major retailer to announce and kick off its Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale for 2026, and they're actually holding three major shopping events between now and the December holidays.

Walmart will hold three sales between Nov. 12 and Dec. 2, as outlined in a recent press release. The sales will be both online and in-store, and will target a mix of Walmart+ members and general shoppers.

The events will take place on three different dates:

Walmart's Black Friday Deals Event 1: Nov. 12–15

Available online and in stores starting at 6 a.m. local time

Walmart+ members get six hours of early access beginning online at 12:01 a.m. ET on Nov. 12

Walmart's Black Friday Deals Event 2: Nov. 23–29

Online only: Nov. 23 starting at 12:01 a.m. ET

Online and in stores: Nov. 27 starting at 6 a.m. local time

Walmart+ members get six hours of early access online beginning Nov. 23 at 12:01 a.m. ET

Walmart's Cyber Monday Deals Event: Nov. 30-Dec. 2

Walmart's physical stores will open at 6:00 a.m. local time on Nov. 27 for their Black Friday events. Of course, they will start online earlier, so make sure to check their website as well.

Walmart says that they will have discounts on electronics, toys, fashion, beauty, home goods, gifts, and everyday essentials. No. But if you are a Walmart+ member, you'll get early access to the sale. You can sign up for a free 30-day Walmart+ subscription and cancel it afterwards or get the annual plan for $98 ($8.17/month).

In short, yes. Though they aren't quite as impactful as they once were, Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales offer discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. Whether it's a major purchase you've been saving up for or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts, especially on items like appliances and electronics. Last year's sales included categories such as tech, home improvement, and fitness.

Black Friday used to be when major retailers offered their best deals on expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Now, however, the distinction is almost meaningless: Every major retailer offers sales on both days, which means the smart move is to know what you want, use price trackers to monitor the deals, and refer to our Black Friday coverage, where we do all the searching, curating, and price tracking for you.

The mother of the missing baby who was buried alive is speaking out after her ex's arrest.

Dezarae Sharp broke her silence in a new interview with The New York Times, detailing her rocky relationship and the harrowing texts she got from her baby's father before he allegedly buried their son alive.

According to court records, things with her son's father, Michael Comer, took a turn in May, when he allegedly tripped her, kicked her and shoved her into a dryer while she was holding baby Koah.

After that, they broke up, he spent a few months in jail -- for a different charge -- and Comer moved in with his mother.

Dezarae says Comer's mother had reached out to her asking if he could see Koah, explaining he'd stopped drinking and was on schizophrenia meds ... so she agreed to let the baby spend weekends with Comer and his mother.

But recently, Comer sent her texts about not being satisfied with co-parenting, allegedly writing ... "I don’t want to take him. I want us to be a family."

And after sending several unanswered messages, Comer allegedly wrote ... "I got toooo heated about the situation so I get not speaking to me anymore. I want to be a family with real trust."

As you know, Koah was found buried alive inside a dog crate in the woods last week ... 24 hours after his father allegedly ran off with him.

The 11-month old was discovered under some freshly disturbed dirt, with muffled cries coming from underground.

Dezarae told NYT she "didn’t think he could go that far," saying ... "It’s something you would see in a movie. It’s something you would see on TV. And the fact that it happened to [Koah] -- I don’t know."

Comer was arrested and charged with attempted murder, unlawful conduct toward a child, custodial interference and burglary.

#3416. Hunger Games: Every Known Winner (& How They Won)

Spoilers ahead for Sunrise On The Reaping!Katniss Everdeen may be the most famous Hunger Games victor ever, but she's just one of many who have survived the Capitol's competition. Across the franchise, Suzanne Collins has introduced several winners whose stories have helped shed light on Panem's violent history, the evolution of the games, and the Capitol's lasting cruelty towards the Districts.

The original trilogy follows Katniss and her journey, while the prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes expands the story, focusing on District 12 winner Lucy Gray Baird. Then, with the second prequel, Sunrise on the Reaping, the universe expanded even more with the full story of Haymitch's Games, aka the Second Quarter Quell.

In Panem, the annual Hunger Games were first established by the Capitol after the First Rebellion as a way to punish the districts. This way, it serves as a constant reminder of the Capitol's power. Each year, one boy and one girl between the ages of 12 and 18 are selected from each district and forced to fight to the death inside a televised arena. The lone survivor is crowned victor and earns a lifetime of wealth, fame, and status.

Between the books and movie series, Collins has filled in the blanks surrounding the many victors of Panem, revealing how they won and what became of them after leaving the arena. Though 75 Hunger Games took place, only 74 were completed. That said, Katniss' first games featured special circumstances, meaning there were 74 total victors before the games came to an end. Through the movies and the books, a lot can be revealed about the various Hunger Games winners, how they became victorious, and what happened to them afterward.

With Sunrise on the Reaping, there's now even more to explore about the Games and their origin, way before Katniss ever volunteered as tribute.

Years before District 12's Haymitch Abernathy won the games, 16-year-old Lucy Gray Baird took the honor as the victor in the 10th annual event. Lucy Gray was mentored by Coriolanus Snow, the future president of Panem, and their relationship is the focus of the prequel movie The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. The tribute hid for the duration of the games while receiving help from Snow from the outside before poisoning some of the participants. In the movie, she won after being the only tribute not attacked by snakes in the arena.

Lucy Gray Baird is played by Rachel Zegler in the prequel movie. It is revealed that Lucy Gray was purposely reaped for the Hunger Games because of her relationship with Mayor Lipp's daughter's boyfriend. As she makes plans to escape District 12, Snow attempts to kill her, but it is unclear if he succeeded or if she made it to freedom. Though Lucy Gray is different from Katniss in many ways, she shares that heroic rebellious spirit.

The following year after Lucy Gray Baird's victory, another female tribute emerged as the Hunger Games winner. Mags Flanagan became the first victor from District 4, living off of nuts and her survival skills by creating fishhooks. She was also the first victor to move to Victor’s Village before serving as a mentor. During the 75th Hunger Games, Mags volunteered in place of Annie Cresta, but she passed away during the event from an acid fog.

Mags was played by Lynn Cohen in The Hunger Games: Catching Fire. She was the oldest tribute to fight in the 75th Hunger Games which was made up of past victors. Mags was also very close with fellow District 4 winner Finnick Odair who she mentored and practically raised. During the games, she was unable to move quickly and got carried by Finnick until she decided to sacrifice herself to allow the group to continue. Many Hunger Games fans have been hoping for a prequel story about the fan-favorite character.

Beetee and Wiress were two victors from District 3. Beetee was victorious by building an electronic trap in the arena, while Wiress won the Hunger Games by being able to figure out how to hide in her year's mirror arena, navigating light beams to find safety until all the other tributes eliminated each other. Both former victors were chosen for the 75th Hunger Games where they aligned with Katniss. While both assisted with Katniss' survival in the Quarter Quell, Wiress died during the event.

In Catching Fire, Beetee is played by Jeffrey Wright while Wiress is played by Amanda Plummer. While Wiress was killed during the games, Beetee managed to survive and was revealed to be a key ally in the Second Rebellion, helping Katniss destroy the forcefield around the arena so they could escape. He returned in The Hunger Games: Mockingjay Part 1 using a wheelchair due to his injuries in the games and remained a big part of the rebellion.

At only 16 years old, Haymitch Abernathy became the second District 12 tribute to win the Hunger Games. Unlike a typical year, the 50th Hunger Games were celebrated as the Second Quarter Quell. This time around, the tributes were doubled. So, now, each district had to send four tributes to compete in the Games.

Haymitch's victory ultimately came down to a confrontation with District 1's last-remaining tribute, Silka. After throwing an axe at Haymitch, the weapon ricocheted off the arena's invisible force field hitting her instead. She accidentally killed herself and Haymitch won.

However, Haymitch's win came at a massive cost. Because he discovered the force field and used it to his advantage, President Snow felt that he'd embarrassed the Capitol. As punishment, all of Haymitch's loved ones were killed, thus sending him into a lifelong alcohol addiction.

Haymitch is played by Woody Harrelson in the original film series and Joseph Zada is taking on the younger version of the character in the Sunrise on the Reaping film adaptation. He becomes an integral part of the Second Rebellion using everything he learned from his Games, and the aftermath, to help Katniss and Peeta destroy the system that ruined his life.

Finnick Odair won the 65th Hunger Games when he was just 14 years old. As a male tribute from District 4, he was mentored by Mags. He was already skilled in fighting but the use of a trident in the arena led to his big win, as did the various gifts sent by sponsors. Like Mags, Finnick participated in the Third Quarter Quell and made an alliance with Katniss.

While Katniss didn't initially want to ally with him, she also didn't know how he had been used by the wealthy members of society of the Capitol or about his relationship with Annie Cresta. The more she learned about Finnick's dark story post-victory, the more she bonded with him.

Finnick is played by Sam Clafin when the character is introduced in Catching Fire. After allying with Katniss and the others in the 75th games, Finnick was rescued and became part of the rebellion. Sadly, Finnick was killed off in The Hunger Games: Mockingjay Part 2 during the attack on the Capitol.

Johanna Mason, a tribute from District 7, was the 71st Hunger Games winner. She pretended to be weak so that she wasn't viewed as a threat, but when the opportunity arose, Johanna attacked with fierce intensity. Being from the lumber district, she was skilled at ax-wielding. Johanna was reaped in the Third Quarter Quell since she was the only living female tribute from her district.

Johanna was played by Jenna Malone in the movies. As Katniss was key to the rebellion, Johanna was recruited to help her survive the 75th Games and to facilitate her rescue. While Johanna succeeded in her mission, she was captured along with Peeta. After being tortured by the Capitol, Johanna was freed by the rebel forces and later joined them when she recovered. She managed to survive, lived in what used to be District 13 during the uprising, and presumably was able to return to District 7.

Whereas Peeta Mellark was reaped into the 74th Hunger Games, Katniss Everdeen volunteered in place of her little sister. Both tributes from District 12 survived deep into the games before reuniting. Katniss had her archery skills while Peeta was skilled in camouflage. As the last two tributes, the pair made a suicide pact until the Gamemaker announced that they could share the victory. Katniss and Peeta returned as tributes in the Third Quarter Quell.

Jennifer Lawrence plays Katniss in the movies while Peeta is played by Josh Hutcherson. The fabricated romance between Katniss and Peeta was a popular narrative among the public and a big reason why they survived the games. While the games were used by President Snow to keep the districts in line, Katniss became a symbol within the Games which was ultimately used to bring down Snow and the Capitol.

Woof (unknown games): District 8 male who hid during the entire event. He joined the 75th Hunger Games in his 70s and quickly died.

Seeder (unknown games): District 11 female who outlived opponents by going without food. She was in her 60s during the 75th Hunger Games and died during the Cornucopia fight at the beginning.

Porter Millicent Tripp (38th Hunger Games): District 5 female who won despite a serious spinal cord injury. She was in her mid-50s and avoided the 75th games, but as she is not present among the surviving Hunger Games winners for President Coin's vote of the final Hunger Games, she presumably died during the Second Rebellion.

Chaff (45th Hunger Games): District 11 male who won with his brute power while fighting. He was in his mid-40s when he fought in the 75th Hunger Games. He made it late into the games but was killed by Brutus.

Brutus (unknown games): District 2 male career tribute. He was in his late 40s during the 75th Hunger Games and was killed by Peeta.

Lyme (unknown games): District 2 female career tribute. She was a middle-aged victor by the time the 75th Hunger Games began, and while she was not reaped, she was part of the rebellion afterward.

Blight (unknown games): District 7 male who used an ax to win his event. He was in his 30s during the 75th Hunger Games when he was killed after running into the forcefield.

Cecelia (unknown games): District 8 female that used intelligence and sword fighting. She was a mother in her 30s by the time she was reaped in the 75th Hunger Games where she was killed in the opening massacre at the Cornucopia.

Enobaria (62nd Hunger Games): District 2 female career tribute that had sharpened teeth to rip competitors' throats out. She was in her mid to late teens when she first was reaped and is in her late 20s or early 30s during the 75th Hunger Games. Though she fought against Katniss and her allies in the games, she was rescued by the rebels and joined them.

Gloss (63rd Hunger Games): District 1 male career tribute who had knife-throwing skills and was in his mid to late teens when he won. He returned in his late 20s for the 75th Hunger Games where he was killed by Katniss.

Cashmere (64th Hunger Games): District 1 female career tribute who was also skilled in knife-throwing. She joined the 75th Hunger Games in her late 20s and was killed by Johanna.

Augustus Baun (67th Hunger Games): District 1 male career tribute. He was not reaped in the 75th Hunger Games but died sometime during the Second Rebellion.

Annie Cresta (70th Hunger Games): District 4 female who won due to her swimming skills. She was in her early 20s when the 75th Hunger Games took place but was spared when Mags volunteered as tribute. She later married Finnick and had his child after he was killed.

Out of all the Hunger Games winners that are known in the movies and books, it is clear one district rises above the others. As the entire list of winners is not known, judging by the information known, it appears that District 2 has the most Hunger Games victors with five in total.

That isn't surprising given that they produce "Career Tributes" along with District 1 which has three victors and District 3, which has two winners. District 12 has the most prominent victors with Katniss, Peeta, Haymitch, and Lucy Gray making up its four winners. As for the rest, District 4 has three while Districts 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11 have two each.

Although not all 74 winners are mentioned or known to readers and viewers throughout the series, there are some intriguing facts about certain winners that help them stand out. As noted, District 2 having the most winners is important, as are the prominent winners from District 12.

Gloss and Cashmere won in consecutive years and were both from District 1, which is the only time that a District had repeat winners in back-to-back years (though District 12 was likely to do so in the 75th Games). Gloss and Cashmere are also the only sibling winners in Hunger Games history. District 12 also had the distinction of having three previous winners still living by the end of the war in Katniss, Peeta, and Haymitch, which was incredibly rare since the Capitol made sure living winners were executed during the events of the Second Rebellion.

With The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, Sunrise on the Reaping, as well as other lines about unnamed victors in the Hunger Games novels, it's evident that Suzanne Collins has plenty more Hunger Games history to explore.

The Hunger Games is a multi-movie franchise starring Jennifer Lawrence as Katniss Everdeen. The films are based on the young adult dystopian book series by author Suzanne Collins. The first film was released in 2012, followed by Catching Fire in 2013, Mockingjay Part 1 in 2014, and Mockingjay Part 2 in 2015. In 2023, the fifth film in the series was released, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.

#3409. Google announces Gemini 4 Hydrogen with ‘significant leaps’ in speed, intelligence

After this week’s Carbon availability, Google today unveiled Gemini 4 Hydrogen instead of keeping the “Flash” branding. This model is billed as bringing “cutting-edge intelligence to everyone.”

Compared to Gemini 3.8 Flash (which launched in September), Hydrogen is billed as a “major standalone upgrade” with “significant leaps in both speed and intelligence.” It offers native 1 million-token input and up to 1 million output tokens. Specifically:

“Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class.”

In the Gemini app, Hydrogen is better at following and sticking to your tone, format, and rules, while offering clear tables and visual breakdowns. As such, “email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try.” Additionally, Hydrogen “more frequently calls the right tools (i.e., Connected Apps) and skills for the job.”

In the model picker, 4 Hydrogen is billed as providing “Everyday help.”

Free users in the Gemini app get access to Hydrogen via the “[Auto] model selection when it’s the appropriate model for the prompt.”

Google says Hydrogen significantly upgrades Search (AI Mode) by better understanding your intent:

…you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for.

Responses get more visual and will feature a wider range of relevant links. Hydrogen is the default model for AI Mode and is used for “your hardest questions” in AI Overviews.

This was a nice surprise when I opened the app an hour or two ago. It seems to be noticeably better, too.

In Google Antigravity, 4 Hydrogen has an “Extra” thinking tier alongside Low, Medium, and High. Then there’s Orchestrator: “Carbon that may offload routine steps to Hydrogen. Same Carbon-level quality, fewer tokens used.”

To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity. Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session.

For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.

For developers, Hydrogen costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.

#3404. Kid Rock's Nashville Bar Sued By Man Who Claims Security Guards Beat Him Up

Kid Rock's honky tonk has been dealing with some legal drama all summer long ... because the controversial rock star's Nashville bar is being sued by a man who claims security guards went overboard and beat him senseless.

A man named Joshua Welch is suing Kid Rock's Big Honky Tonk and Steakhouse over an alleged incident he says took place in December 2025 ... and the alleged beatdown kicked off after he says he "lightly tapped" a performer's guitar with his finger.

Welch's lawyer says he touched the guitar in a "moment of poor judgment" -- and didn’t even touch the instrument hard ... but he claims he was still approached by a security guard and 86'd from the joint.

On his way out of the venue, Welch's lawyer says he doubled down by trying to touch the guitar again ... which is when he claims the security guard became "disproportionately agitated."

Welch claims he was beaten by 3 men in the elevator. He alleges he was slammed against the wall of the elevator and then thrown out when it reached the ground floor. He says he was then pushed to the floor and repeatedly shoved down when he tried to get off the ground multiple times ... including once when he says he landed hard on his right hand and badly injured his ring finger.

He says he underwent surgery to fix the damaged digit about a month later.

Welch is suing for assault and battery, negligence, negligent hiring and training, and false imprisonment. To be clear, he's suing Kid Rock's restaurant -- not the star himself.

In its reply, the restaurant denied all wrongdoing ... and insisted its security guards were justified in their use of force.

Sony has some of the biggest price cuts, with savings of up to 32% across select Bravia Theater models, including more than $700 off its premium Theater Trio system.

Samsung's Dolby Atmos soundbars are also discounted by as much as $400, while Bose and LG have more affordable options for anyone looking to improve dialogue clarity, add some bass, or enjoy surround sound without a complicated setup. Whether you're shopping for a compact speaker for a bedroom TV or a more immersive system for movie nights, here are the deals worth considering.

For anyone building a premium home theater around a large TV, the Sony Bravia Theater Trio is down to $1,498 from $2,199.99, saving you $701.99, or roughly 32%. Unlike a conventional soundbar, the Trio uses three separate front speakers for the left, center, and right channels, helping spread dialogue and effects across a wider soundstage. You can read PCMag’s “excellent” review for more details.

The Sony Bravia Theater Bar 7 is down to $718 from $869 for anyone who wants a single soundbar under the TV. Its nine speakers include upward- and side-firing drivers that widen the soundstage and give Dolby Atmos some height, but there’s no subwoofer, so the now $898 Bar 7 with a wireless sub bundle (down from $1,099.99) might be the better pick for deeper bass.

Moving down Sony's lineup, the Bravia Theater Bar 6 is $548, down from $699.99, and pairs a 3.1.2-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer and upward-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos height effects. Spending $100 more gets you the Bravia Theater System 6, now $648 from $799.99, which adds rear speakers in a 5.1-channel setup for movies and games where sound moves behind you.

For a more affordable upgrade, the Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is down to $278 from $349.99, saving you nearly $72. It's a 3.1-channel system with a dedicated center speaker and wireless subwoofer, so dialogue should come through more clearly while music and movie effects get some additional low-end presence.

Sony’s older systems are discounted too, including the HT-S400 at $258, down from $299, which pairs a 2.1-channel soundbar and wireless subwoofer with S-Force Pro Front Surround to widen the sound for everyday TV, sports, and casual movies. The HT-S40R is arguably the better deal at the same $258, down from $329.99, since it adds two rear speakers for a full 5.1-channel setup, though neither model supports Dolby Atmos.

For smaller rooms or for anyone who mainly wants dialogue to come across more clearly, Bose has two compact soundbars on sale: The newer Bose TV Speaker (2nd Gen) is down to $239 from $299, with an updated acoustic design that Bose says improves clarity and overall sound performance. Meanwhile, the original Bose TV Speaker is $199, down from $279, and offers a similarly compact design with a dedicated dialogue mode and adjustable bass.

Samsung’s HW-Q800H is down to $697.99 from $1,097.99, a $400 cut on a 5.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos soundbar with a wireless subwoofer. Its side- and upward-firing speakers help place effects around and above you, while a dedicated center channel keeps dialogue clear during busy action scenes.

For something that takes up less space, the Samsung HW-S60D is $277.99, down from $399.99, and fits seven speakers, including side-firing drivers, into a compact 5.0-channel soundbar. It also supports Dolby Atmos, Adaptive Sound, and a voice enhancement mode, along with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, AirPlay, and Chromecast for music streaming. That said, it has no upward-firing speakers or subwoofer, so its height effects and bass won’t match that of the Q800H.

If you're looking for a complete surround sound system without spending several hundred dollars, the LG S6FTR is down to $249.99 from $399.99, saving you $150, or roughly 38%. It's a 5.1-channel home theater package with a soundbar, subwoofer, and dedicated rear speakers. That makes it particularly appealing for action movies and games, where directional sound adds to the experience.

The LG S40TR is another affordable option for anyone who wants rear speakers included in the box. It's currently $199.99, down from $279.99, and offers a 4.1-channel arrangement with a wireless subwoofer and two rear speakers. This should give movie soundtracks a greater sense of direction than a basic soundbar, while the subwoofer handles the lower frequencies that smaller TV speakers often struggle to reproduce.

At just under $187, the S60T is the least expensive system in this roundup, pairing a 3.1-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer for clearer dialogue and fuller sound than your TV’s speakers. That said, it lacks rear speakers and Dolby Atmos height channels, so it’s better suited to someone who wants a simple, affordable upgrade without filling the room with additional hardware.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

#3400. iOS 27’s Find My app adds convenient feature I’ve long wished for

iOS 27 is packed with new features, including several for the Find My app. One upgrade to Find My—custom sharing durations—grants a feature request I’ve had for years.

Apple’s Find My app is a great way to share your location with friends or family members on either permanent or a temporary basis.

But the “temporary” option just got a very welcome upgrade in iOS 27.

That’s because you can now set up location sharing in Find My for a custom duration. Per Apple:

users [now] have more control over how they share their location with friends and family using Find My, with new options to share for a custom duration — either for a number of minutes, hours, or days — or even set a date and time for when sharing will stop. This makes it easy for users to share their location while attending an event, or for a long weekend getaway with friends and family.

Until iOS 27, you could only choose from a very limited set of “temporary” options for sharing: for one hour, or until end of day. The only other option was “indefinitely.”

The main time I find myself adding new people to share my location with, I’m either traveling or they’re visiting me. On these occasions, the “one hour” and “until end of day” options never cut it.

So of course, I have to choose “indefinitely.” Then there’s the decision after the trip ends of either continuing to let location sharing happen, or ending sharing immediately (if I remember to). And the latter option has always felt a little awkward to me. I’d much rather schedule the sharing duration upfront.

And now with iOS 27 I can. When sharing location with someone, a new ‘Custom’ duration option allows choosing an end date and time, and/or manually setting a given number of days, hours, and minutes for sharing to continue.

It’s a great change, long overdue, and works perfectly for the scenarios Apple outlined.

Have you ever wished for custom sharing durations in Find My? Let us know in the comments.
